title: Progressive Wealth Taxation
by: Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman
summary: Brookings Papers on Economic Activity paper on the revenue potential, enforcement and economic effects of a tax on the wealth of the richest US families, with lessons from other countries.

title: A blueprint for a coordinated minimum effective taxation standard for ultra-high-net-worth individuals
by: Gabriel Zucman, for the Brazilian G20 presidency (EU Tax Observatory)
summary: Commissioned by the G20 presidency: proposes a minimum tax of 2% of wealth a year for individuals worth over $1 billion, which countries could levy as a wealth tax or by other means.

title: A wealth tax for the UK: final report
by: Wealth Tax Commission (Arun Advani, Emma Chamberlain, Andy Summers)
summary: Independent commission (LSE, Warwick and a tax barrister) concluding that a one-off wealth tax is the better choice if the government wants to raise more revenue from wealth.

title: Ultra-Millionaire Tax Act of 2021 (S. 510 and H.R. 1459, 117th Congress)
by: Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Reps. Brendan Boyle and Pramila Jayapal
status: Introduced 1 March 2021 in the Senate (S. 510, Warren) and the House (H.R. 1459, Jayapal) and referred to the Finance and Ways and Means committees; no later action is recorded in the bill status data
summary: A yearly 2% tax on net worth between $50 million and $1 billion and 3% above $1 billion (6% if a Medicare for All law is in effect), with a 40% exit tax on those who renounce citizenship.
overview:
The Ultra-Millionaire Tax Act of 2021 is the first of three versions that Senator Elizabeth Warren and Representatives Pramila Jayapal and Brendan Boyle have introduced. It taxes net worth every year: 2% between $50 million and $1 billion, 3% above $1 billion, and 6% above $1 billion if a Medicare for All law is in effect. People who renounce citizenship face a 40% exit tax.

It was introduced on 1 March 2021 as S. 510 in the Senate and H.R. 1459 in the House and referred to the Finance and Ways and Means committees. The bill status data records no later action, and the bill lapsed with the 117th Congress. The official sponsor lists were compared with the register: 33 members on the House bill and 9 on the Senate bill. The 2024 and 2026 bills carry the proposal forward.

title: Proposition de loi n° 768 instaurant un impôt plancher de 2 % sur le patrimoine des ultra riches
by: Eva Sas, Clémentine Autain and the Écologiste et Social group
status: Adopted by the Assemblée nationale at first reading on 20 February 2025 (text no. 58). Rejected by the Sénat at first reading on 12 June 2025 (text no. 143). Returned to the Assemblée on 12 June 2025 as no. 1579 for a second reading; the Assemblée's dossier (read 12 November 2026) shows no outcome after that.
summary: The "taxe Zucman": a floor tax that makes households with net wealth above EUR 100 million pay at least 2% of that wealth in tax each year, counting the income tax, wealth tax on property (IFI), social contributions and high-income levy they already pay.

links.label: Text adopted by the Assemblée nationale, no. 58 (20 February 2025)
Text rejected by the Sénat, no. 143 (12 June 2025)

overview:
The "taxe Zucman" is a minimum tax, not an extra wealth tax on top of existing ones. It applies to people whose net assets exceed 100 million euro on 1 January, counted worldwide for people who live in France and in France only for those who do not. Each year they must pay at least 2% of their net wealth in total tax. Income tax, the real-estate wealth tax (IFI), the CSG and CRDS social contributions and the high-income levy (CEHR) already paid count towards the 2%, and the new tax is only the difference, if there is one. Succession-tax exemptions do not apply, the principal home gets a flat abatement of 1 million euro, and the tax returns and sanctions follow the inheritance-tax rules. The tax would start on 1 January 2026.

The explanatory memorandum says it would hit about 4,000 taxpayers, 0.01% of the total, and bring in 15 to 25 billion euro a year according to the economist Gabriel Zucman. The authors argue that the richest hold their fortunes in holding companies that pay little income tax, so that their effective tax rate is lower than the average household's. They note that almost 80% of French people want a wealth tax back and cite the finding by France Stratégie that only 0.2% of ISF-eligible taxpayers left the country in 2017.

Eva Sas, Clémentine Autain and the members of the Écologiste et Social group filed it on 7 January 2025. The Assemblée's finance committee reported on it on 12 February 2025 and the full chamber adopted it on 20 February 2025. It added a new 3° to article 885 A, which makes people domiciled in France for more than ten years and during at least one of the last five liable on their assets in France and abroad.

The Sénat's finance committee, with the rapporteur Emmanuel Capus, proposed rejection in a report of 4 June 2025, calling the tax weak on constitutional, operational and economic grounds, did not adopt the single article, and the Sénat rejected the bill in plenary on 12 June 2025. It went back to the Assemblée for a second reading the same day. The Assemblée and Sénat pages give no vote counts.

title: Antrag 21/4029: Vermögensteuer wieder erheben – Länderfinanzen nachhaltig sichern
by: Fraktion Die Linke
status: First reading on 6 March 2026, referred to the Finance Committee. The committee took it up on 7 October 2026 and recommends rejection (Drucksache 21/8481, dated 9 October 2026), with CDU/CSU, AfD, SPD and Greens against Die Linke. No plenary vote on the recommendation had been found as of 12 November 2026.
summary: Asks the government to bring in a bill that levies the wealth tax again: a net wealth tax from 1% above 1 million euro, rising to 5% at 50 million and 12% above 1 billion.

links.label: Finance Committee report and recommendation, Drucksache 21/8481 (PDF)

overview:
Die Linke's motion asks the government to bring in a bill that levies the wealth tax again. It would tax personal net wealth above 1 million euro, with a further allowance of 5 million euro for business assets. The rate rises in a straight line from 1% to 5% at 50 million euro, then jumps to 12% above 1 billion euro, a rate the motion says is meant to reduce billion-euro fortunes. Companies would not pay the tax themselves. The motion also asks the government to examine, and report back on, paying the tax in shares of assets and crediting income tax against it.

Assets would be valued close to market value, as they already are for inheritance tax; the motion puts collection and compliance costs below 5% of the yield. Its modelling (DIW, 2026) puts the revenue, after allowing for behavioural responses, at about 100 billion euro a year, paid by the richest 2%: two thirds of it by people with 100 million euro or more and a third by billionaires. The money goes to the Länder, and through a larger shared pool to the municipalities. The motion lists what it could fund: hundreds of thousands of homes, free local public transport, teachers and nursery staff.

Christian Görke, Janine Wissler and 18 other Left MPs tabled it on 6 February 2026 (Drucksache 21/4029); the group chairs Heidi Reichinnek and Sören Pellmann signed for the group. The Bundestag held the first reading on 6 March 2026 and sent it to the Finance Committee, which discussed it on 7 October 2026 and recommends rejecting it (Drucksache 21/8481). In that debate the SPD said it also wants very large fortunes to contribute more and pointed to Gabriel Zucman's design. The Greens said they want a wealth tax and presented their own, narrower 500-million concept (Drucksache 21/8267).

It is the broadest of the German proposals now before the Bundestag: it starts at 1 million euro, where the Greens' 2026 motion starts at 500 million, and its top rate of 12% is the highest. It continues the line of Left motions since 2010, which asked for 5% above 1 million euro.

title: Ley 38/2022: Impuesto Temporal de Solidaridad de las Grandes Fortunas
by: Cortes Generales
status: In force
summary: Created a state-level tax on net wealth above €3 million, with rates from 0% to 3.5%, on top of the regional wealth tax.
overview:
Law 38/2022 of 27 December 2022 created the Impuesto Temporal de Solidaridad de las Grandes Fortunas, a state tax on the net wealth of individuals above EUR 3 million. The first EUR 3 million is taxed at 0%. Above that the scale is 1.7% on the next slice, 2.1% on the next and 3.5% on net wealth above EUR 10,695,996.06. Residents with unlimited liability get a EUR 700,000 exempt minimum. The tax exempts the same assets that are exempt from the wealth tax, so exemptions such as the family business carry over.

It sits on top of the existing Impuesto sobre el Patrimonio: whatever a person pays under that tax is deducted from this one, so there is no double charge. Unlike the wealth tax, its revenue goes to the central Treasury and is not passed to the regions. The law was published in the BOE on 28 December 2022 and took effect the next day, 29 December 2022. The text applies the tax for the first two years in which it accrues and includes a review clause to decide whether to keep or repeal it. A 2026 Sumar bill describes it as extended since then while wealth taxation is reviewed.

It matters because it put a national floor under wealth taxation, charged on top of whatever the regions levy. The register links the legislators who sponsored or signed it.

title: Wealth Inequality and Closing the Poverty Gap in Arab Countries: The Case for a Solidarity Wealth Tax
by: Khalid Abu-Ismail and Vladimir Hlasny, UN ESCWA
summary: A UN ESCWA technical paper estimating that a solidarity wealth tax on the richest tenth of adults, about 1.2% a year in the middle-income Arab countries, could cover the cost of closing the poverty gap there; the least developed countries would need outside help.

title: Commitment to Reducing Inequality Index: Malawi Country Profile 2025
by: Jo Walker and Matthew Martin (with Oxfam in Malawi, MEJN, and NCA-DCA)
summary: Evaluates Malawi's fiscal framework and inequality gap, recommending a moderate wealth tax of 0.7% on accumulated wealth (raising ~$70M) to fund universal essential healthcare for 890,000 citizens.

title: Motion 20.3174: Millionäre besteuern, um Gemeinwesen zu finanzieren und Arbeitsplätze zu retten
by: Denis de la Reussille (Swiss Party of Labour)
status: Rejected by the National Council on 22 September 2021 (65 yes, 118 no)
summary: Asks the Federal Council to introduce a Covid-19 solidarity tax on wealth over CHF 3 million and use the proceeds for workers, families and small businesses.
overview:
Denis de la Reussille of the Swiss Party of Labour tabled motion 20.3174 on 4 May 2020, at the start of the Covid-19 crisis. It instructs the Federal Council to introduce a "Covid-19 solidarity tax" on wealth over 3 million francs and to use the proceeds to support employees, families, craft businesses and small firms. The text names no rate, but the reasoning says a one-off levy of 2% on wealth over 3 million francs would raise about 17.5 billion francs.

The Federal Council recommended rejection. It said it wanted to finance the crisis measures from existing revenue, that announcing a new tax during the downturn would deepen the recession and weaken legal certainty, and that the federal government can levy a tax only with an express constitutional basis, which a wealth tax lacks. A constitutional amendment would therefore need the approval of the people and the cantons.

The National Council rejected the motion on 22 September 2021 by 118 votes to 65.

title: Motion 20.3203: Solidaritätsabgabe auf Milliardenvermögen zur Bekämpfung der Corona-Krise
by: Social Democratic group (SP)
status: Rejected by the National Council on 15 March 2022 (66 yes, 126 no)
summary: Asks the Federal Council to set up a Covid-19 fund financed by a temporary solidarity levy on wealth of CHF 1 billion and above.
overview:
The Social Democratic group tabled motion 20.3203 on 4 May 2020. It instructs the Federal Council to set up a fund against the economic and social effects of the Covid-19 pandemic, fed by a temporary solidarity levy on very high wealth, from 1 billion francs up. The reasoning gives 2 Rappen per franc above 1 billion francs, 2%, as an example. The fund would finance care, childcare, climate measures such as building renovation and renewable energy, the digital transition, and measures against poverty in Switzerland and abroad.

The Federal Council recommended rejection. It repeated that a federal wealth tax needs a constitutional amendment and argued that a higher wealth-tax burden would cut declared wealth through emigration, shifts into tax-favoured investments and non-declaration. It also noted that Swiss wealth taxes already bring in about 1.1% of GDP, more than in the few other OECD countries that still have a general wealth tax, and that a tax paid by very few people conflicts with the constitutional principle that taxation be general.

The National Council rejected the motion on 15 March 2022 by 126 votes to 66.

title: Motion 23.3361: Für eine Steuer auf dem Vermögen der Superreichen!
by: Stefania Prezioso Batou (Ensemble à Gauche)
status: Rejected by the National Council on 13 March 2024 (60 yes, 132 no)
summary: Asks the Federal Council to amend Article 128 of the Federal Constitution so that a direct federal tax on the wealth of natural persons can be levied.
overview:
Stefania Prezioso Batou (Ensemble à Gauche) tabled motion 23.3361 on 17 March 2023. It instructs the Federal Council to amend Article 128 of the Federal Constitution so that a direct federal tax on the wealth of natural persons can be levied, with the aim that the very rich contribute to the ecological and social transition. The motion sets no threshold or rate.

The reasoning refers to a petition by 130 members of the European Parliament for a global tax on the superrich, whose authors consider 1.5% on wealth of 50 million or more worthwhile, and says the richest 1% of people worldwide cause 17% of CO2 emissions. It asks Switzerland to follow.

The Federal Council, which had answered the similar motions 20.3335, 20.3174 and 20.3203 in 2020, again recommended rejection. It said Switzerland already has a high wealth tax by international comparison, with revenue of about 1.2% of GDP (OECD data for 2020), and that raising the burden would shrink declared wealth through emigration, shifts to tax-favoured assets and non-declaration, which would also hurt cantonal wealth-tax and income-tax revenue.

The National Council rejected the motion on 13 March 2024 by 132 votes to 60.

title: Vote 22 (43rd Parliament, 2nd Session): opposition motion for a new 1% tax on wealth over $20 million
by: Peter Julian (NDP)
summary: Opposition motion asking the government to put in place a new one percent tax on wealth over $20 million and an excess profit tax on big corporations, and to spend the proceeds on income security, health care and housing.
status: Negatived on 16 November 2020, 27 yeas to 292 nays (the House of Commons vote record)
overview:
On 16 November 2020, in the second session of the 43rd Parliament, NDP member Peter Julian moved an opposition motion asking the government to put in place a new 1% tax on wealth over $20 million and an excess profits tax on large corporations. The motion cited a claim that Canadian billionaires gained $37 billion during the pandemic. It asked that the proceeds fund a guaranteed basic income, expanded health care including national dental care and single-payer public pharmacare, and a national housing strategy with a dedicated Indigenous-led part.

The House of Commons voted it down, 27 yeas to 292 nays. All 27 yeas were from the NDP (23), the Greens (Jenica Atwin, Paul Manly and Elizabeth May) and one independent, Marwan Tabbara. The Liberals (145 nays), the Conservatives (117) and the Bloc Québécois (30) all voted against.

The register lists the 27 members who voted yes. It is a non-binding opposition motion: even if passed it would not have created a tax, but it is a recorded House vote on a wealth tax.

title: Motion M-43: Wealth tax
by: Peter Julian (NDP), seconded by Gord Johns and Alistair MacGregor
summary: Private member's motion: "the government should immediately implement a 1% wealth tax on fortunes over $20 million".
status: Reinstated from the previous session on 23 September 2020; the page shows no debate or vote. The 43rd Parliament has since ended.
overview:
Motion M-43 was a private member's motion by NDP MP Peter Julian (New Westminster—Burnaby). It said the government should immediately implement a 1% wealth tax on fortunes over $20 million. It was seconded by Gord Johns (30 September 2020) and Alistair MacGregor (15 October 2020), both NDP.

The motion was reinstated from the previous session on 23 September 2020. The House of Commons record shows no debate and no vote on it. It lapsed when the 43rd Parliament ended, and Julian is no longer an MP.

The same 1% rate on wealth over $20 million was put to a recorded vote in an NDP opposition motion on 16 November 2020, which the House rejected (see Vote 22).

title: Motion M-68: Wealth inequality
by: Nathaniel Erskine-Smith (Liberal), seconded by Paul Manly and Elizabeth May
summary: Private member's motion asking the government to levy a one-time tax on extreme wealth to help pay for the pandemic response (3% on assets over $10 million, 5% over $20 million), alongside an inheritance tax on estates over $5 million and a fairer tax treatment of investment income.
status: Placed on notice on 11 February 2021; the page shows no later activity. The 43rd Parliament has since ended.
overview:
Motion M-68, "Wealth inequality", was a private member's motion put on notice on 11 February 2021 by Liberal MP Nathaniel Erskine-Smith (Beaches—East York). It was seconded by Paul Manly (18 February 2021) and Elizabeth May (22 February 2021), both Green.

It asked the government to act on extreme wealth inequality in three ways: a one-time tax on extreme wealth to help pay for the pandemic response, at 3% on assets over $10 million and 5% over $20 million; new taxes on the transfer of extreme wealth, including an inheritance tax on estates over $5 million; and fairer taxation of investment income relative to employment income.

The House record shows it was only placed on notice, with no scheduled debate and no vote. It lapsed when the 43rd Parliament ended, and Erskine-Smith is no longer an MP. It is a wealth-tax proposal from a Liberal MP, not an opposition party.

title: Net wealth tax on Canadian resident economic families
by: Nigel Wodrich, Parliamentary Budget Officer, at the request of Peter Julian MP
summary: Official costing of an annual tax of 1% on family net wealth above $20 million: the PBO estimates 13,800 families would pay it and that it would raise $5.6 billion net in 2020-21.

title: Implementing annual wealth tax (45th General Election costing)
by: Parliamentary Budget Officer, for the New Democratic Party
summary: Election costing of the NDP's annual household wealth tax (1% on net worth from $10 million to $50 million, 2% to $100 million, 3% above): about $22.8 billion net in 2025-26 and $121.3 billion over five years, assuming 35% of each household's wealth is hidden.

title: Multi-Millionaires and Fair Taxes: The Case for a Wealth Tax in Canada
by: Andrew Jackson (Broadbent Institute), edited by Katrina Miller
summary: Argues for an annual wealth tax to help pay for the pandemic, reviews the NDP's 2019 proposal of 1% above $20 million and the practical objections, and concludes that it is a feasible political choice.

title: Report: It's Time To Tax Extreme Wealth Inequality
by: Toby Sanger and Erika Beauchesne (Canadians for Tax Fairness)
summary: Proposes a graduated annual wealth tax of 1% above $10 million, 2% above $100 million and 3% above $1 billion, which it estimates would raise close to $20 billion a year.

title: Un nouvel impôt sur le patrimoine
by: Guillaume Hébert (IRIS)
summary: Proposes a Québec tax on household net assets above $2 million, at 0.2% from $2 to 5 million, 0.5% to $25 million, 0.75% to $100 million and 1.25% above, aimed at the richest 10% of households and estimated to raise about $6.8 billion.

title: Proposición de Ley 122/000213: Impuesto sobre la titularidad, tenencia, disponibilidad, disfrute o uso de bienes o derechos por personas con grandes fortunas
by: Grupo Parlamentario Confederal de Unidas Podemos-En Comú Podem-Galicia en Común
summary: Would create a tax on the net wealth of people with large fortunes (from EUR 10 million), with an eight-bracket scale of marginal rates from 3.6% to 5% on total net wealth after debts and a EUR 1 million reduction of the base.
status: Rechazada (the Pleno of the Congreso debated its taking into consideration and rejected it, 7 June 2022)
overview:
This bill was introduced by the Unidas Podemos group in the Congress of Deputies. It would have created a new state tax on the net wealth of people with large fortunes, as a complement to the existing wealth tax. The group's spokesperson Pablo Echenique signed the filing on 4 April 2022, the Congress Bureau admitted it on 19 April 2022 and it was published on 22 April 2022.

The tax would apply to people whose net wealth, after debts, passes EUR 10 million, with a EUR 1 million reduction of the base. The scale has eight brackets with marginal rates from 3.6% to 5%. The bill's preamble says the rates are 0.1 to 1.5 points above the wealth-tax scale and that the tax paid under the wealth tax would be deducted. Exemptions for shares in firms would be limited to companies with fewer than 250 employees and turnover up to EUR 50 million or a balance sheet up to EUR 43 million. The bill also targets holding structures with no real substance, and caps the combined bill with income tax so that it can reduce the tax by at most 70%. It was meant to start on 1 January 2023.

The Congress rejected it when it came to the floor on 7 June 2022, by 277 votes against, 58 for and 4 abstentions, according to press reports (not the official record). The Socialists, the People's Party, Vox, Ciudadanos, PNV and PDeCAT voted against; EH Bildu, CUP, BNG, Compromís and ERC supported it.

title: Proposición de Ley 122/000045: Impuesto sobre la titularidad, tenencia, disponibilidad, disfrute o uso de bienes o derechos por personas con grandes fortunas
by: Grupo Parlamentario Mixto (Podemos deputies)
summary: Re-presents the Podemos bill for a tax on the net wealth of people with large fortunes, with the same eight-bracket scale of marginal rates from 3.6% to 5% and a EUR 1 million reduction of the base.
status: Admitida a trámite por la Mesa del Congreso (9 January 2024); published in the BOCG on 12 January 2024. Lapsed when the Cortes were dissolved on 5 October 2026 (Royal Decree 806/2026)
overview:
This is the Podemos wealth-tax bill filed again in the 15th legislature. Four Podemos deputies in the Mixed Group (Lilith Verstrynge, Javier Sánchez Serna, Martina Velarde and Noemí Santana) signed it on 19 December 2023, with Ione Belarra as the group's deputy spokesperson. The Congress Bureau admitted it on 9 January 2024 and it was published on 12 January 2024.

The preamble matches the 2022 bill (122/000213). It would tax the net wealth of people above EUR 10 million, with a EUR 1 million reduction of the base and an eight-bracket scale with marginal rates from 3.6% to 5%, as a complement to the existing wealth tax. The preamble says the scale would add between 0 and 0.7 points of burden for people who already pay the wealth tax, and 1.7% to 4% for those who do not. Exemptions for shares in companies would be limited to firms under 250 employees. The 2022 version had been rejected on 7 June 2022.

The official publication shows only that the bill was admitted for processing and sent to the Government. The sources read here show no debate or vote on taking it into consideration. The Cortes Generales were dissolved on 5 October 2026 (Royal Decree 806/2026), ahead of the general election on 29 November 2026, so the bill lapsed with them. The Congress record shows it as "Caducado".

title: Proposición de Ley 122/000303: creación del Gravamen sobre la Concentración de Riqueza
by: Grupo Parlamentario Plurinacional SUMAR
summary: Would levy a single 3% rate each year on the part of a person's net wealth above EUR 50 million, and cap the marginal rate of the Impuesto sobre el Patrimonio at 3.5% on that part.
status: Admitida a trámite por la Mesa de la Cámara (22 September 2026). Lapsed when the Cortes were dissolved on 5 October 2026 (Royal Decree 806/2026)
overview:
The Sumar group in the Congress of Deputies filed this bill on 16 September 2026, signed by ten deputies including Enrique Santiago and the group spokesperson Verónica Martínez Barbero. The Bureau admitted it on 22 September 2026 and it was published on 25 September 2026.

It would create a Levy on the Concentration of Wealth, a state payment that the bill itself describes as non-tax in nature, owed by people whose net wealth exceeds EUR 50 million. The base is the part above EUR 50 million, charged at a single 3% rate a year, and the bill also caps the marginal rate of the Impuesto sobre el Patrimonio at 3.5% on that part. Exemptions are narrow: historic heritage, some artworks, household goods and a main home up to EUR 300,000. Unlike the wealth tax, there is no general exemption for business assets or shareholdings.

The money would go to a Child Protection Fund. The Government would have six months after the law takes effect to send Parliament a bill for a universal child-raising benefit for under-18s. The bill takes effect the day after publication, with the first levy on 31 December of that year if it starts before 30 June, otherwise a year later. Its preamble argues the EUR 3 million threshold of the Temporary Solidarity Tax is too low to reach very large fortunes. The official publication shows it was admitted and sent to the Government; no vote is shown. The Cortes Generales were dissolved on 5 October 2026 (Royal Decree 806/2026), ahead of the general election on 29 November 2026, so the bill lapsed with them. The Congress record shows it as "Caducado".

title: Norma Foral 23/2023, de 15 de diciembre, por la que se regula el Impuesto Temporal de Solidaridad de las Grandes Fortunas (Álava)
by: Juntas Generales de Álava
summary: Regulates in Álava the temporary solidarity tax on large fortunes, a complement to the wealth tax that applies to net wealth above EUR 3,000,000.
status: Approved by the Juntas Generales de Álava on 15 December 2023; published in the BOTHA no. 150 of 29 December 2023
overview:
Norma Foral 23/2023 is the Álava version of the Temporary Solidarity Tax on Large Fortunes. The Juntas Generales de Álava approved it on 15 December 2023 and it was published in the Territory's official bulletin (BOTHA) no. 150 on 29 December 2023. The Basque Economic Agreement treats this tax, which complements the wealth tax, as one the Basque provinces regulate under their own rules.

The tax charges individuals whose net wealth exceeds EUR 3 million. The taxable base is reduced by an exempt minimum of EUR 800,000, higher than the EUR 700,000 in the state law. The scale has four rates: 1.7%, 2.1%, 2.5% and 3.5%. It accrues each 31 December on the wealth held that day. A cap applies to the combined bill of this tax, the wealth tax and income tax. People who pay income tax to the Álava authorities owe it on worldwide wealth.

It took effect the day after publication, 30 December 2023. The register lists the Álava legislators linked to it.

title: Un Tope a la Riqueza para España: Evidencia sobre su Potencial Impacto
by: Marina Alcázar, Olga Cantó and Francisco García-Rodríguez (The Wealth Cap Project)
summary: Finds that Spain's billionaires pay an effective rate of about 0.09% of their wealth through the Impuesto sobre el Patrimonio and the solidarity tax, and estimates that a wealth cap could raise about EUR 50.3 billion.

title: Un impuesto al patrimonio para el siglo XXI: opciones para rediseñar el IP y recaudar más de los que más tienen
by: Íñigo Macías Aymar (Oxfam Intermón)
summary: Argues for redesigning the Impuesto sobre el Patrimonio to raise substantially more revenue and restore progressivity among the super-rich, with estimates by Julio López Laborda and Anabel Zárate Marco and by Carmen Durrer.

title: El Impuesto Temporal de Solidaridad de las grandes fortunas y su encaje con el Impuesto sobre el Patrimonio
by: Diego Martínez, Manuel Díaz and Carmen Marín (Fedea)
summary: Sets out the main features of the planned solidarity tax on net wealth above EUR 3 million and analyses how it fits with the regional Impuesto sobre el Patrimonio and what it means for the finances of the autonomous communities, without assessing the tax itself.

title: Three ways Australia can tax wealth better
by: David Richardson and Matt Grudnoff (The Australia Institute)
summary: Recommends an annual 2% wealth tax on net assets above $5 million (family home and superannuation exempt), which it estimates would raise $41 billion a year, alongside an inheritance tax and scrapping the CGT discount.

title: Greens will tax 150 billionaires as part of revenue plan to fund dental into Medicare, GP for free and other cost of living measures
by: Australian Greens
summary: Announces a Parliamentary Budget Office-costed plan under which Australia's 150 billionaires would pay an annual 10% tax on their net wealth, expected to raise $23 billion over the forward estimates and $50 billion over the decade.

title: Matters of Urgency: Cost of Living (tax billionaires), urgency motion by Senator Nick McKim
by: Senator Nick McKim (Australian Greens)
summary: Urgency motion calling on the Government to support the Greens plan to tax Australia's billionaires and use the revenue for cost of living relief, including dental in Medicare and free GP visits; the Greens plan is an annual 10% tax on billionaires' net wealth.
status: Matter of urgency motion put to a Senate division on 11 February 2025 and not passed, 12 ayes to 25 noes

links.label: Senate Hansard, 11 February 2025 (OpenAustralia XML copy: motion, speeches and division)

overview:
This is a Senate urgency motion, not a bill, so it sets no tax itself. On 11 February 2025 Greens senator Nick McKim moved that the Senate treat as a matter of urgency "the need for the Albanese Labor Government to support the Greens plan to tax Australia's billionaires and use the revenue to help fund urgent cost of living relief, including getting dental into Medicare and making it free to see the GP."

In his speech McKim described the plan as a 10% tax on net wealth over $1 billion. He said Australia has 150 billionaires holding about $585 billion between them, and that the tax would raise about $50 billion over ten years, the amount the Parliamentary Budget Office costed for free GP visits for every Australian. Another Greens senator, speaking the same day, described it as an annual 10% tax on the 150 billionaires' net wealth, with a 10% limit on capital flight in any year.

The Senate voted on the motion at 5.42 pm and it failed, 12 ayes to 25 noes. The 12 ayes were the Greens senators and Lidia Thorpe, and the register lists them. Other senators who spoke called the idea of taxing billionaires overly simplistic. The Hansard record of the sitting was read for this page.

title: Wealth taxes and the post-COVID future of the state
by: Jane Andrew, Max Baker, Christine Cooper and Jonathan Tweedie (Critical Perspectives on Accounting)

title: Ley 27.605: Aporte Solidario y Extraordinario para ayudar a morigerar los efectos de la pandemia
by: Congreso de la Nación Argentina
summary: Creates a one-off emergency contribution on the assets in Argentina and abroad of residents whose total assets exceed ARS 200 million, on a scale from 2% to 3.5%.
status: Bill 4534-D-2020 (Cámara de Diputados), passed by the Chamber on 17 November 2020 and sanctioned by the Senate on 4 December 2020 as Ley 27.605; promulgated by Decreto 1024/20 of 17 December 2020 and published in the Boletín Oficial (no. 34.544) on 18 December 2020

links.label: Senate record of the bill (expediente 49/20 CD, Exp. HCD 4534-D-2020)
Bill text as filed in the Chamber (Trámite Parlamentario PDF, Internet Archive copy of 3 November 2025)

overview:
Carlos Heller filed the bill as 4534-D-2020 in the Cámara de Diputados, with fourteen co-signers led by Máximo Kirchner. The text creates, as an emergency measure and once only, an extraordinary contribution on the assets that people held on 31 December 2019, in the country and abroad for residents, valued under Ley 23.966. It applies when the total is ARS 200 million or more, with no tax-free minimum.

The scale runs from 2% on the band from ARS 200 to 300 million to 3.5% above ARS 3 billion. Assets held abroad pay rates 50% higher, and the difference is removed if at least 30% of the person's foreign financial holdings are repatriated within 60 days. The explanatory statement says the contribution reaches about 12,000 people, fewer than 400 of them at the top rate. Article 7 earmarks the proceeds: 20% for medical equipment and supplies, with further shares for the other purposes the article lists, among them the Progresar scholarships. The tax authority AFIP collects it.

The Senate's record shows the Chamber's sanction on 17 November 2020, a committee giro to Presupuesto y Hacienda, and the Senate's approval on 4 December 2020. The sanctioned text became Ley 27.605.

title: Ley 2277 de 2022: reforma tributaria para la igualdad y la justicia social (impuesto al patrimonio, arts. 35 to 37)
by: Congreso de la República de Colombia (project of the Ministry of Finance under José Antonio Ocampo)
summary: Adds articles 292-3, 294-3 and 295-3 to the Estatuto Tributario, creating a permanent annual wealth tax on net assets of 72,000 UVT or more held on 1 January, with the first 12,000 UVT of a person's home excluded.
status: Ley 2277 de 2022 (Diario Oficial No. 52.247 of 13 December 2022); the Senate's text page was last updated on 15 October 2026

links.label: Compiled text with articles 35 to 39 (DIAN normograma)
Reform bill file 118/2022C and 131/2022S (Cámara de Representantes)
Senate plenary record of 2 November 2022 with the named vote (Gaceta del Congreso 121 of 2023)
Who paid in 2025 (La República, DIAN figures)

overview:
Ley 2277 of 13 December 2022 made Colombia's wealth tax permanent. It charges individuals and undivided estates on net wealth held on 1 January once it reaches 72,000 UVT, about US$1.0 million in 2026, and excludes the first 12,000 UVT of the home. The scale is marginal: nothing up to 72,000 UVT, 0.5% from 72,000 to 122,000 UVT, 1% from 122,000 to 239,000 UVT and 1.5% above that. The 1.5% band applies only for 2023 to 2026.

Finance Minister José Antonio Ocampo filed the reform on 8 August 2022 with a permanent tax from COP 3 billion at two rates. Congress added the third. The register holds the named vote on the article: on 2 November 2022 the Senate plenary rejected a proposal to delete it, with the Secretariat reporting 18 for and 68 against. Sixty-five of the 66 senators printed under "no" are on the register; the other has died.

The tax raised about COP 1.2 trillion, US$320 million, in 2025 from 34,229 filers, and fortunes above 239,000 UVT paid 72% of it. The Constitutional Court declined to rule on challenges in sentences C-395 of 2024 and C-031 of 2025, so the tax stands.

In August 2026 President Abelardo de la Espriella announced that the wealth tax will be eliminated. The bill his government filed on 29 October 2026, Proyecto de Ley 477 de 2026 Cámara, does not repeal it. It keeps the tax for individuals only for 2027 to 2030, lifts the threshold to 95,500 UVT and sets rates of 0.5% and 1%. The president sent Congress a message of urgency on 3 November. As of 7 November 2026 the bill had not passed.

title: Proyecto de Ley 070 de 2020 Cámara: modifica el Decreto Ley 568 de 2020 (impuesto solidario por el COVID-19)
by: Opposition senators and representatives led by Iván Marulanda, Aida Avella and León Fredy Muñoz
summary: Would make Colombia's wealth tax permanent: individuals above 84,253 UVT (about COP 3,000 million) and companies above 2,246,749 UVT, with top marginal rates of 4% and 6%.
status: Filed with the signatures of senators and representatives and published in Gaceta del Congreso 650 (10 August 2020). The report for first debate in the Comisión Tercera of the Cámara (22 September 2020) asks the commission to archive it.

links.label: Report for first debate (Cámara de Representantes, 22 September 2020)

overview:
Bill 070 of 2020 in the Colombian Chamber of Representatives rewrote Decreto Legislativo 568 of 2020, the emergency "solidarity tax" created during the COVID-19 emergency. Its article 3 made the wealth tax permanent and extended it to companies; until then it ran only to 2021. The tax would apply to individuals with net wealth above 84,253 tax units (UVT), about COP 3,000 million, and to legal persons above 2,246,749 UVT, about COP 80,000 million. The top marginal rates were 4% for individuals and 6% for companies.

The same bill raised the tax on dividends from 10% to 20% and the top marginal income-tax rate for individuals from 39% to 55%. It was filed with the signatures of opposition senators and representatives, among them Iván Marulanda, Aida Avella, Victoria Sandino, Pablo Catatumbo and León Fredy Muñoz, and published in Gaceta del Congreso 650 on 10 August 2020.

In the Comisión Tercera of the Chamber, the appointed rapporteurs, led by coordinators Carlos Alberto Carreño and Erasmo Zuleta, asked on 22 September 2020 that the bill be archived. They argued that it rewrote articles of the decree that the Constitutional Court had already struck down, that it was premature in the middle of the pandemic, and they cited the tax authority DIAN's opinion. The register lists 41 of the signers.

title: Proyecto de Ley 066 de 2021 Cámara: Ley de Equidad Fiscal
by: Victoria Sandino, Pablo Catatumbo, Aida Avella, Gustavo Petro and others
summary: Part of the Ley de Equidad Fiscal: a wealth tax for 2022 to 2025 on net wealth of COP 5,000 million or more, at 1% to 3% a year, with all revenue for social programmes for the poorest households.
status: Filed on 21 July 2021. Gaceta del Congreso 1634 (16 November 2021) publishes both a positive report and a negative report for first debate in the Comisión Tercera; the negative report, received on 11 October 2021, asks the commission to archive the bill. No vote found.

links.label: Reports for first debate (Gaceta del Congreso 1634, 16 November 2021)

overview:
Bill 066 of 2021 in the Chamber of Representatives, the "Ley de Equidad Fiscal", was filed on 21 July 2021 by senators and representatives, among them Victoria Sandino, Pablo Catatumbo, Aida Avella and Gustavo Petro. The positive report published in the Gazette proposes a wealth tax for the years 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025, changing the wealth tax that Ley 2010 of 2019 had created.

The tax falls on net wealth of COP 5,000 million or more on 1 January of each year. The rates are 1% a year for wealth from COP 5,000 to 10,000 million, 1.5% up to 20,000 million, 2% up to 50,000 million and 3% above that. The first 13,500 UVT of a person's home are excluded, and all the revenue is earmarked for social plans and programmes for households in strata 1, 2 and 3. The same bill also proposes a tax on ultra-processed food and sweetened drinks.

The bill was assigned to the Comisión Tercera of the Chamber. Gaceta 1634 of 16 November 2021 carries two reports for first debate: a positive one, and a negative one, received on 11 October 2021 and signed by Armando Zabaraín, Víctor Ortiz, Bayardo Betancourt, Wadith Manzur and Christian Moreno, which asks the commission to archive the bill. The register lists the 15 signers.

by: Leopoldo Fergusson and Marc Hofstetter (Universidad de los Andes)
summary: Proposes a marginal wealth tax only on net worth above COP 1,000 million, at 0.5%, 1% above COP 3,000 million and 2% above COP 5,000 million, which it estimates would raise close to 1% of GDP.

title: Boletín 13555-07: constitutional reform for a one-time tax on the wealth of certain individuals
by: Deputies Gabriel Ascencio, Karol Cariola, Giorgio Jackson, Daniel Núñez, Luis Rocafull, Alexis Sepúlveda, Alejandra Sepúlveda, Raúl Soto, Camila Vallejo and Esteban Velásquez
summary: Motion to amend the Constitution to set, once only, a tax on the wealth of certain individuals to finance an emergency basic income.
status: Approved in general on 21 April 2021 (105 votes to 18, 26 abstentions) and in particular on 18 May 2021 by the Chamber of Deputies, which sent it to the Senate the same day (second constitutional step). The Senate's tracking service (read 12 November 2026) shows it in the Constitution Committee, waiting for its first report, without urgency; the last action is 18 May 2021, when the Senate admitted it as admissible, 18 votes to 13.

links.label: Motion with exposición de motivos (Chamber of Deputies, PDF)

overview:
Boletín 13555-07 is a motion to amend the Constitution so that a tax on wealth can be levied once, to pay for an emergency basic income during the COVID-19 pandemic. Ten deputies filed it on 1 June 2020, and the register lists all ten. The text as filed adds a transitory provision that taxes at 2.5% the gross wealth, in Chile or abroad, of people domiciled in Chile who held 22 million US dollars or more on 31 December 2019. The tax is due within thirty days of the reform's publication.

The explanatory statement argues that the richest 0.1% of Chileans, about 5,840 people, hold roughly 250 billion dollars, close to the country's GDP in 2019. It puts the revenue at 6.5 billion dollars. That would pay a basic income above the poverty line to at least 80% of the most vulnerable households for three months, reaching about 11.5 million people. It sets this against Chile's land, inheritance and financial-transaction taxes, which together raise 0.85% of GDP.

The Chamber approved it in general on 21 April 2021 and voted its provisions one by one on 18 May 2021, then sent it to the Senate. There the Constitution Committee received it, and the Senate admitted it as admissible by 18 votes to 13. The Senate's tracking service shows no action since that day and no urgency. The figures above are those of the motion as filed. What distinguishes it from the other Latin American bills is that it is a constitutional reform, a single levy tied to a named emergency programme.
