summary: Builds a model of the wealth of the richest groups, reviews international experience and the standard objections, and applies a designed net wealth tax to Chile.

title: Wealth Tax Act, 1975 (Number 25 of 1975)
by: Oireachtas
summary: Charges a wealth tax each year at one per cent of the net market value of the taxable wealth of individuals, discretionary trusts and private non-trading companies, from 5 April 1975.
status: Enacted 16 August 1975; section 38 of the Finance Act, 1978 stops the charge for any valuation date on or after 5 April 1978

links.label: Finance Act, 1978, section 38 (abolition of wealth tax)

overview:
The Wealth Tax Act, 1975 set up an annual net wealth tax in Ireland. It charged one per cent each year on the net market value of the taxable wealth of an assessable person on the valuation date, with effect from 5 April 1975. Assessable persons were individuals, discretionary trusts and private non-trading companies. An individual domiciled and ordinarily resident in the State was taxed on property anywhere in the world; anyone else only on property in the State.

Individuals had an exclusion before the tax applied: £100,000 for a married man living with his wife, £90,000 for a widow or widower, and £70,000 for anyone else, plus £2,500 for each minor child whose property was counted with theirs. The Act was enacted on 16 August 1975 (Number 25 of 1975).

It was short-lived. Section 38 of the Finance Act, 1978 provided that wealth tax is not charged for any valuation date on or after 5 April 1978, which ended it after three years. The same section lowered the interest rate on unpaid tax from 1.5 to 1.25 per cent.

It matters because it shows Ireland has legislated, collected and then repealed a wealth tax. This summary is based on the Act's own text and section 38 of the 1978 Act, both read on the Irish Statute Book.

title: Finance (No. 2) Bill 2023, Report Stage recommendation 3: report on a 2% wealth tax
by: Senator Frances Black, seconded by Senator Paul Gavan
summary: Would oblige the Minister to lay a report on the revenue and distributional impact of a wealth tax of 2 per cent on all households with assets over 20 million euro.
status: Recommendation put and declared lost in Seanad Éireann on 12 December 2023
overview:
Recommendation 3 was an amendment moved at Report Stage of the Finance (No. 2) Bill 2023 in Seanad Éireann on 12 December 2023. It would have inserted a new section requiring the Minister for Finance, within six months of the Act passing, to lay before both Houses of the Oireachtas a report on the potential revenue raised from, and the distributional impact of, a wealth tax of 2 per cent on all households with assets over 20 million euro.

Senator Frances Black moved it and Senator Paul Gavan seconded it. Black said the threshold had been revised upwards after an exchange on Committee Stage. Gavan said Sinn Féin's consistent policy is to support a wealth tax and that the recommendation only asked for a report.

The Government's reply, given by Minister of State Jennifer Carroll MacNeill, rejected it. She said existing taxes such as capital gains tax, capital acquisitions tax and local property tax already tax wealth, that revenue from a new tax might not be additional, and that the Commission on Taxation and Welfare (2022) advised against a new net wealth tax before first trying to amend existing taxes on capital and wealth. The recommendation was put and declared lost; the record shows no division on it.

It matters as a recent test of Irish parliamentary support: it asked only for a costing, not a tax, and was still refused. The summary is based on the Seanad debate record of 12 December 2023, read for this recommendation.

title: Confronting Wealth Inequality in Ireland
by: Tom McDonnell and Ciarán Nugent (NERI) and Sorley McCaughey, for Oxfam Ireland
summary: Models an annual net wealth tax on the top 1% of the population, with a high threshold of about 3 million euro, and puts the yield of a 1% rate at around 1 billion euro a year (2% about 1.7 billion, 3% about 2.5 billion), as Oxfam Ireland's release states it.

title: Net Wealth Tax for Ireland - Possibilities and Pitfalls (NERI Working Paper 78)
by: Tom McDonnell and Ciarán Nugent (NERI) with Sorley McCaughey
summary: Concludes that a recurrent tax on net household wealth is viable in Ireland if it is simple, has few reliefs and a high threshold reaching about the wealthiest 1%, raising roughly 800 million euro a year.

title: Scenarios and distributional implications of a household wealth tax in Ireland
by: Martina Lawless and Donal Lynch (ESRI; ifo DICE Report 16(2))
summary: Estimates what a household wealth tax could raise in Ireland and how many households would be liable, by applying other European countries' designs and testing combinations of thresholds and asset exemptions.

title: PLP 277/2008: regulates the Imposto sobre Grandes Fortunas (art. 153, VII of the Constitution)
by: Chico Alencar, Ivan Valente, Luciana Genro
summary: Regulates the Tax on Large Fortunes: 1% to 5% a year on net wealth above R$ 2 million (2009 money), worldwide assets included; the bill to which some 34 later wealth-tax bills in the Câmara are attached.
status: Câmara dos Deputados, situation "Pronta para Pauta". The main bill of a group: later Tax on Large Fortunes bills are attached to it. Archived at the end of the legislature in 2011, 2015 and 2019 and reactivated each time at a deputy's request (14 Mar 2011, 10 Feb 2015, 19 Feb 2019); the history shows no archiving in 2023. Requests to put it on the Plenary agenda on 30 May 2019 and 9 Jun 2020; the history shows no vote. Last entry 2 Jun 2023 (attaching PLP 69/2023). Checked against the Câmara open data on 12 November 2026: no later entry.

links.label: Bills related to PLP 277/2008 (Câmara open data)

overview:
PLP 277/2008 is the oldest wealth-tax bill still before the Câmara and the one the later ones are attached to. Luciana Genro, then leader of the PSOL, filed it on 26 March 2008 with Chico Alencar and Ivan Valente. It would put into law article 153, VII of the 1988 Constitution, which lets the Union levy a tax on large fortunes by complementary law. No such law has ever been passed.

The tax falls on net wealth held on 1 January each year above R$ 2 million, in 2009 money and indexed to inflation. Individuals living in Brazil pay on assets at home and abroad, and non-residents pay on what they own in Brazil. Rates rise by band: 1% from R$ 2 million, 2% from R$ 5 million, 3% from R$ 10 million, 4% from R$ 20 million and 5% above R$ 50 million. Tools of a trade are excluded up to R$ 300,000, and an asset missing from the return is presumed bought with income hidden from the income tax.

The justification recalls that a 1989 bill by Senator Fernando Henrique Cardoso passed the Senate and reached the Câmara. The authors say it let the tax be deducted from income tax, which defeats the purpose, and that its bands and rates were out of date. They cite the Atlas da Exclusão Social figure that the 5,000 richest families hold wealth equal to 42% of GDP, and they call for better tax inspection.

Under the Câmara's rules the bill was archived at the end of the 2007-2011, 2011-2015 and 2015-2019 legislatures and revived each time at a deputy's request. It is ready for the Plenary agenda, and the register's history shows no vote. About 34 later complementary bills on large fortunes are attached to it, among them PLP 26/2011, PLP 130/2012, PLP 188/2020, PLP 193/2020, PLP 130/2021 and PLP 69/2023, and PLP 9/2019 through PLP 62/2011. Each has its own page.

title: PLP 26/2011: institutes the Imposto sobre Grandes Fortunas (IGF)
by: Amauri Teixeira
summary: Institutes the Tax on Large Fortunes on net wealth above R$ 5 million, with five bands from 1% to 5% a year; Amauri Teixeira's version of the PLP 277/2008 design.
status: Câmara dos Deputados, situation "Tramitando em Conjunto": attached to PLP 277/2008 on 23 Mar 2011, so it moves with it. Archived at the end of the legislature in 2015 and 2019 and reactivated on 10 Feb 2015 and 19 Feb 2019. Last entry 22 Feb 2019; no action of its own since. Checked against the Câmara open data on 12 November 2026: no later entry.
overview:
PLP 26/2011 was filed on 11 March 2011 by Amauri Teixeira (PT, Bahia). It copies the structure of Luciana Genro's PLP 277/2008 article by article but raises the entry point to R$ 5 million, in 2012 money and indexed to inflation.

Individuals living in Brazil, estates and non-residents with assets in Brazil pay on net wealth held on 1 January. Rates by band: 1% from R$ 5 million, 2% from R$ 7 million, 3% from R$ 15 million, 4% from R$ 25 million and 5% above R$ 50 million. Tools of a trade are excluded up to R$ 300,000, and assets missing from the return are presumed bought with hidden income.

The justification answers the usual objections one by one. It says the tax would not drive capital out, would not clash with other taxes because its base is total wealth, and could be valued through electronic records and bank positions. It puts the revenue above that of the old CPMF bank-transaction tax, and says the money would reduce the regressivity of the system, send more resources to states and municipalities and allow payroll taxes to be cut.

The Câmara attached it to PLP 277/2008 on 23 March 2011. It was archived at the end of the 2011-2015 and 2015-2019 legislatures and revived on 10 February 2015 and 19 February 2019. It has had no action of its own since.

title: PLP 130/2012: institutes the Imposto sobre Grandes Fortunas
by: Amauri Teixeira, Assis Carvalho, Cláudio Puty, Jilmar Tatto, José Guimarães, Paulo Teixeira and 3 other deputies
summary: Institutes the Tax on Large Fortunes at 0.5%, 0.75% and 1% on net wealth above 8,000 times the monthly income-tax exemption (R$ 11.99 million in 2011), aimed at about 10,000 families and a first-year yield of at least R$ 6 billion.
status: Câmara dos Deputados, situation "Tramitando em Conjunto": attached to PLP 277/2008 on 27 Feb 2012, so it moves with it. Archived at the end of the legislature in 2015 and 2019 and reactivated on 10 Feb 2015 and 19 Feb 2019. Last entry 19 Mar 2019; no action of its own since. Checked against the Câmara open data on 12 November 2026: no later entry.
overview:
PLP 130/2012 was filed on 7 February 2012 by nine PT deputies, with Paulo Teixeira first on the bill and Amauri Teixeira, Jilmar Tatto, José Guimarães, Pedro Eugênio, Pepe Vargas, Ricardo Berzoini, Cláudio Puty and Assis Carvalho. It is the moderate-rate design from the Workers' Party, in contrast to the 1% to 5% bands of PLP 277/2008 and PLP 26/2011.

The tax applies to net wealth on 31 December above 8,000 times the monthly exemption of the personal income tax. The justification puts that at R$ 11.99 million in 2011. Rates are 0.5% up to 25,000 times the exemption, 0.75% up to 75,000 times and 1% above. Taxpayers are individuals living in Brazil and non-residents with assets there; spouses are taxed on their own share and children's assets are added to their parents'. A home is excluded up to 20% of the taxpayer's wealth, work tools and art up to 10% each. Payment in instalments is barred.

The authors say the tax would reach about 10,000 families, 0.04% of income-tax filers, and above all the 5,000 families they credit with wealth equal to 40% of GDP. They estimate revenue of at least R$ 6 billion in the first year, to go mainly to social security: health, pensions and assistance. They point to Argentina and Uruguay, where taxes on wealth raise 1.2% and 6.3% of tax revenue according to the IPEA.

It was attached to PLP 277/2008 on 27 February 2012. It was archived at the end of the 2011-2015 and 2015-2019 legislatures and revived on 10 February 2015 and 19 February 2019. Assis Carvalho, a co-author, died in 2020 and is not in the register.

title: PLP 9/2019: institutes the Imposto sobre Grandes Fortunas
by: Alessandro Molon, Bira do Pindaré, Camilo Capiberibe, Danilo Cabral, Elias Vaz, João H. Campos and 3 other deputies
summary: Institutes the Tax on Large Fortunes as a flat 5% on net wealth above R$ 20 million, which the author estimates would raise about R$ 38.9 billion a year from 0.09% of income-tax filers.
status: Câmara dos Deputados, situation "Tramitando em Conjunto": attached on 3 Apr 2019 to PLP 62/2011, which is itself attached to PLP 277/2008, so it moves with that bill. A request to withdraw the bill was refused on 27 Jun 2019, and the signature of Deputy Rodrigo Coelho was withdrawn on 18 Feb 2020 (rectified 21 Feb 2020). Last entry 21 Feb 2020. Checked against the Câmara open data on 12 November 2026: no later entry.
overview:
PLP 9/2019 was filed on 4 February 2019 by Danilo Cabral (PSB, Pernambuco) with eight other deputies: Alessandro Molon, Bira do Pindaré, Camilo Capiberibe, Elias Vaz, João H. Campos, João Roma, Lídice da Mata and Ted Conti. It is the shortest of the Câmara's wealth-tax bills, with seven articles.

The tax is a single rate. Anyone holding more than R$ 20 million in assets at home or abroad on 31 December pays 5% a year on the part above that line, less debts shown on the income-tax return and backed by documents. The threshold moves with the income-tax table. The tax is filed with the annual income-tax return, collected on the same dates and run by the federal revenue service, which is told to look for sham sales made to cut taxable wealth.

The justification uses the 2016 income-tax statistics. 25,785 filers, 0.09% of the total, declared net assets of R$ 1.294 trillion, an average of about R$ 50 million, which is more than the combined assets of the 53% of filers earning up to five minimum wages. About 68% of this group's income was exempt, largely because dividends are not taxed. The author estimates R$ 38.9 billion a year.

The Câmara attached it on 3 April 2019 to PLP 62/2011, which is itself attached to PLP 277/2008. A request to withdraw it was refused on 27 June 2019, and Deputy Rodrigo Coelho's signature was withdrawn in February 2020.

title: PLP 188/2020: institutes the Imposto sobre Grandes Fortunas (IGF)
by: Afonso Florence, Airton Faleiro, Alencar Santana Braga, Alexandre Padilha, Beto Faro, Bohn Gass and 36 other deputies
summary: Institutes the Tax on Large Fortunes at 1%, 1.5% and 2% on wealth above R$ 15 million, filed in July 2020 by Zé Neto and about 40 PT deputies as a response to the Covid-19 crisis.
status: Câmara dos Deputados, situation "Tramitando em Conjunto": attached to PLP 277/2008 on 7 Dec 2020, so it moves with it. Last entry 8 Dec 2020 (publication); no action of its own since. Checked against the Câmara open data on 12 November 2026: no later entry.
overview:
PLP 188/2020 was filed on 17 July 2020 by Zé Neto (PT, Bahia) and 41 other deputies, the PT group, among them Gleisi Hoffmann, Alexandre Padilha, Paulo Pimenta, Maria do Rosário and Patrus Ananias.

The tax applies to assets above R$ 15 million on 1 January each year. Taxpayers are residents, estates and non-residents on their Brazilian assets. Debts taken to buy the assets, work tools (to R$ 100,000) and a home (to R$ 1 million) are deducted, and property taxes actually paid on the same assets are credited against the tax. Rates are 1% from R$ 15 million, 1.5% from R$ 30 million and 2% above R$ 50 million, with assets valued at market price. A missing asset is presumed bought with hidden income.

The justification says the Constitution has authorised the tax for more than 30 years and Congress owes the Constituent Assembly the follow-through. It argues that the better-off should help the public finances through the Covid-19 pandemic, for health and for the needy, and notes Argentina's one-off tax on large fortunes then under discussion. Property taxes were 4.64% of Brazilian tax revenue in 2018, while taxes on goods and services were 44.74%.

It was attached to PLP 277/2008 on 7 December 2020 and has had no action of its own since. PLP 203/2024 repeats its text.

title: PLP 193/2020: institutes the Imposto sobre Grandes Fortunas
by: Áurea Carolina, David Miranda, Edmilson Rodrigues, Fernanda Melchionna, Glauber Braga, Ivan Valente and 3 other deputies
summary: Institutes the Tax on Large Fortunes at 1% to 5% on wealth above R$ 5 million and earmarks the revenue for the PSOL's Permanent Minimum Income Programme.
status: Câmara dos Deputados, situation "Tramitando em Conjunto": attached to PLP 277/2008 on 7 Dec 2020, so it moves with it. Last entry 8 Dec 2020 (publication); no action of its own since. Checked against the Câmara open data on 12 November 2026: no later entry.
overview:
PLP 193/2020 was filed on 24 July 2020 by the PSOL group: Áurea Carolina, David Miranda, Edmilson Rodrigues, Fernanda Melchionna, Glauber Braga, Ivan Valente, Luiza Erundina, Marcelo Freixo and Sâmia Bomfim. It continues the line of PLP 277/2008 by the same party and ties the tax to a policy the PSOL was pressing at the time.

The tax applies to assets above R$ 5 million on 1 January, in 2020 money and indexed. Tools of a trade and assets of high social, economic or ecological value are excluded up to R$ 500,000 each. Rates rise in seven bands: 1% from R$ 5 million, 1.5% from R$ 10 million, 2% from R$ 20 million, 3% from R$ 30 million, 4% from R$ 40 million and 5% above R$ 50 million. An asset missing from the return is presumed bought with hidden income.

All revenue is assigned to the Programa de Renda Mínima, the PSOL's permanent minimum income programme. The justification describes it as a benefit of R$ 600 to R$ 1,200 per family for about 80 million people living on up to half a minimum wage a month. Using a Cedeplar (UFMG) model, it puts the net annual cost at R$ 365 billion, or 5.37% of GDP in 2018. It lists the large-fortunes tax as the first of four funding sources, ahead of a 20% tax on profits and dividends and a higher bank profit levy.

It was attached to PLP 277/2008 on 7 December 2020 and has had no action of its own since.

title: PLP 130/2021: institutes the Imposto sobre Grandes Fortunas
by: Afonso Florence, Airton Faleiro, Alencar Santana Braga, Alice Portugal, Benedita da Silva, Beto Faro and 49 other deputies
summary: Institutes the Tax on Large Fortunes on assets above R$ 10 million: 1%, 2% and 3% for the first five years, then 0.5%, 1% and 1.5%; about 55 deputies as authors, 20% of revenue for health, and an estimate of over R$ 40 billion a year.
status: Câmara dos Deputados, situation "Tramitando em Conjunto": attached to PLP 277/2008 on 28 Sep 2021, so it moves with it. Last entry 24 May 2022 (attaching PLP 74/2022 to it). Checked against the Câmara open data on 12 November 2026: no later entry.
overview:
PLP 130/2021 was filed on 2 September 2021 by Pedro Uczai (PT, Santa Catarina) and 54 other deputies. The signers include Fernanda Melchionna, Ivan Valente, Jandira Feghali, Danilo Cabral and Marcelo Freixo, from several parties of the left.

A large fortune is defined as assets of any kind, in Brazil or abroad, above R$ 10 million on 1 January, a line the authors set to reach the richest 0.3% of residents. Non-residents with assets in Brazil pay regardless of the line and must name a representative in Brazil. Rates apply in bands. For the first five years: 1% from R$ 10 million, 2% from R$ 40 million and 3% above R$ 80 million. After that: 0.5%, 1% and 1.5% on the same bands. A single home is excluded up to R$ 2 million and work tools up to R$ 500,000. Debts taken to buy assets can be deducted. Of the revenue, 20% goes to health services, first of all to support Covid-19 victims.

The justification draws on Oxfam Brazil's finding that five people hold more than half of the population's combined wealth. Applying an average 2.5% to the amounts above R$ 10 million declared on income-tax returns gives about R$ 32 billion. The authors count foreign owners and assets understated at historic cost and expect more than R$ 40 billion. They say the bill came out of consultations with civil society after the pandemic.

It was attached to PLP 277/2008 on 28 September 2021. On 24 May 2022 PLP 74/2022 was attached to it. Pedro Uczai filed a new version in February 2026 as PLP 5/2026.

title: PLP 69/2023: institutes the Imposto sobre Grandes Fortunas (IGF)
by: Jorge Goetten
summary: Institutes a one-off Tax on Large Fortunes on assets above R$ 10 million, at 1.5% to 3.5% plus an extra 1% to 1.75% on assets held abroad, by Jorge Goetten (PL) to cut the deficit and public-debt interest.
status: Câmara dos Deputados: attached to PLP 277/2008 on 2 Jun 2023, so it moves with it, although the situation field still reads "Aguardando Encaminhamento". Last entry 2 Jun 2023 (publication). Checked against the Câmara open data on 12 November 2026: no later entry.
overview:
PLP 69/2023 was filed on 21 March 2023 by Jorge Goetten, a deputy for Santa Catarina in the Liberal Party (PL). It differs from the other Câmara bills in that the tax is paid once.

The tax falls on assets above R$ 10 million held on 31 December of the year the law is published, and is due by 30 April of the following year. Residents pay on their worldwide assets, non-residents on Brazilian ones, and estates are covered. Market value is used, with the book value of private companies and the quoted price of listed shares. Rates are 1.5% from R$ 10 million, 2.5% from R$ 30 million and 3.5% above R$ 50 million. On the part of the assets held abroad, an additional 1% from R$ 10 million and 1.75% above R$ 30 million apply, which takes the top rate to 5.25%.

The justification says the aim is to cut the public-sector deficit and the interest bill on public debt. It points to the cost of the Covid-19 emergency aid and the returned Bolsa Família, and argues that the more favoured part of the population should contribute more to overcome the difficulties of the economy.

The Câmara attached it to PLP 277/2008 on 2 June 2023, although its situation field still reads "Aguardando Encaminhamento". It has had no action since.

title: PLP 203/2024: institutes the Imposto sobre Grandes Fortunas (IGF)
by: Elisangela Araujo
summary: Institutes the Tax on Large Fortunes at 1%, 1.5% and 2% on wealth above R$ 15 million; Elisangela Araujo's filing repeats the text of PLP 188/2020.
status: Câmara dos Deputados, situation "Aguardando Despacho do Presidente da Câmara dos Deputados (Chancela)": the history shows only the filing on 19 Nov 2024, with no referral to a committee and no other action since. Checked against the Câmara open data on 12 November 2026: no later entry.
overview:
PLP 203/2024 was filed on 19 November 2024 by Elisangela Araujo (PT, Bahia). Its articles, rates and justification are those of PLP 188/2020, which Zé Neto and about 40 PT deputies filed in July 2020.

The tax applies to assets above R$ 15 million on 1 January each year, for residents, estates and non-residents on their Brazilian assets. Debts taken to buy the assets, work tools (to R$ 100,000) and a home (to R$ 1 million) are deducted, and property taxes paid on the same assets are credited against the tax. Rates are 1% from R$ 15 million, 1.5% from R$ 30 million and 2% above R$ 50 million, on market values. The federal revenue service administers it.

The justification was written for 2020. It speaks of the Covid-19 pandemic and a debt to the Constituent Assembly, and notes that property taxes were 4.64% of Brazilian tax revenue in 2018 against 44.74% for taxes on goods and services.

The Câmara page shows only the filing and has not yet shown a referral to a committee or attachment to PLP 277/2008.

title: PLP 5/2026: institutes the Imposto sobre Grandes Fortunas
by: Pedro Uczai
summary: Institutes the Tax on Large Fortunes at 1% to 3% on wealth above R$ 10 million, with property taxes credited and all revenue going to the Fund to Combat and Eradicate Poverty; Pedro Uczai's 2026 filing.
status: Câmara dos Deputados, situation "Aguardando Despacho do Presidente da Câmara dos Deputados (Chancela)": the history shows only the filing on 2 Feb 2026, with no referral to a committee and no other action since. Checked against the Câmara open data on 12 November 2026: no later entry.
overview:
PLP 5/2026 was filed on 2 February 2026 by Pedro Uczai (PT, Santa Catarina), the first author of PLP 130/2021. It is his shorter 2026 version of that bill and the newest wealth-tax bill in the Câmara.

The tax applies to assets above R$ 10 million on 1 January each year, less debts and liens. Residents pay on all assets, non-residents on those in Brazil, and estates are covered. Shares are valued at the last closing quote, private companies at market value, and real estate at the reference value set in Complementary Law 214 of 2025, the tax-reform law. Spouses and co-owners are taxed individually on their share. The table gives 1% for the band from R$ 10 million to R$ 100 million, 2% from R$ 100 million (with R$ 1 million deducted) and 3% from R$ 200 million (with R$ 3 million deducted). Property taxes (ITR, IPVA and IPTU) paid the year before on the same assets are credited. Payment falls due on the last working day of April.

All revenue goes to the Fund to Combat and Eradicate Poverty. The justification cites article 80, III of the transitional constitutional provisions, which assigns the tax to that fund. It describes the fund as paying for income transfers and for health, education, housing and sanitation in the poorest regions.

The Câmara page shows only the filing, with no referral to a committee and no attachment to PLP 277/2008 yet. The earlier Uczai bill, PLP 130/2021, is attached to it.

title: PLS 534/2011: taxation of large fortunes
by: Senator Antonio Carlos Valadares (PSB)
summary: Regulates art. 153, VII of the Constitution: an annual tax on net wealth above R$ 2,500,000 held at 31 December, on Brazilian-born individuals worldwide and on foreigners resident in Brazil for assets there.
status: Senado Federal: "Arquivada ao final da legislatura" (20 December 2018)
overview:
Complementary bill PLS 534/2011 was read in the Brazilian Senate on 31 August 2011 and sent to the Social Affairs and Economic Affairs committees. Its author is Senator Antonio Carlos Valadares of the PSB, and it aims to regulate article 153, VII of the 1988 Constitution, which allows a federal tax on large fortunes that Congress has never regulated.

The bill taxes individuals whose wealth exceeds R$ 2,500,000 on 31 December each year. Residents in Brazil would be taxed on assets anywhere in the world, and foreigners domiciled in Brazil on assets located in Brazil. It sets valuation rules and a progressive rate table, allows deductions for property and vehicle taxes paid and for the upkeep of assets, requires an annual declaration with advance payment, and sets penalties for late filing, undervaluation, omission and fraud.

In the Social Affairs Committee the rapporteurship changed hands many times, ending with Lindbergh Farias in August 2017. Benedito de Lira's 2015 report recommended approval with four amendments, but the committee vote was postponed and never held. The Senate archived the bill on 20 December 2018 at the end of the legislature. In the Senate's public consultation, 105 people voted in favour and 40 against.

title: PLS 315/2015: institutes the Imposto sobre Grandes Fortunas
by: Senator Paulo Paim (PT)
summary: Institutes the Tax on Large Fortunes as a flat 1% a year on net wealth above R$ 50 million, by Senator Paulo Paim; revived in March 2023 and back before the Economic Affairs Committee.
status: Senado Federal. Archived at the end of the legislature on 22 Dec 2022 (RISF art. 332 §1), then reactivated on 16 Mar 2023 when the Plenary approved RQS 98/2023 (Paulo Paim) and sent it back to the Economic Affairs Committee (CAE). Last entry 16 Mar 2023; no committee report shown. Checked against the Senate open data on 12 November 2026: the situation is still "Desarquivada" and the last entry is 16 Mar 2023.
overview:
PLS 315/2015 is a complementary bill that Senator Paulo Paim (PT, Rio Grande do Sul) filed on 26 May 2015.

The tax is a flat 1% a year on net wealth above R$ 50 million at 31 December, with the threshold indexed. It covers Brazilian-born individuals and their estates on assets anywhere, and foreigners living in Brazil on assets in Brazil. The family home and small household goods, tools of a trade, protected heritage and environmental land, and assets given to cultural and charitable bodies are excluded. Property and inheritance taxes already paid on the assets, and the cost of keeping them up, are credited. The return is filed annually, instalments are allowed, and penalties run from 50% for understating an asset to 150% for fraud. The federal revenue service runs it.

The justification places the tax in the constitutional goals of a more just society and the end of poverty. It says that the tax system should ask more of those who can pay more, and describes wealth as income that has not been consumed.

The Senate archived the bill at the end of the legislature on 22 December 2022. On 16 March 2023 the Plenary approved Paim's request RQS 98/2023 and sent the bill back to the Economic Affairs Committee (CAE). No committee report appears on the bill page.

title: PLS 139/2017: institutes the Imposto sobre Grandes Fortunas
by: Senator Vanessa Grazziotin (PCdoB)
summary: Regulates art. 153, VII of the Constitution to institute the Tax on Large Fortunes, taxing net wealth at progressive rates with deductions from the tax owed.
status: Senado Federal: "Arquivada ao final da legislatura" (21 December 2018)
overview:
Complementary bill PLS 139/2017 was filed on 9 May 2017 by Senator Vanessa Grazziotin of the PCdoB and read in the Senate that day. It regulates article 153, VII of the Constitution, the federal tax on large fortunes that has been in the text since 1988 and has never been put into law. The bill defines net wealth as the taxable event, sets progressive rates and provides for certain deductions from the tax owed.

It went to the Senate's Economic Affairs Committee the same day. Senator Romero Jucá was named rapporteur on 9 June 2017, and the bill was never voted on. On 21 December 2018 it was archived at the end of the legislature under article 332 of the Senate rules.

On the Senate's public consultation page, 2,387 people voted in favour of the bill and 1,033 against.

title: PLP 183/2019: institutes the Imposto sobre Grandes Fortunas
by: Senator Plínio Valério (PSDB)
summary: Institutes the Tax on Large Fortunes at 0.5%, 0.75% and 1% on net wealth above 12,000 times the monthly income-tax exemption; the only Senate wealth-tax bill with a favourable committee report, but no vote has been taken.
status: Senado Federal, Economic Affairs Committee (CAE). Rapporteur Major Olímpio presented a favourable report with two amendments on 25 Mar 2020 and returned the bill on 8 Apr 2021 because he had left the committee. His successor, Veneziano Vital do Rêgo, presented a favourable report on 5 Dec 2022 and the bill was on the committee agenda for 7 Dec 2022; the history shows no vote. It continued under RISF art. 332 on 21 Dec 2022 and has awaited a new rapporteur since 2 Feb 2023. Checked against the Senate open data on 12 November 2026: no later entry.

links.label: CAE report of Senator Veneziano Vital do Rêgo, 5 Dec 2022 (PDF)

overview:
PLP 183/2019 was filed on 6 August 2019 by Senator Plínio Valério (PSDB, Amazonas). It follows the design of PLP 130/2012 from the Câmara, with a higher entry point, and the justification thanks the members of both houses whose bills it draws on.

The tax applies to net wealth on 31 December above 12,000 times the monthly exemption of the personal income tax. The justification put that at R$ 22.8 million at the time. Rates are 0.5% up to 20,000 times the exemption, 0.75% up to 70,000 times and 1% above. Individuals living in Brazil, estates and non-residents with Brazilian assets pay. The home (up to 20% of wealth), work tools (up to 10%), intellectual property and small items are excluded. ITR, IPTU, IPVA, ITBI and ITCMD paid on the same assets are credited. Instalments are barred.

The author says the bill is not a Robin Hood tax and will not end poverty, but that those who earn more should pay more. He notes that a group of US billionaires had recently asked for a federal wealth tax, and that revenue goes to the Fund to Combat and Eradicate Poverty. He describes the design as simple, cheap to run and no burden on the middle class.

In the Economic Affairs Committee two rapporteurs have recommended approval. Veneziano Vital do Rêgo's report finds the bill sound in law, says it would reduce inequality and add stable revenue, and says capital flight is unlikely given the evidence. The rapporteur's vote is for approval. The bill has not been put to the vote and awaits a new rapporteur. PLP 125/2021 by Senator Jorge Kajuru has the same design.

title: PLP 38/2020: Extraordinary Tax on Large Fortunes during the public calamity
by: Senator Reguffe (PODE)
summary: Institutes an extraordinary tax on large fortunes for the duration of the public calamity declared for covid-19: 0.5% a year on individuals with net wealth above 50,000 minimum wages.
status: Senado Federal: "Arquivada ao final da legislatura" (21 December 2022)
overview:
Complementary bill PLP 38/2020 was presented in the Brazilian Senate on 24 March 2020 by Senator Reguffe (Podemos, Federal District) and read in plenary that day. It creates an "Imposto Extraordinário sobre Grandes Fortunas", a tax on large fortunes that would apply only while a public calamity is in force in Brazil, which at the time meant the COVID-19 emergency.

The tax would apply to individuals with net wealth above 50,000 minimum wages, at a rate of half a percentage point per year.

The bill was published in the Senate gazette on 26 March 2020. On 30 March 2020 Senator Paulo Paim filed a request, RQS 151/2020, to process it together with PLS 315/2015 and PLPs 183/2019 and 50/2020, other bills on the same tax. It was never voted on. The Senate archived it on 21 December 2022 at the end of the legislature. In the Senate's public consultation, 85 people voted in favour and 36 against.

title: PLP 50/2020: tax on large fortunes and compulsory loan for covid-19 social protection
by: Senator Eliziane Gama (Cidadania)
summary: Institutes a temporary Tax on Large Fortunes (0.5%, 0.75%, 1%) plus a refundable 4% compulsory loan on the same wealth in 2020, to pay for Covid-19 health and income support; by Senator Eliziane Gama.
status: Senado Federal, Economic Affairs Committee (CAE): it continued under RISF art. 332 on 21 Dec 2022, and Senator Jaques Wagner was named rapporteur on 19 Apr 2023. Last entry 19 Apr 2023; no report shown. Checked against the Senate open data on 12 November 2026: no later entry.
overview:
PLP 50/2020 was filed on 26 March 2020 by Senator Eliziane Gama (Cidadania, Maranhão), at the start of the Covid-19 emergency. It has two parts and both fall on net wealth above 12,000 times the monthly exemption of the personal income tax.

The first part is a tax on large fortunes that lasts as long as the spending cap of Constitutional Amendment 95. Rates are 0.5% up to 20,000 times the exemption, 0.75% up to 70,000 times and 1% above. The second is a compulsory loan on the same wealth at four centavos per real above the line. It is collected in 2020 only, since a loan is not bound by the one-year wait that applies to new taxes. It is repaid from 2021 as credits against the tax, with interest at the TR rate. Both tax individuals living in Brazil, estates and non-residents on their Brazilian assets, and the loan is assessed on wealth at the end of 2019. The federal revenue service is to set the rules within 20 days.

The money is to go first to health, social assistance and social security, including larger Bolsa Família benefits or a basic income. The justification argues that income falls in a quarantine, so the stock of wealth is the right base. It notes that people earning over 320 minimum wages declare assets above R$ 1 trillion, and that only a tenth of the income of the richest 1% is taxable.

The bill is before the Economic Affairs Committee. Senator Jaques Wagner was named rapporteur in June 2022 and again on 19 April 2023, and no report is on the page. The committee asked the Economy Ministry in April and August 2021 to review the bill's budget compatibility. It continued under RISF art. 332 on 21 Dec 2022.

title: PLP 101/2021: Extraordinary Contribution on Large Fortunes
by: Senator Randolfe Rodrigues (Rede)
summary: Institutes a one-off Extraordinary Contribution on Large Fortunes of 0.5% to 5% on wealth above R$ 4.67 million, split between Covid-19 health spending and emergency aid; by Senator Randolfe Rodrigues, inspired by the Unafisco study.
status: Senado Federal: since 9 May 2023 handled together with PLP 125/2021 (RISF art. 48 §1). The Presidency sent the pair to the Constitution and Justice Committee (CCJ) and then the Economic Affairs Committee (CAE), and they await a rapporteur. It continued under RISF art. 332 on 21 Dec 2022. Checked against the Senate open data on 12 November 2026: no later entry.
overview:
PLP 101/2021 was filed on 2 July 2021 by Senator Randolfe Rodrigues (Rede, Amapá). It does not create the tax of article 153, VII. It creates an Extraordinary Contribution on Large Fortunes, paid once, as a response to the Covid-19 emergency.

The contribution falls on assets above R$ 4.67 million, at home or abroad, for residents, and on Brazilian assets for non-residents. Rates rise in five bands: 0.5% from R$ 4.67 million, 1% from R$ 7 million, 2% from R$ 10 million, 3% from R$ 15 million and 5% above R$ 30 million, each with a fixed amount to deduct. Wealth is taken from the latest income-tax return, or declared within 60 days of the law's approval. Half the money goes to health, first of all the fight against Covid-19, and half to topping up emergency aid for the poorest families, on top of the 2021 budget.

The justification says that the number of Brazilian billionaires grew from 45 in 2020 to 65 in 2021, with combined wealth of R$ 1.6 trillion, about a fifth of annual output, while 7.9 million people were expected to be in extreme poverty. It credits the design to the study by Unafisco, the federal tax auditors' union. A contribution was chosen over a tax because it can be charged 90 days after publication, whereas a tax must wait for the next year. The constitutional basis is the power to create new sources of social-security funding.

Since 9 May 2023 it has been handled together with PLP 125/2021, which taxes large fortunes as a regular tax instead. Both await a rapporteur.

title: PLP 125/2021: institutes the Imposto sobre Grandes Fortunas
by: Senator Jorge Kajuru (PODE)
summary: Institutes the Tax on Large Fortunes at 0.5%, 0.75% and 1% on net wealth above 10,000 times the monthly income-tax exemption, by Senator Jorge Kajuru; processed together with PLP 101/2021.
status: Senado Federal: since 9 May 2023 handled together with PLP 101/2021 (RISF art. 48 §1). The Presidency sent the pair to the Constitution and Justice Committee (CCJ) and then the Economic Affairs Committee (CAE), and they await a rapporteur. It continued under RISF art. 332 on 21 Dec 2022. Checked against the Senate open data on 12 November 2026: no later entry.
overview:
PLP 125/2021 was filed on 26 August 2021 by Senator Jorge Kajuru (Podemos, Goiás). It has the same structure as Senator Plínio Valério's PLP 183/2019, with a lower threshold.

The tax applies to net wealth on 31 December above 10,000 times the monthly exemption of the personal income tax, R$ 19.0 million at the time. Rates are 0.5% up to 20,000 times the exemption, 0.75% up to 50,000 times and 1% above. Individuals living in Brazil, estates and non-residents with Brazilian assets pay. The home (to 20% of wealth), work tools (to 10%), protected heritage and environmental land, and assets given to cultural and charitable bodies are excluded. ITR, IPTU, IPVA, ITBI and ITCMD paid on the same assets are credited. Whoever helps hide the true owner of assets is jointly liable. The law takes effect on 1 January of the second year after publication.

The justification says the Brazilian system leans on regressive indirect taxes, and that taxes on income and wealth are the way to progressivity. It admits that the tax is controversial, since some European countries dropped it and the United States never had one. It answers that a short law with few rates and bands keeps administration cheap, and that the revenue offsets the cost as with the IPTU and IPVA. The threshold was R$ 19,039,800 when the bill was filed, and the revenue goes to the Fund to Combat and Eradicate Poverty.

Since 9 May 2023 it has been handled together with PLP 101/2021, Senator Randolfe Rodrigues's one-off contribution. The pair goes to the Constitution and Justice Committee and then the Economic Affairs Committee, and awaits a rapporteur.

title: Tributar os super-ricos para reconstruir o país (executive report)
by: Fenafisco, Anfip, Instituto Justiça Fiscal and Auditores Fiscais pela Democracia
summary: Eight tax-law proposals that include regulating the Imposto sobre Grandes Fortunas (rates of 0.5%, 1% and 1.5%, raised for five years to 1%, 2% and 3%), which it estimates at R$ 40 billion of a total R$ 292 billion a year, falling on the richest 0.3%.

title: Imposto sobre Grandes Fortunas: o recente debate internacional e a situação no Brasil (One Pager 378)
by: Pedro Carvalho Jr. (Ipea) and Luana Passos (UFF)
summary: Reviews the recent international debate on taxing large fortunes and the situation of the Imposto sobre Grandes Fortunas, still unregulated in Brazil since the 1988 Constitution.

title: Antrag 17/2944: Auswege aus der Krise: Steuerpolitische Gerechtigkeit und Handlungsfähigkeit des Staates wiederherstellen
by: Fraktion Die Linke (Barbara Höll, Axel Troost, Sahra Wagenknecht and others)
summary: Among its demands, asks the government to bring back the wealth tax as a millionaires' tax, at 5% of net wealth above an allowance of 1,000,000 euro.
status: Motion tabled in the Bundestag (Drucksache 17/2944); the 17th Bundestag has since ended
overview:
Drucksache 17/2944 is a motion from the Die Linke group in the Bundestag, tabled on 14 September 2010 and titled "Ways out of the crisis: restoring fairness in tax policy and the state's ability to act". It is a broad tax programme, not a single-tax bill. Its first demand is to bring back the wealth tax in the form of a "millionaires' tax": net private wealth above an allowance of 1,000,000 euro would be taxed at 5 per cent.

The second demand is to reform inheritance and gift tax, with one personal allowance of 150,000 euro for all heirs (300,000 euro for minor children, surviving spouses and people over 60) and rates rising to 60 per cent on the largest bequests. The motion argues that the financial crisis grew out of redistribution from the bottom to the top over the previous ten years and that the government's cuts fall on low and middle incomes.

The motion asks the government to present the necessary bills. The register records it as tabled; the 17th Bundestag has since ended, so it lapsed. A wealth tax of this kind has not been introduced.

It matters as an early statement of the 5 per cent millionaires' tax that Die Linke repeated in 2012 and 2017. This summary comes from the motion's own text; its committee fate was not checked.

title: Antrag 17/8792: Wer Schulden bremsen will, muss Millionäre besteuern
by: Fraktion Die Linke (Barbara Höll, Axel Troost, Sahra Wagenknecht and others)
summary: Asks the government for a bill that brings back the wealth tax as a millionaires' tax: 5% on net wealth above 1,000,000 euro.
status: Debated on 23 March 2012 and referred to committees (Bundestag text archive); no vote shown there. The 17th Bundestag has since ended
overview:
Drucksache 17/8792, "Whoever wants to brake debt must tax millionaires", is a motion from the Die Linke group in the Bundestag, tabled on 29 February 2012. It asks the government to present a bill that brings back the wealth tax as a millionaires' tax. Wealth would be assessed on 31 December 2012 as private financial assets plus the market value of private property and other assets, minus private debts. Net wealth per person up to 1,000,000 euro would be tax-free and the part above taxed at 5 per cent.

The reasoning ties the tax to the constitutional debt brake and the cost of the financial crisis. It cites a DIW study that a 1 per cent tax with a 500,000 euro allowance could raise 16 to 21 billion euro a year, and estimates that this 5 per cent model would raise up to 80 billion euro.

The Bundestag text archive shows the motion was debated on 23 March 2012 and referred to committees; no vote is shown there. The 17th Bundestag has since ended, so it lapsed.

It matters because it put a concrete rate, allowance and revenue estimate on the table in Germany's debate on reviving the wealth tax, which has not been levied since 1997. This summary is based on the motion's full text.

title: Gesetzentwurf 17/10770: Entwurf eines Gesetzes zur Erhebung einer Vermögensabgabe
by: Fraktion Bündnis 90/Die Grünen (Lisa Paus, Kerstin Andreae, Britta Haßelmann and others)
summary: Bill for a one-off wealth levy on the richest, modelled on the post-war Lastenausgleich, to reduce the public debt caused by the financial crisis.
status: Roll call in the Bundestag on 27 June 2013: 66 yes, 318 no, 195 abstentions (official name list)
overview:
Drucksache 17/10770 is a bill by the Bündnis 90/Die Grünen group in the Bundestag, tabled on 25 September 2012, for a one-off wealth levy (Vermögensabgabe) modelled on the post-war Lastenausgleich. Its stated aim is to pay down the public debt, which had grown by more than 400 billion euro in three years of financial-crisis rescue and stimulus.

The levy would be 15 per cent of taxable wealth on a cut-off date of 1 January 2012, paid in ten equal annual instalments of 1.5 per cent that cover repayment and interest. Each person gets an allowance of 1,000,000 euro, plus 250,000 euro per child, and domestic business and farm assets get a further allowance of 5,000,000 euro. The allowances shrink euro for euro for wealth above them. Statutory social insurance claims and similar pension entitlements are exempt. The group, citing a DIW study, expected about 100 billion euro over ten years from roughly 330,000 people, under 1 per cent of the population.

The Bundestag voted on it by roll call on 27 June 2013: 66 yes, 318 no and 195 abstentions, so it was rejected.

It matters as a fully drafted law, with article-by-article reasoning, rather than a request to the government. The summary comes from the bill's own text; the vote count is from the official name list noted in the status.

title: Antrag 17/10778: Reichtum umFAIRteilen – in Deutschland und Europa
by: Fraktion Die Linke (Alexander Ulrich, Gregor Gysi, Sahra Wagenknecht and others)
summary: Among its demands, asks the government to work at EU level for a Europe-wide coordinated wealth levy (Vermögensabgabe).
status: Motion tabled in the Bundestag (Drucksache 17/10778); the 17th Bundestag has since ended
overview:
Drucksache 17/10778, "Redistribute wealth: in Germany and Europe", is a motion from the Die Linke group in the Bundestag, tabled on 25 September 2012. It is a long crisis programme. Among its demands, it asks the government to work at EU level for a coordinated wealth levy (Vermögensabgabe) on private net wealth that was above 1 million euro on a past cut-off date. The levy would cover financial and physical assets, be paid over several years, spare small and medium businesses, and be paired with a debt cut for heavily indebted states.

It also asks the government to bring bills to the Bundestag for a levy under Article 106(1) no. 5 of the Basic Law on the model of the 1952 Lastenausgleich, and for the wealth tax to return as a 5 per cent millionaires' tax on wealth above 1 million euro. Other demands include a financial transactions tax, an end to austerity conditions on EU rescue loans and the nationalisation of large private banks.

The register records it as tabled; the 17th Bundestag has since ended, so it lapsed. Its committee fate was not checked.

It matters because it links a national wealth levy to a Europe-wide one during the euro crisis. The summary is from the motion's own text.

title: Antrag 19/94: Reichtum gerechter verteilen – Vermögensteuer als Millionärsteuer wieder erheben
by: Fraktion Die Linke (Klaus Ernst, Fabio De Masi, Bernd Riexinger and others)
summary: Asks the government for a bill that brings back the wealth tax as a millionaires' tax: 5% above 1 million euro, with a higher allowance of 5 million euro for business assets.
status: Motion tabled in the Bundestag (Drucksache 19/94); the 19th Bundestag has since ended
overview:
Drucksache 19/94 is a motion from the Die Linke group in the Bundestag, tabled on 22 November 2017 at the start of the 19th term, titled "Distribute wealth more fairly: bring back the wealth tax as a millionaires' tax". It asks the government to present a bill that reinstates the wealth tax, aimed at the richest 1 to 2 per cent of the population.

The design: net wealth per person is valued on 31 December 2016 (financial assets plus the market value of private property and other assets, minus private debts). The first 1,000,000 euro is tax-free and the part above is taxed at 5 per cent. For business assets of sole proprietors and partnerships, a higher allowance of 5,000,000 euro applies.

The motion notes that the wealth tax has been suspended since 1997 and that, according to the OECD, property-related taxes in Germany were only 0.9 per cent of GDP in 2013, against a GDP-weighted OECD average of 2.5 per cent. The 19th Bundestag has since ended, so the motion lapsed; its committee fate was not checked.

It matters as the 2017 version of the group's standing proposal, with a special allowance for business assets added. The summary is from the motion's full text.

title: Antrag 19/28908: Einmalige Vermögensabgabe für Milliardäre und Multimillionäre
by: Fraktion Die Linke (Fabio De Masi, Stefan Liebich, Klaus Ernst and others)
summary: Asks the government for a one-off wealth levy under Article 106(1) no. 5 of the Basic Law, aimed at no more than the richest 0.7% of adults and at least 300 billion euro.
status: Motion tabled in the Bundestag (Drucksache 19/28908); the 19th Bundestag has since ended
overview:
Drucksache 19/28908, "One-off wealth levy for billionaires and multimillionaires", is a motion from the Die Linke group in the Bundestag, tabled on 22 April 2021. It asks the government to present a bill for a one-off levy under Article 106(1) no. 5 of the Basic Law, to help pay for the Covid-19 crisis, on the model of the 1952 Lastenausgleich.

The levy should hit at most the richest 0.7 per cent of adults and raise at least 300 billion euro. It would be charged per person on net wealth on 1 January 2021 at market value, with a personal allowance of 2,000,000 euro and a separate 5,000,000 euro allowance for business assets (including holdings of at least 25 per cent in companies). Pension assets stay free up to 1,000,000 euro. The rate is progressive, from 10 per cent rising to 30 per cent for wealth of 100 million euro and above. The payments are spread over 20 years with interest, which the motion equates to at most 1.5 per cent a year at the top rate.

The 19th Bundestag has since ended, so the motion lapsed; its committee fate was not checked. It matters because it is a detailed levy design backed by a DIW costing. The summary is from the motion's full text.

title: Antrag 20/4307: Einmalige Vermögensabgabe für Multimillionäre und Milliardäre
by: Fraktion Die Linke (Christian Görke, Gesine Lötzsch, Klaus Ernst and others)
summary: Asks the government for a bill creating a one-off wealth levy on multimillionaires and billionaires under Article 106(1) no. 5 of the Basic Law, on the model of the Lastenausgleich.
status: Rejected by the Bundestag on 10 November 2022 in a named vote: 36 yes, 649 no (Bundestag text archive)
overview:
Drucksache 20/4307, "One-off wealth levy for multimillionaires and billionaires", is a motion from the Die Linke group in the Bundestag, tabled on 8 November 2022 during the energy-price crisis. It asks the government to present a bill creating a one-off levy on multimillionaires and billionaires under Article 106(1) no. 5 of the Basic Law, on the model of the post-war Lastenausgleich. It names no rate or allowance, and points instead to proposals from the SPD, the Greens and Die Linke and to a DIW study of the group's earlier levy.

It argues that the richest 1 per cent hold almost a third of German net wealth and that those with the largest financial buffer should carry more of the crisis costs.

The Bundestag rejected the motion on 10 November 2022 in a named vote: 36 yes and 649 no, according to the Bundestag text archive noted in the status.

It matters because it shows how little support a levy had in the 20th Bundestag. The summary is based on the motion's text; the vote count is from the record cited in the status.

title: Antrag 21/8267: 500-Millionen-Steuer – Extremvermögen fairer beteiligen
by: Fraktion Bündnis 90/Die Grünen (Karoline Otte, Katharina Beck, Katharina Dröge and others)
summary: Asks the government to introduce a tax on net wealth above an allowance of 500 million euro, at 2% rising to 3% above 1 billion and 4% above 10 billion euro.
status: Tabled by the Greens group on 29 September 2026 (Drucksache 21/8267, dated 22 September; Bundestag notice hib 758/2026 of 30 September). The first reading is scheduled for 12 November 2026 (30 minutes), with referral to the committees and the Finance Committee in the lead; its outcome was not yet published when checked on 12 November.
overview:
The Greens' "500-Millionen-Steuer" asks the government to tax net wealth above an allowance of 500 million euro. The rate starts at 2% above 500 million euro, rises to 3% from 1 billion and tops out at 4% from 10 billion, in a straight-line progression. Income tax a person has already paid is credited against the new tax, so a billionaire who already pays income tax at the level of an average earner owes nothing extra. The motion says only a few hundred people in Germany, the richest 0.0007% of 84 million, would be liable, and it expects more than 20 billion euro a year.

The case rests on how the tax system treats the very rich. The motion says people with more than 500 million euro pay about a third less in tax and contributions, as a share of their means, than an average earner, because profits pile up in holding companies that pay about 1.5% on distributions where a private shareholder would pay about 26%. It also names loopholes in inheritance tax, worth about 20 billion euro a year if closed, as a separate gap. The revenue is meant to ease the squeeze on the federal budget and on municipalities, which the motion says miss more than 30 billion euro a year.

On valuation, the motion relies on the Bewertungsgesetz routines already used for inheritance and gift tax: earnings-value and cash-flow methods for unlisted companies. It puts collection costs below 1% of the yield and says hardship cases can be handled by deferral. It grounds the federal power to tax in Article 106(2) no. 1 of the Basic Law and cites the economist Gabriel Zucman's proposals.

Karoline Otte, Katharina Beck and 13 other Green MPs tabled it, with the group chairs Katharina Dröge and Britta Haßelmann. The Greens presented the concept to the Finance Committee on 7 October 2026, in its debate on the Left's motion 21/4029, as a more workable route that could be put in place at once. The Bundestag takes up the motion on 12 November 2026.

title: Antrag 19/1952: Vermögensteuer wieder einführen – Reiche müssen ihren fairen Beitrag leisten!
by: Fraktion Die Linke (Abgeordnetenhaus von Berlin)
summary: Asks the Berlin Senate to start a Bundesrat initiative to bring back the wealth tax and to commission a legal opinion on whether the Land now has the power to do so.
status: Committees recommended rejection (Drucksache 19/2364, 3 April 2025: Ausschuss für Bundes- und Europaangelegenheiten 12 March, Hauptausschuss 2 April; CDU, SPD and AfD against Greens and Linke). The plenary decision was not found. The 19th term ended when the newly elected Abgeordnetenhaus met on 29 October 2026, so the motion is no longer pending.
overview:
Drucksache 19/1952 is a motion from the Die Linke group in the Berlin Abgeordnetenhaus, tabled on 8 October 2024, titled "Bring back the wealth tax: the rich must make their fair contribution!". It asks the Berlin Senate to start a Bundesrat initiative to reintroduce the wealth tax at federal level as soon as possible. It also asks the Senate to commission a legal opinion on whether the Land itself has acquired the power to legislate on it, because the federal government has failed to act since the Federal Constitutional Court's 1995 ruling. The motion cites legal literature (Epping/Hillgruber, 2023) for that view.

It gives as reasons Berlin's budget cuts of about 3 billion euro, a study by Netzwerk Steuergerechtigkeit and Oxfam that it says shows more than 380 billion euro of revenue lost since 1997, and a survey it reports in which 62 per cent of Germans favour reintroduction. It notes that until 1996 wealth was taxed at 1 per cent a year.

According to the register's status, committees recommended rejecting it on 12 March and 2 April 2025 (Drucksache 19/2364), with CDU, SPD and AfD against Greens and Linke. The plenary decision was not found, and the term ended when the newly elected Abgeordnetenhaus met on 29 October 2026, so the motion is no longer pending.

title: Antrag 7/845: Wiederbelebung der Vermögensteuer als Teil einer gerechten Steuerpolitik
by: Fraktion Die Linke (Landtag von Sachsen-Anhalt)
summary: Asks the state government to work for a Bundesrat initiative to bring back the wealth tax in Germany.
status: Motion tabled in the Landtag of Saxony-Anhalt (Drucksache 7/845); the 7th term has since ended
overview:
Drucksache 7/845 is a motion from the Die Linke group in the Landtag of Saxony-Anhalt, tabled on 19 January 2017 and signed by its group leader Swen Knöchel. It is titled "Reviving the wealth tax as part of fair tax policy and as a contribution to lasting consolidation of the state budget".

The Landtag would state that a wealth tax is an important part of tax policy based on fairness and ability to pay, and that a consolidation policy focused only on spending is not enough to secure the state's long-term freedom to act. It then asks the state government to work toward a Bundesrat initiative to bring back the wealth tax in Germany, which the motion says must be a nationwide rule because a tax in single Länder would not make sense. The reasoning points to the end of the Solidarity Pact II, falling EU funds and demographic revenue losses. The motion sets no rate or allowance.

The register records it as tabled; the 7th term of the Landtag has since ended, so it lapsed. Its fate in the Landtag was not checked. It matters as one of two near-identical Linke motions in German Länder in early 2017. The summary is from the motion's full text.

title: Antrag 19/4497: Wiederbelebung der Vermögensteuer als Teil einer gerechten Steuerpolitik
by: Fraktion Die Linke (Hessischer Landtag)
summary: Asks the state government to work for a Bundesrat initiative to bring back the wealth tax in Germany.
status: Motion tabled in the Hessian Landtag (Drucksache 19/4497); the 19th term has since ended
overview:
Drucksache 19/4497 is a motion from the Die Linke group in the Hessian Landtag, tabled on 7 February 2017 by group leader van Ooyen, titled "Reviving the wealth tax as part of a fair tax policy". It is almost word for word the Saxony-Anhalt motion tabled in January 2017.

The Landtag would state that a wealth tax is an important part of tax policy based on fairness and ability to pay, and that a spending-only consolidation policy does not secure the state budget. It then asks the Hessian state government to work toward a Bundesrat initiative to bring back the wealth tax in Germany. It sets no rate or allowance, and says a nationwide rule is needed because a wealth tax in single Länder would not make sense.

The reasoning recalls the Federal Constitutional Court's decision of 22 June 1995, which found the old wealth tax law incompatible with the equality principle because property and other assets were valued differently, and says no constitutional rewrite followed, so the law could not be applied from 1 January 1997. It also cites under-funded municipalities, staff shortages in the public service and housing shortages in Hesse.

The register records it as tabled; the 19th term has since ended, so it lapsed. Its fate in the Landtag was not checked. The summary is from the motion's full text.

title: Vermögensteuer: Erhebliches Aufkommenspotential trotz erwartbarer Ausweichreaktionen (DIW Wochenbericht 42/2012)

summary: Models a 1% wealth tax with a personal allowance of 2 million euro and finds it would still raise about 11.6 billion euro a year after avoidance responses.

summary: Uses a microsimulation model to estimate that a reinstated wealth tax could raise ten to twenty billion euro a year even with high allowances, though avoidance could cut that noticeably.

summary: A legal opinion that concludes the Basic Law does not stand in the way of reintroducing a wealth tax.

title: Vedtak om skatt av inntekt og formue mv. for inntektsåret 2026 (Stortingets skattevedtak, Vedtak 212)
by: Stortinget (Prop. 1 LS and Innst. 3 S, 2025–2026)
status: Vedtak 212 in the Storting's decisions on Skatter og avgifter 2026 (Prop. 1 LS, Innst. 3 S, 2025–2026); the page shows no decision date
summary: The annual decision that sets Norway's net wealth tax for income year 2026: a state rate of 0.65% above NOK 1.9 million (0.75% above NOK 21.5 million), a municipal rate of at most 0.35%, and 1.0% and 1.1% for taxpayers under skatteloven § 2-3 first paragraph letters k to n.
overview:
Every year the Storting passes a tax decision (skattevedtak) that sets the rates of Norway's taxes on income and wealth. Decision 212 covers income year 2026 and was handled in the Storting's budget case 'Skatter og avgifter 2026' (Prop. 1 LS and Innst. 3 S, 2025 to 2026).

The state wealth tax for a person or estate is 0.65% of net wealth above NOK 1.9 million, rising to 0.75% on the part above NOK 21.5 million. Spouses taxed together pay on wealth above NOK 3.8 million, with the higher rate above NOK 43 million. People taxed under skatteloven section 2-3 first paragraph letters k to n pay 1.0% and 1.1% on the same bands. Companies and similar entities pay 0.3%.

Municipalities also levy a wealth tax on the same base, with the same NOK 1.9 million deduction (NOK 3.8 million for spouses). The municipal rate may not exceed 0.35%.

Norway is one of the few countries that still has an annual net wealth tax. The rules for what counts as wealth are in the Tax Act, chapter 4. The Storting's page shows the decision text but no decision date.

title: NOU 2022: 20 Et helhetlig skattesystem
by: Skatteutvalget (chair Ragnar Torvik), for the Ministry of Finance
summary: The expert committee's majority keeps a net wealth tax but would cut its revenue by NOK 8.4 billion (a much higher threshold, lower rates, a wider base without valuation discounts) and replace part of it with an inheritance tax; a minority wants a still smaller wealth tax.

title: Wealth Taxation and Household Saving: Evidence from Assessment Discontinuities in Norway
by: Marius A. K. Ring (University of Texas at Austin)
summary: Uses geographic discontinuities in Norway's annual net wealth tax and third-party saving data to find that each krone of wealth tax raises annual net financial saving by 3.76 kroner, mostly through higher labour earnings.

title: Proposta di legge di iniziativa popolare "Imposta grandi patrimoni" (campagna 1%Equo)
by: Comitato 1%Equo, promoted by Rifondazione Comunista with economists and researchers (first signatory Maurizio Acerbo)
status: Presented to the Corte di Cassazione on 7 May 2026 under art. 71 of the Constitution. Signature collection runs from 15 May to 15 November 2026; a press report of 8 June 2026 says 50,000 signatures were reached in about three weeks, while the campaign page (read 12 November 2026) shows its official count as still being updated. No parliamentary number was found.
summary: An annual personal tax on net wealth above €2 million, excluding the main home, at 1% to €5 million, 1.7% to €8 million, 2.1% to €20 million and 3.5% above, with IMU, IVIE and IVAFE deducted.

links.label: Campaign page, 1% Equo (signature count and deadline)
L'Indipendente, 8 June 2026: the initiative reaches 50,000 signatures
Il Fatto Quotidiano, 7 May 2026: filing at the Corte di Cassazione

overview:
The 1% Equo bill is a popular-initiative proposal for an annual tax on the net wealth of individuals above EUR 2 million. The main home is left out of the base and comes on top of the EUR 2 million, so the tax reaches only the part of total wealth above the threshold. Four slices are taxed: 1% from EUR 2 million to 5 million, 1.7% from 5 to 8 million, 2.1% from 8 to 20 million and 3.5% above 20 million. The existing IMU, IVIE and IVAFE are deducted from what is owed.

Residents pay on all their wealth, non-residents on assets in Italy, and trustees on assets placed in trust (trusts for severely disabled people under law 112/2016 are excluded). Property is valued at its revalued cadastral value, financial assets at market value on 31 December and unlisted holdings at tax value. The money is earmarked for the national health service, public schools and early-years education, public housing, the green transition, safety at work, disability policy and income support, and what is left goes to easing the income-tax drag on wages through a fund at the Ministry of Economy. A second part of the bill reforms inheritance tax, with rates of 8%, 12% and 15% in the direct line and 15%, 18% and 22% for other heirs.

The promoters' report puts the wealth tax at about EUR 26 billion a year in a cautious scenario (about 215,000 taxpayers) and about EUR 65 billion in a wider one (about 505,000), plus EUR 5.5 to 8 billion from the inheritance reform. The bill was filed at the Corte di Cassazione on 7 May 2026 by the 1% Equo committee, promoted by Rifondazione Comunista with economists and researchers, and is collecting the 50,000 voter signatures that article 71 of the Constitution requires to send it to Parliament. Its eleven first signatories named at the filing, Maurizio Acerbo, Pier Giorgio Ardeni, Anna Bruna Camposampiero, Elena Coccia, Francesca Fornario, Alfonso Gianni, Matteo Prencipe, Rosa Rinaldi, Nadia Rosa, Benedetta Sabene and Marco Veronese Passarella, are all in the register.

title: L'agenda TaxTheRich per l'Italia: Manifesto degli economisti e delle economiste italiani/e
by: 134 Italian economists, drafted by Demetrio Guzzardi, Elisa Palagi and Andrea Roventini (Sant'Anna School), presented with Oxfam Italia
summary: Asks for a progressive tax on the richest 0.1% of citizens, with net wealth above €5.4 million, in line with the European Citizens' Initiative, within a year, together with higher inheritance tax and more top income-tax brackets.

title: Tackling the regressivity of the Italian tax system: An optimal taxation framework with heterogeneous returns to capital
by: Matteo Dalle Luche, Demetrio Guzzardi, Elisa Palagi, Andrea Roventini and Alessandro Santoro (World Inequality Lab WP 2024/23)
summary: Using ECB distributional wealth accounts, finds the Italian tax system regressive over the top 7% and estimates the revenue and inequality effects of higher optimal rates on capital income or of a progressive wealth tax.

title: 富裕税法 (Wealth Tax Act, Law No. 174 of 1950)
by: The Diet of Japan, after the 1949 Shoup recommendations
status: Promulgated 11 May 1950 as Law No. 174; repealed with effect from 1 August 1953 by Law No. 164 of 1953 (Nagoya University law database)
summary: Japan's only permanent net wealth tax: a yearly progressive tax on net worth over ¥5 million at 0.5%, rising to 1% above ¥10 million, 2% above ¥20 million and 3% above ¥50 million.
overview:
Japan's Wealth Tax Act, called the Net Worth Tax Law in the Nagoya University translation, was Law No. 174 of 1950, promulgated on 11 May 1950. It was a yearly tax on net worth, the only permanent one Japan has had. The database lists the Diet's finance committee meetings on it from February 1950.

It applied to individuals who lived in Japan or had stayed more than one year, on all their property, and to other individuals on their property located in Japan. Net worth was measured at midnight on 31 December each year: property at market value minus debts, including taxes owed. Family members living together were combined and the tax shared out between them. Rates were set in four brackets of taxable value: 0.5% on the part over 5 million yen, 1% over 10 million, 2% over 20 million and 3% over 50 million.

The database lists five amending laws between 1950 and 1952, and the Act was repealed by Law No. 164 of 1953, effective 1 August 1953, so it was levied for only a few years. It matters as an early, fully legislated example of a progressive annual wealth tax. The English and Japanese text of the law, the amendment list and the repeal were read on the Nagoya University database.

title: 「富裕税法」再導入論
by: Masato Kikuya (菊谷正人), Keieishirin vol. 53 no. 2 (Hosei University)
summary: Compares the one-off 1946 property tax law with the 1950 wealth tax law and proposes reintroducing a general net wealth tax, with concrete rules on taxable persons and revaluation of property.

title: 부유세와 종합부동산세: 부유세의 조세정책적 의미 (Wealth tax and the comprehensive real estate tax)
by: Korea Institute of Public Finance (KIPF)
summary: Examines proposals for a net wealth tax in Korea, the Swedish and French experience, the comprehensive real estate tax as a wealth tax, and the revenue and distribution effects of alternative designs.

title: 감세정국에서 부유세 도입을 말하다 (forum proceedings)
by: Keynote by Jung Se-eun (Chungnam National University) with discussants from the Labour, Green and Justice parties and civil society; posted by the Labour Party
summary: Proceedings of a forum on introducing a wealth tax amid tax cuts, with a keynote on the issues in creating one and six discussant papers, one of which argues for strengthening asset taxes instead.

title: Que reforma y adicionan diversas disposiciones a la Ley del Impuesto sobre la Renta, en materia de impuesto a las grandes riquezas
by: Dip. José Luis Sánchez González (Partido del Trabajo)
summary: Initiative in the Chamber of Deputies to add an annual tax on the net wealth of individuals above 100 million pesos to the income tax law, with rates of 1.5%, 2.5% and 3.5%, debts deducted, paid into a new Fondo para la Justicia Social.
status: Presented to the Chamber of Deputies and published in the Gaceta Parlamentaria no. 6987-II-4 of 3 March 2026; turned to the Comisión de Hacienda y Crédito Público. The Gaceta's initiative index (copy of 14 October 2026) lists no extension, committee report or vote.

links.label: Initiative in the Gaceta Parlamentaria no. 6987-II-4, 3 March 2026 (Cámara de Diputados)
Gaceta index of initiatives, second ordinary period of the second year, LXVI Legislature (committee turn)
Initiative on the sponsor's group page (Partido del Trabajo, 29 April 2026)

overview:
Deputy José Luis Sánchez González of the Partido del Trabajo presented this initiative on 3 March 2026 and the Gaceta Parlamentaria published it that day, in number 6987-II-4. He is the only signatory. The Chamber turned it to the Comisión de Hacienda y Crédito Público, and the Gaceta's index of initiatives, in the copy of 14 October 2026, lists no extension, committee report or vote.

The decree adds a fraction XIX to article 142 of the Ley del Impuesto sobre la Renta, which counts income from the accumulation of wealth in the patrimony, and two new articles, 146 Bis and 146 Ter. Article 146 Bis taxes, at the end of each fiscal year, net wealth above 100 million pesos held by individuals who live in Mexico or who live abroad with a permanent establishment in the country. Net wealth is the value of the taxpayer's assets minus debts and enforceable liabilities. The assets listed are real estate; vehicles, boats and aircraft; shares and stakes in companies and other financial entities; bank deposits, investments, rights, titles and securities; and works of art, jewellery and other goods. The text sets no exemption for any asset class and no deduction beyond debts.

Article 146 Ter sets three annual rates: 1.5% on net wealth from 100 million to 500 million pesos, 2.5% from 500 million to 1,000 million, and 3.5% above 1,000 million. The whole yield goes to a new Fondo para la Justicia Social, for poverty reduction and vulnerable groups, the environment, education from early childhood to university, science and technology, and decent housing. The Treasury (SHCP), with the tax authority (SAT), issues the general rules. Failure to comply carries a fine of twice the contribution not paid, plus criminal liability under the Código Fiscal de la Federación. The decree takes effect the day after publication in the Diario Oficial, and the authorities have 180 calendar days to update the rules.

The statement of reasons argues from inequality and from low tax collection. It cites the World Inequality Lab for the finding that in 2023 the top 1% held about 30% of national wealth and the poorer half less than 5%, and Oxfam México on the ten richest Mexicans. It presents Colombia's 2025 decree raising its tax on large fortunes as a precedent and names Spain, Norway and Switzerland as experience that such taxes are compatible with investment and growth when the threshold is high. It estimates, from preliminary data of the tax authority and wealth surveys, that fewer than 0.1% of the population would pay and that the tax would raise between 40,000 and 60,000 million pesos a year. The sponsor's group page dates its entry 29 April 2026.

title: Proyecto de Ley 5163/2020-CR: Ley de Impuesto a las Grandes Fortunas
by: Rocío Silva Santisteban and Mirtha Vásquez (Frente Amplio)
summary: Bill to create a permanent annual tax on the net personal wealth of resident individuals above 400 tax units (UIT), with rates rising from 1% to 5%, justified as a way to cut inequality after the COVID-19 crisis.
status: Received by Congress on 12 May 2020; no committee report or vote found, and the 2020-2021 Congress has ended
overview:
Bill 5163/2020-CR, the "Ley de Impuesto a las Grandes Fortunas", was filed in the Peruvian Congress on 12 May 2020 by the Frente Amplio parliamentary group, on the initiative of Rocío Silva Santisteban and Mirtha Vásquez. It creates a tax on the net personal wealth of individuals who live in Peru. Companies are left out on purpose, so that the cost does not fall on consumers or workers.

The tax applies to wealth above 400 tax units (UIT). It is progressive: 1% on the part between 400 and 700 UIT, 2% up to 1,000 UIT, 3% up to 1,300 UIT, 4% up to 1,600 UIT and 5% above that. It covers property, vehicles, shares and bonds, bank deposits, and collectibles, art and jewellery worth more than two UIT, with liabilities linked to those assets deductible. The tax authority SUNAT would collect it and keep a register of wealth.

The explanatory memorandum presents it as a permanent measure to reduce inequality, which it calls the country's main structural problem, and not as a one-off crisis levy. It cites Decreto Legislativo 451, an earlier personal wealth tax that is no longer in force. The bill was received on 12 May 2020. No committee report or vote has been found, and the 2020-2021 Congress has ended. The register lists six of its signers.

title: Proyecto de Ley 06615/2020-CR: Ley que crea el Impuesto de Solidaridad sobre la Fortuna
by: Betto Barrionuevo Romero and other members of the Somos Perú group
summary: Bill to create a progressive tax on the net wealth of individuals, conjugal partnerships and undivided estates above 250 tax units (UIT), at rates from 0.5% to 4%.
status: Sent to the Economy, Banking, Finance and Financial Intelligence Committee on 9 November 2020 and marked 'en comisión' on 10 November 2020; no vote found, and the 2020-2021 Congress has ended
overview:
Bill 6615/2020-CR, the "Impuesto de Solidaridad sobre la Fortuna", was filed in the Peruvian Congress on 5 November 2020 by members of the Somos Perú group, on the initiative of Betto Barrionuevo Romero. It would tax the net wealth of individuals, conjugal partnerships and undivided estates living in Peru.

The tax starts at 250 tax units (UIT) for a person and at 500 UIT for a conjugal partnership. The rates are 0.5% on the part between 250 and 500 UIT, 1% up to 750 UIT, 2% up to 1,000 UIT, 3% for the next band and 4% above 1,500 UIT; the table as printed skips the band between 1,000 and 1,250 UIT. The base includes real estate other than the family home up to 250 UIT, vehicles and pleasure boats, works of art and antiques, bank deposits and shareholdings. The ministry of economy would issue rules against avoidance within 90 days.

The explanatory memorandum calls it the first step of a tax reform aimed at the richest 1% to 2% of Peruvians, in the context of the pandemic and of Peru's high inequality. It was sent to the Economy, Banking, Finance and Financial Intelligence Committee on 9 November 2020. No vote has been found, and the 2020-2021 Congress has ended.
