title: House Bill No. 10253: An Act imposing a 'Super-Rich Tax' on individuals with net value assets exceeding one billion pesos
by: Reps. Ferdinand Gaite, Carlos Zarate, Eufemia Cullamat, France Castro, Arlene Brosas and Sarah Jane Elago (Makabayan bloc)
summary: Proposes a yearly tax of 1% on net assets above 1 billion pesos, 2% above 2 billion and 3% above 3 billion, amending the National Internal Revenue Code, with 60% of the revenue for health and 40% for education, social protection, employment and housing.
status: Pending with the Committee on Ways and Means since 22 September 2021; filed 20 September 2021, Eighteenth Congress, Third Regular Session; the House shows no later action and the Congress ended in June 2022 (House bill-tracking page, checked 12 November 2026).

links.label: House bill-tracking page: authors, committee referral and status

overview:
The Super-Rich Tax Act of 2021 was filed on 20 September 2021 by Bayan Muna Representatives Ferdinand Gaite, Carlos Isagani Zarate and Eufemia Cullamat, ACT Teachers Representative France Castro, Gabriela Women's Party Representative Arlene Brosas and Kabataan Representative Sarah Jane Elago. It was referred to the Committee on Ways and Means on 22 September 2021 and the House shows no further action. Its provisions returned in the 20th Congress as House Bill 8123.

It imposes an individual wealth tax on the net value of taxable assets above PHP 1 billion, defined as the market value of real or personal, tangible or intangible assets wherever situated, less debts. It applies to resident citizens on assets from all sources at home and abroad, to citizens living abroad, including overseas contract workers, on assets in the Philippines, and to resident aliens on assets in the Philippines. The rates, from 1 January 2022, are 1% on wealth above PHP 1 billion, 2% above PHP 2 billion and 3% above PHP 3 billion. Spouses compute their tax separately, with unattributable assets split equally. All the revenue is earmarked: 60% for medical assistance and the Health Facilities Enhancement Program, and 40% for education, social protection, employment and housing for poor and near-poor households.

The explanatory note estimates that the tax would raise PHP 236.7 billion a year from the 50 richest Filipinos alone.

title: House Bill No. 4304: An Act imposing Solidarity Contribution on the most affluent Filipinos for the benefit of public health and climate change resiliency
by: Reps. Percival Cendaña, Jose Manuel Diokno, Dadah Kiram Ismula (Akbayan) and Kaka Bag-ao, with 25 co-authors
summary: Imposes a Solidarity Contribution on the net worth of Filipino citizens above PHP 300 million, at 1.5% rising to 3% above PHP 2.5 billion, with the revenue earmarked for health and climate resilience.
status: Pending with the Committee on Ways and Means since 8 September 2025; filed 3 September 2025, Twentieth Congress, First Regular Session. Twenty-five further members were entered as co-authors between 26 May and 9 November 2026 (House bill-tracking page, checked 12 November 2026).

links.label: House bill-tracking page: authors, committee referral and status
DZRH, 19 March 2026: report on the bill

overview:
The Solidarity Contribution Act is the Akbayan bill. It was filed on 3 September 2025 by Representatives Percival Cendaña, Chel Diokno and Dadah Kiram Ismula of Akbayan and by Kaka Bag-ao of Dinagat Islands, and referred to the Committee on Ways and Means on 8 September 2025. The House's tracking page shows it still pending there. The explanatory note says Akbayan drafted it together with Third World Network, the Freedom from Debt Coalition and the NAGKAISA labor coalition. Since 26 May 2026 the House Journal has entered 25 more members as co-authors, the last on 9 November 2026; the tracking page prints each by surname, mostly with initials, and the register records 24 of them whose identity is clear.

The tax falls on the net worth of a natural person who is a Filipino citizen, wherever the person lives. Assets are defined broadly: houses and real estate, shares and options, partnership and club interests, mutual fund certificates, deposits, securities, bonds, receivables, trusts, expected insurance benefits, annuities, intangible property, jewellery and any other property with value. Liabilities, such as loans and accounts payable, are deducted; unused credit lines are not. Net worth is taken on 31 December. The bill sets no other exemption.

It has the lowest threshold of the Philippine bills and eight marginal bands: nothing up to PHP 300 million, then 1.5% of the excess over PHP 300 million, PHP 3 million plus 1.75% over PHP 500 million, PHP 6.5 million plus 2% over PHP 700 million, PHP 12.5 million plus 2.25% over PHP 1 billion, PHP 19.25 million plus 2.5% over PHP 1.3 billion, PHP 31.75 million plus 2.75% over PHP 1.8 billion, and PHP 51 million plus 3% over PHP 2.5 billion. A return is due to the Bureau of Internal Revenue by 31 May; half the tax is paid on filing, 25% by 31 August and 25% by 30 November. The Bureau assesses and collects it with the powers it holds over income, estate and donor's tax, including fines, penalties and criminal charges, and the Secretary of Finance issues the rules. The contribution is part of internal revenue, inserted into the tax code as Title III-A.

The revenue is reserved by law for six uses: the Universal Health Care Act, other health spending including new hospitals, training medical students and hiring doctors for public hospitals, the People's Survival Fund and the Calamity and Quick Response Funds, research on climate adaptation, public health and disaster risk reduction, and immediate aid from local governments to people displaced by climate disasters.

The explanatory note argues from inequality. It says rising asset values are not taxed, that the estate tax is a flat 6% (down from 60% in 1950), and that the corporate income tax has fallen to 20%. It cites a PHP 200 billion yearly shortfall for universal health care priorities and PHP 673.30 billion of losses from tropical cyclones in 2011 to 2021. It gives no estimate of what the contribution would raise.

title: House Bill No. 8123: An Act imposing a 'Billionaire Wealth Tax' on individuals
by: Reps. Antonio Tinio, Sarah Jane Elago and Renee Louise Co (Makabayan bloc)
summary: Proposes an annual tax of 1% on wealth above 1 billion pesos, 2% above 2 billion and 3% above 3 billion on individual billionaires.
status: Pending with the Committee on Ways and Means since 3 March 2026; filed 26 February 2026, Twentieth Congress, First Regular Session (House bill-tracking page, checked 12 November 2026).

links.label: House bill-tracking page: authors, committee referral and status
House Bill 10253 (18th Congress), the first version of this bill

overview:
The Billionaire Wealth Tax Act was filed on 26 February 2026 by Representatives Antonio Tinio (ACT Teachers), Sarah Jane Elago (Gabriela Women's Party) and Renee Louise Co (Kabataan). It had its first reading on 3 March 2026 and went to the Committee on Ways and Means, where the House's tracking page still shows it. The tracking page lists no co-authors. The explanatory note says the bill was first filed by Bayan Muna, ACT Teachers, Gabriela and Kabataan members as House Bill 10253 in the 18th Congress.

The tax falls on individuals whose net taxable assets exceed PHP 1 billion: citizens whether resident or not, resident aliens, and non-resident aliens on assets in the Philippines. Net taxable assets are the fair market value of all real and personal, tangible and intangible assets wherever situated, less debts, at 31 December. Listed shares are valued at the closing price, real property at the higher of the BIR zonal value and the appraised value, and private companies at the last arm's-length transaction or, if none, the higher of book value and a capitalisation of earnings. The rates are 1% on wealth above PHP 1 billion, 2% above PHP 2 billion and 3% above PHP 3 billion, effective 1 January 2026. Married people compute their tax separately, with assets that cannot be attributed to one spouse split equally.

Every person above the threshold must file a sworn annual statement of all assets, held directly or through companies and trusts, at home and abroad, by 15 May of the following year; the burden of declaring accurately rests on the taxpayer and the government need not prove undeclared assets at first assessment. Quarterly instalments may be elected. Real-property tax can be credited against the tax up to 25% of the tax due, with no carry-over, assets are revalued every three years, and changes of more than 20% must be declared within 30 days. Arrangements whose main purpose is avoiding the tax are disregarded, and a 3% exit tax applies if a taxpayer loses Philippine citizenship or permanent residence. Within 180 days the Bureau of Internal Revenue must set up a Wealth-Tax Unit with lifestyle audits and access to financial records, and the Commissioner may join international transparency standards such as the OECD Common Reporting Standard. Wilful misdeclaration carries a penalty of at least 20% of the undeclared value, confiscation of concealed assets in cases of fraud and criminal charges.

All the revenue is earmarked: 60% for public health, towards a public health spending target of 5% of GDP, and 40% for education (20%), social protection and employment (15%) and housing (5%). The money must add to the regular appropriations, the Department of Budget and Management certifies this, the Commission on Audit audits it every year, and the department publishes collections and disbursements each quarter.

The explanatory note cites the IBON Foundation's estimate of at least PHP 508 billion a year from the country's 3,000 billionaires and PHP 289 billion from the 50 richest. It says billionaires are 0.0026% of the population.

title: House Bill No. 8860: An Act establishing a more progressive and targeted tax system by increasing income tax exemptions and imposing solidarity wealth tax and windfall profits tax (PATAS Act)
by: Rep. Raymond Democrito C. Mendoza (TUCP party-list)
summary: A tax-reform package that raises the income tax exemption to PHP 600,000, adds a windfall profits tax on oil, gas and electricity companies, and imposes an annual Solidarity Wealth Tax of 1% to 3% on net worth of PHP 1 billion and above.
status: Pending with the Committee on Ways and Means since 4 May 2026; filed 14 April 2026, Twentieth Congress, First Regular Session (House bill-tracking page, checked 12 November 2026).

links.label: House bill-tracking page: authors, committee referral and status

overview:
The PATAS Act (Patas na Ambag sa Tax para sa Angat-Sahod) was filed on 14 April 2026 by Representative Raymond Mendoza of the TUCP party-list. It was referred to the Committee on Ways and Means on 4 May 2026, where the House's tracking page still shows it. The bill has three parts, and only one is a wealth tax; the register lists it for that part.

The wealth tax is a new Section 27 of the tax code, the Solidarity Wealth Tax, an annual tax on every individual whose net worth is at least PHP 1 billion. Net worth is the fair market value of all real or personal, tangible or intangible assets wherever situated, owned directly or indirectly, less liabilities, at 31 December. Assets held through companies, partnerships, trusts or similar arrangements are attributed to the beneficial owner. The schedule is 1% on net worth from PHP 1 billion up to PHP 2 billion, 2% over PHP 2 billion up to PHP 3 billion and 3% over PHP 3 billion; the text does not say whether each rate applies only to the slice within its band. The return is due on 15 April of the following year. The Secretary of Finance, on the Commissioner of Internal Revenue's recommendation, sets uniform valuation standards, audit procedures and anti-avoidance rules. The bill does not earmark the revenue.

The other two parts are an income tax cut and a windfall tax. The income tax exemption rises to PHP 600,000 a year, with new brackets at 15% from PHP 600,000, 20% from PHP 850,000, 25% from PHP 1.5 million, 30% from PHP 3.4 million and 35% above PHP 13 million; the tax-exempt ceiling on 13th-month pay and other benefits rises from PHP 90,000 to PHP 250,000; and holiday, overtime, night-shift and hazard pay and service charges are exempt. The windfall profits tax covers oil, gas and petroleum companies and electric power generation, transmission and distribution, and taxes profit above the lower of the three-year average taxable income and a 12% rate of return, at 15% on profit up to 20% above that threshold, 25% from 20% to 50% above, and 35% beyond.

The explanatory note says the wealth tax offsets the income tax revenue loss. It cites 15 Filipino billionaires on the Forbes 2026 list with combined net worth of USD 44.5 billion, about PHP 2.49 trillion, the IBON Foundation's estimate that a wealth tax on 3,000 billionaires could raise at least PHP 500 billion a year, and a study by the UP Center for Integrative and Development Studies that calls a wealth tax feasible and not double taxation.

title: House Bill No. 9274: An Act imposing an 'Ultra-Wealth Tax' on individuals with net assets exceeding one billion pesos
by: Rep. Leila M. de Lima
summary: Imposes an annual Ultra-Wealth Tax of 1% on wealth above 1 billion pesos, 2% above 2 billion and 3% above 3 billion, with revenue for health, education, social protection and housing.
status: Pending with the Committee on Ways and Means since 20 May 2026; filed 18 May 2026, Twentieth Congress, First Regular Session (House bill-tracking page, checked 12 November 2026).

links.label: House bill-tracking page: authors, committee referral and status
House Bill 8123, the Billionaire Wealth Tax bill whose provisions this bill adopts

overview:
The Ultra-Wealth Tax Act is a bill by Representative Leila de Lima of the ML party-list, filed on 18 May 2026. It had its first reading on 20 May 2026 and went to the Committee on Ways and Means, where the House's tracking page still shows it; no co-authors are listed. Its explanatory note says similar bills had already been filed in the 20th Congress by Representatives Percival Cendaña, Chel Diokno, Dadah Ismula, Kaka Bag-ao, Antonio Tinio, Sarah Elago, Renee Co and Raymond Mendoza, and that this bill adopts several of their provisions.

The tax is the same as in House Bill 8123: an annual tax on individuals with net taxable assets above PHP 1 billion, at 1% on wealth above PHP 1 billion, 2% above PHP 2 billion and 3% above PHP 3 billion from 1 January 2026, covering citizens, resident aliens and non-resident aliens on Philippine assets. It repeats that bill's sworn self-assessment by 15 May with the burden on the taxpayer, the valuation rules, separate computation for spouses, the credit for real-property tax capped at 25% of the tax due, the three-year revaluation, the anti-avoidance rule with a 3% exit tax, the Wealth-Tax Unit in the Bureau of Internal Revenue, the cooperation with international transparency standards and the penalties (at least 20% of undeclared value, confiscation in cases of fraud, criminal charges). It also bars the revenue from replacing existing social-service appropriations, with the Department of Budget and Management certifying the levels and the Commission on Audit checking them each year.

What differs is the split of the revenue, all of which is earmarked. De Lima's bill gives 50% to public health, including hospital infrastructure and staffing, and 50% to social measures: education 20%, a local government support fund 15%, social protection and employment 10% and housing 5%. House Bill 8123 gives 60% to health and has no local government share.

The explanatory note gives no revenue estimate. It argues from the World Bank's 2022 finding that the Philippines ranked 15th of 63 countries for income inequality, from the growth of the fifty richest Filipinos' net worth from PHP 3.95 trillion in 2022 to PHP 4.44 trillion in 2023, and from the burden of consumption taxes on the poor.

by: Eduardo C. Tadem (UP Center for Integrative and Development Studies, Program on Alternative Development)
summary: Monograph that sets out the case for a Philippine wealth tax and traces the civil-society and labour campaign for it.

summary: IBON estimates that a tax of 1% on wealth above 1 billion pesos, 2% above 2 billion and 3% above 3 billion would raise at least 502 billion pesos a year from about 3,000 billionaires.

title: Varallisuusverolaki ja laki tuloverolain ja eräiden muiden verolakien muuttamisesta (Wealth Tax Act and amendment of the Income Tax Act; LA 81/2006 vp)
by: Kari Uotila and six other Left Alliance MPs
summary: Left Alliance initiative to bring back the repealed wealth tax at 0.8% above EUR 185,000 of taxable wealth, from 1 January 2007, alongside a social income deduction for benefit recipients.
status: Lakialoite tabled 27 September 2006; the Eduskunta's processing page shows the matter ended at second reading with the overall decision 'Hylätty' (rejected).
overview:
Initiative LA 81/2006 vp was signed on 27 September 2006 by Kari Uotila and six other Left Alliance MPs. It was a companion to the government's own tax bill HE 144/2006 vp and part of the party's alternative budget for 2007. It proposed to re-enact the wealth tax Finland had abolished from 2006, with the scale of the 2004 tax year: wealth tax would be paid on taxable wealth above EUR 185,000, at a marginal rate of 0.8%.

Two allowances would be more generous than in 2005: the deduction per child would be EUR 3,000 (it was EUR 2,000) and the deduction for a person's own home EUR 20,000 (it was EUR 10,000). The initiative says that, set this way, about thirty thousand of Finland's wealthiest taxpayers would pay. A company would pay 1%. The new Wealth Tax Act would take effect on 1 January 2007 and apply first to the 2007 assessment.

The same initiative paired the wealth tax with a new social income deduction for people on unemployment benefit, training allowance, sickness and similar benefits, on the argument that benefits are taxed harder than wages. The aim, in its words, is that the richest help pay for common needs while small benefits are freed from tax.

The Eduskunta's processing page shows the matter ended at second reading with the overall decision 'Hylätty' (rejected). The wealth tax was not restored.

title: Varallisuusverolaki (Wealth Tax Act; LA 84/2009 vp)
by: Pietari Jääskeläinen and three other Finns Party MPs
summary: Finns Party initiative to reinstate the wealth tax abolished from 2006, from 1 January 2010, estimating about EUR 150 million a year to fund basic social security.
status: Lakialoite tabled 25 September 2009; the Eduskunta's processing page shows the matter ended with the overall decision 'Rauennut' (lapsed) after committee stage.
overview:
Initiative LA 84/2009 vp was signed on 25 September 2009 by Pietari Jääskeläinen, Raimo Vistbacka, Pirkko Ruohonen-Lerner and Pertti Virtanen of the Finns Party. It contains a full draft Wealth Tax Act. The tax would take effect on 1 January 2010 and apply first to the 2010 assessment. The annual rates and the progressive scale would be set each year in a separate scale act.

The explanatory text recalls that the rate was 0.9% from 1989 to 2005 and was cut to 0.8% from 2005. In 2003 the tax brought in just under EUR 120 million from fewer than 40,000 taxpayers. It was abolished from the start of 2006, which the authors say benefited mainly about 30,000 of the best-off, and they estimate the state lost over EUR 600 million between 2006 and 2009.

With state borrowing heading towards nearly EUR 13 billion the next year, they argue that the tax should return. They estimate about EUR 150 million a year and want it used to raise the labour-market and income-support benefits that lost purchasing power for people made unemployed.

The Eduskunta's processing page shows the matter ended with the overall decision 'Rauennut' (lapsed) after committee stage. The wealth tax was not restored.

title: Varallisuusverolaki (Wealth Tax Act; LA 63/2010 vp)
by: Pietari Jääskeläinen and four other Finns Party MPs
summary: Finns Party initiative with a full draft Wealth Tax Act to restore the tax from 1 January 2011, estimating about EUR 150 million a year to fund basic social security.
status: Lakialoite tabled 17 September 2010; the Eduskunta's processing page shows the matter ended with the overall decision 'Rauennut' (lapsed) after committee stage.
overview:
Initiative LA 63/2010 vp was signed on 17 September 2010 by Pietari Jääskeläinen, Pertti Virtanen, Pentti Oinonen, Pirkko Ruohonen-Lerner and Raimo Vistbacka of the Finns Party. It repeats their 2009 initiative LA 84/2009, with the same explanatory text, and carries a full draft Wealth Tax Act that would take effect on 1 January 2011 and apply first to the 2011 assessment. Annual rates and the progressive scale would be set in a separate scale act.

The text recalls that the wealth tax rate was 0.9% from 1989 to 2005 and was cut to 0.8% from 2005. In 2003 it brought in just under EUR 120 million from fewer than 40,000 taxpayers. After abolition from 2006 the authors estimate the state lost over EUR 600 million in revenue.

They estimate that restoring it would bring in about EUR 150 million a year and propose to spend it on basic security for people out of work.

The Eduskunta's processing page shows the matter ended with the overall decision 'Rauennut' (lapsed) after committee stage. The wealth tax was not restored.

by: Kaj Turunen and other Finns Party MPs
summary: Finns Party initiative to restore the wealth tax at 0.8% a year on taxable assets above EUR 300,000 (companies 1%), estimating about EUR 135 million of revenue in 2013.
status: Lakialoite tabled 12 October 2012; the Eduskunta's processing page shows the matter ended at second reading with the overall decision 'Hylätty' (rejected).
overview:
Initiative LA 55/2012 vp, an Act on a wealth tax, was signed on 12 October 2012 by Kaj Turunen and 38 other Finns Party MPs. It proposes to restore the wealth tax with a single rate: 0.8% a year on taxable wealth above EUR 300,000 for people, estates and joint interests, and 1% for companies as before.

The authors say it is reasonable that the better-off carry more of society's costs. Counting wealth growth since 2005, they estimate revenue of about EUR 135 million in 2013. The Act would take effect on 1 January 2013 and apply first to the 2013 assessment.

It is among the best-supported wealth-tax bills in Finland, with nearly forty Finns Party MPs signing. The Eduskunta's processing page shows the matter ended at second reading with the overall decision 'Hylätty' (rejected); the committee's recommendation to reject was adopted without a roll call.

status: Lakialoite tabled 24 October 2014; the Eduskunta's processing page shows the matter ended with the overall decision 'Rauennut' (lapsed) after committee stage.

The authors say it is reasonable that the better-off carry more of society's costs. Counting wealth growth since 2005, they estimate revenue of about EUR 150 million in 2015. The Act would take effect on 1 January 2015 and apply first to the 2015 assessment.

title: Toimenpidealoite miljonääriveron käyttöönoton valmistelun aloittamisesta (motion to start preparing a millionaire tax; TPA 25/2022 vp)
by: Pia Lohikoski and other Left Alliance MPs
summary: Motion asking the government to prepare a millionaire tax of 0.5% on wealth above EUR 1 million (home excluded), estimated at over EUR 500 million a year.
status: Toimenpidealoite tabled 10 March 2022; the Eduskunta's processing page shows it as handled, stage 'Raukeaminen', overall decision 'Rauennut' (lapsed).
overview:
Motion for action TPA 25/2022 vp was tabled on 10 March 2022 by Pia Lohikoski and 11 other Left Alliance MPs. It asks the government to start preparing a 'millionaire tax' on wealth above EUR 1 million, excluding the home. At a rate of 0.5% the Parliament's information service estimated it would raise over EUR 500 million a year.

The motion cites Statistics Finland: the wealthiest tenth owned 49.6% of household net wealth in 2019, up from under 44% in 2009. It also cites ECB data that the richest 1% owned about 15% of net wealth in 2014.

It lists design lessons from the old tax: a tighter tax base including deposits, bonds and savings life insurance; equal treatment of companies and sole traders; and exemption for unproductive or public-interest assets such as protected forest and protected buildings.

The Eduskunta's processing page shows it as handled, stage 'Raukeaminen', overall decision 'Rauennut' (lapsed). A motion for action asks the government to act and is not itself a law.

title: Kansainvälinen minimivero varakkaimmille yksityishenkilöille (An international minimum tax on the wealthiest individuals)
by: Finnwatch
summary: Research article that sets out the details of Gabriel Zucman's G20 proposal for a minimum tax on the wealth of the richest individuals and why existing taxes leave billionaires lightly taxed.

title: Forslag til folketingsbeslutning om indførelse af en progressiv formueskat (B 70, 2021-22)
by: Sikandar Siddique, Uffe Elbæk and Susanne Zimmer (Frie Grønne)
summary: Motion that would require the government to introduce a bill by the end of 2022 for a progressive wealth tax from 1 January 2023: 1% on net wealth from DKK 3.5 million, rising to 20% from DKK 1 billion (thresholds doubled for couples).
status: 2. behandlet/forkastet (second reading, rejected 7 June 2022): 10 for (EL, FG, ALT), 86 against.
overview:
Motion B 70 was introduced on 20 January 2022 by Sikandar Siddique, Uffe Elbæk and Susanne Zimmer of Frie Grønne. It would instruct the government to bring a bill before the end of 2022 for a progressive wealth tax in force from 1 January 2023. Net wealth between DKK 3.5 million and 10 million would be taxed at 1%, DKK 10 million to 50 million at 2%, DKK 50 million to 100 million at 5%, DKK 100 million to 1 billion at 10%, and DKK 1 billion and above at 20%. The thresholds are doubled for married couples.

The base would be as wide as possible: owner-occupied homes, pension wealth (adjusted for deferred tax), financial assets, unlisted shares and cooperative housing, minus all loans including bank and student loans. The lowest threshold matches roughly the bottom of the richest tenth of Danes, which the Tax Ministry put at DKK 3.55 million.

The authors say the aim is to reduce wealth inequality. They note Denmark phased out its wealth tax in 1996 to 1997, when it was 1% of wealth above about DKK 1.6 million and raised about DKK 840 million.

The motion was rejected at second reading on 7 June 2022: 10 votes for (Enhedslisten, Frie Grønne, Alternativet) and 86 against.

title: Wealth Taxation and Wealth Accumulation: Theory and Evidence From Denmark
by: Katrine Jakobsen, Kristian Jakobsen, Henrik Kleven and Gabriel Zucman
summary: Uses Danish administrative wealth records and the sharp cut in the wealth tax from 1989 to show clear effects on reported wealth, larger for the very wealthy, and a sizable long-run elasticity of taxable wealth at the top.

title: Wetsvoorstel tot instelling van een belasting op de grote vermogens / Proposition de loi visant à introduire un impôt sur les grands patrimoines (DOC 54 0770/001)
by: Ahmed Laaouej and other PS members
summary: Proposes a wealth tax on net assets of EUR 1,250,000 or more at 0.40% to 1.50%, leaving out goods used exclusively for an economic activity and the taxpayer's own home.
status: Vervallen (lapsed) in the Chamber, declared 23 May 2019. Taken into consideration 15 January 2015; discussed in the Finance and Budget committee on 27 January 2015, 13 January 2016 and 23 February 2016; Court of Audit advice 10 April 2015. No vote is recorded (Chamber file read 12 November 2026).
overview:
The Parti Socialiste's bill would create a "belasting op de grote vermogens" on the net wealth of natural persons whose assets reach 1,250,000 euro on the last day of the tax period. Residents of Belgium are taxed on their worldwide assets and non-residents on their Belgian assets. The tax covers property, financial investments, cash, furniture, vehicles, yachts and jewels. Goods used exclusively for a professional activity and the home the taxpayer lives in are left out, and companies are not taxed.

The rates apply by slice: 0.40% on wealth up to 1,250,000 euro, 0.80% from there to 2,500,000 euro, 1.20% from there to 5,000,000 euro and 1.50% above that, with the slices indexed to the health index. A safety net caps the tax at half the difference between the taxpayer's wealth and 1,250,000 euro, so nobody ends up with less than someone just under the threshold. Taxpayers file a return, the Income Tax Code rules for assessment and collection apply, and the law would take effect from tax year 2016.

The authors say more than 70% of tax revenue still comes from labour income and household consumption, and that the bill is meant to make "dormant capital" contribute, not the middle class or small savers. The Court of Audit's advice of 10 April 2015 put the yield at between 727.72 million and 2,294.67 million euro depending on the assumptions, according to the PVDA-PTB bill that quotes it.

Ahmed Laaouej, Laurette Onkelinx, Stéphane Crusnière and Alain Mathot filed it on 13 January 2015. The Finance and Budget committee took it up with Vanessa Matz as rapporteur, but no vote is recorded and it lapsed at the end of the legislature. The PS filed the same text again in 2019 as DOC 55 0036.

title: Wetsvoorstel tot instelling van een belasting op de grote vermogens / Proposition de loi visant à introduire un impôt sur les grands patrimoines (DOC 55 0036/001)
by: Ahmed Laaouej and other PS members
summary: Proposes a wealth tax on net assets of EUR 1,250,000 or more at 0.40% to 1.50%, leaving out goods used exclusively for an economic activity and the taxpayer's own home.
status: Vervallen (lapsed) in the Chamber, declared 27 May 2024. Filed 9 July 2019 and taken into consideration 10 July 2019 in the Finance and Budget committee; no vote is recorded (Chamber file read 12 November 2026).
overview:
This is the Parti Socialiste's second attempt at the same bill: its explanatory note says it takes over the text of DOC 54 0770. It would tax the net wealth of natural persons who hold at least 1,250,000 euro on the last day of the tax period, residents on their worldwide assets and non-residents on their Belgian assets. Goods used exclusively for a professional activity and the taxpayer's own home are left out.

The tax is charged by slice: 0.40% on wealth up to 1,250,000 euro, 0.80% to 2,500,000 euro, 1.20% to 5,000,000 euro and 1.50% above that, with the slices indexed to the health index. A safety net caps the tax at half the amount by which wealth exceeds 1,250,000 euro, so that the tax never drops a taxpayer below the threshold. Taxpayers file a return and the Income Tax Code rules on assessment and collection apply. The effect date moves to tax year 2020.

The authors repeat that more than 70% of revenue comes from labour and consumption and that the aim is to make "dormant capital" pay, not the middle class, small savers or companies.

Ahmed Laaouej and seven other PS members (Hugues Bayet, Marc Goblet, Frédéric Daerden, Patrick Prévot, Christophe Lacroix, Malik Ben Achour and Sophie Thémont) filed it on 9 July 2019, in the extraordinary session that opened the 55th legislature. The Chamber page lists only the bill text, records no vote, and shows it lapsed on 27 May 2024. On 18 September 2019 the PVDA-PTB filed its own, higher-rate "miljonairstaks" (DOC 55 0397).

title: Wetsvoorstel tot instelling van een miljonairstaks / Proposition de loi créant une taxe sur les millionnaires (DOC 55 0397/001)
by: Marco Van Hees, Raoul Hedebouw, Peter Mertens and Steven De Vuyst (PVDA-PTB)
summary: Proposes an annual tax on wealth of EUR 1 million or more at 1% on the slice from EUR 1m to 2m, 2% from EUR 2m to 3m and 3% above EUR 3m.
status: Vervallen (lapsed) in the Chamber, declared 27 May 2024. Filed 18 September 2019 and taken into consideration 19 September 2019 in the Finance and Budget committee; no vote is recorded (Chamber file read 12 November 2026).
overview:
The PVDA-PTB's "miljonairstaks" is an annual tax on the net wealth of households worth 1 million euro or more. The rate is 1% on the slice from 1 to 2 million euro, 2% from 2 to 3 million and 3% above 3 million. A household is a single person or a couple (married or cohabiting) with their dependent minor children, and it is taxed if at least one member was a Belgian resident during the year; non-resident households are taxed on their Belgian assets. Wealth is valued on 1 January at market value, estimated by the household. Debts are deducted, except those on exempt assets, and the main home and the assets used in the household's main profession are each exempt up to 500,000 euro.

The tax would be self-declared: the return is due by 30 June and the tax by 30 September. The bill orders a special tax body and a "wealth cadastre" to check the returns, with no bank secrecy and with yearly data from banks, insurers, wealth managers and companies with registered shares. It would take effect on 1 January of the year after publication in the Belgian Official Gazette.

The authors apply the tax to the 2,134 billion euro of net household wealth at the end of 2014 (National Bank figures) and estimate a yield of more than 10 billion euro a year, noting that only part would reach the treasury. Almost 90% would come from the richest 1% of households and the tax would touch about 3% of households. They contrast this with the Court of Audit's 727 million to 2.3 billion euro for the PS bill of 2015, which has a higher threshold, lower rates and an uncapped exemption for the home.

Marco Van Hees, Raoul Hedebouw, Peter Mertens and Steven De Vuyst filed it on 18 September 2019. The party filed a new version in 2024 as DOC 56 0323, with a 5 million euro threshold.

title: Wetsvoorstel tot instelling van een miljonairstaks / Proposition de loi créant une taxe sur les millionnaires (DOC 56 0323/001)
by: Sofie Merckx, Kemal Bilmez, Peter Mertens, Roberto D'Amico, Raoul Hedebouw and Nadia Moscufo (PVDA-PTB)
summary: Proposes a tax on wealth of EUR 5 million or more at 2% on the slice from EUR 5m to 10m and 3% above EUR 10m, exempting the part below EUR 5m.
status: Pending (hangend) in the Chamber's Finance and Budget committee. The plenary rejected the urgency request on 17 October 2024, the day the bill was taken into consideration; committee discussion started on 12 November 2024 and resumed on 17 March, 22 September and 6 October 2026. No vote on the bill itself is recorded (Chamber file read 12 November 2026).
overview:
The PVDA-PTB's "miljonairstaks" taxes the net wealth of households above 5 million euro, which the authors say is about the richest 1%. The part below 5 million (indexed) is exempt. The rate is 2% on the slice from 5 to 10 million euro and 3% above 10 million. Everything counts: property, businesses and farms, shares, savings, jewels, art, vehicles and crypto-assets, less debts. Debts cannot make an asset negative, and debts on partly exempt assets, such as a family home, are only deductible for the taxed part.

Taxpayers value their assets at market value, with royal decrees for annuities, usufruct and similar rights. The tax is self-declared: the household returns the form by 30 June, works out the tax itself and pays by 30 September, and a "Large Fortunes" unit at the federal tax administration audits the biggest returns. It would start on 1 January of the year after the law is published.

The authors put the gross yield at 10.78 billion euro a year and the net at 8 billion, after allowing a 26% loss from avoidance, the figure the Federal Planning Bureau uses. They build on the Bureau's February 2024 method, the National Bank's total household net wealth of 2,852 billion euro and the researchers Apostel and O'Neill's spread of wealth, which uses the rich list. Almost all of the money, 99.7%, would come from the top 1%.

Sofie Merckx, Kemal Bilmez, Peter Mertens, Roberto D'Amico, Raoul Hedebouw and Nadia Moscufo tabled it on 8 October 2024. It takes over, with changes, the PTB-PVDA bill DOC 55 0397 of the previous legislature. Of the three Belgian bills it has the highest rates and the highest yield estimate.

title: Wetsvoorstel tot instelling van een belasting op de grote vermogens / Proposition de loi visant à introduire un impôt sur les grands patrimoines (DOC 56 0901/001)
by: Paul Magnette and nine other PS members
summary: Proposes a tax of 1% on the slices of wealth between EUR 5 million and EUR 100 million and 2% on the slices above EUR 100 million.
status: Pending (hangend) in the Chamber's Finance and Budget committee. The plenary rejected the urgency request on 22 May 2025, the day the bill was taken into consideration. The committee discussed it on 17 March, 22 September and 6 October 2026, and its calendar records the bill as rejected (verworpen) on 6 October 2026. No plenary vote on the bill is recorded (Chamber file read 12 November 2026).
overview:
The Parti Socialiste's bill puts a tax on large fortunes: 1% on the slices of wealth between 5 and 100 million euro and 2% on the slices above 100 million. Only natural persons holding at least 5 million euro in their own name pay. Residents are taxed on their worldwide wealth, subject to tax treaties, and non-residents on what they hold in Belgium. A safety rule stops the tax exceeding half the difference between total wealth and 5 million euro, so a person just above the threshold does not pay far more than one just below.

Assets are valued under the inheritance-tax rules, and trusts and fiducies are counted in the wealth of the founder or beneficiary. The tax is assessed through the income-tax machinery, and the bill sets assessment year 2026 as the start. It is built to work alongside the tax on securities accounts, which is credited so that the same wealth is not taxed twice. The authors estimate it could raise up to 2.5 billion euro.

The explanatory text frames it as a shift of taxation from labour to capital that would pay for lower taxes on low and middle wages and support small businesses. It cites the EU Tax Observatory (a 2% tax on European billionaires would yield 42.3 billion euro), Brazil's G20 proposal of a 2% minimum tax on billionaires, Spain's 2022 solidarity tax and the French proposal for a 2% tax above 100 million euro.

Paul Magnette and nine other PS members of the Chamber tabled it on 15 May 2025: Sophie Thémont, Frédéric Daerden, Caroline Désir, Hugues Bayet, Ludivine Dedonder, Khalil Aouasti, Lydia Mutyebele Ngoi, Christophe Lacroix and Pierre-Yves Dermagne. Unlike the PVDA-PTB bill, it keeps the rate at 1% all the way from 5 to 100 million euro.

title: Wetsvoorstel met het oog op het invoeren van een vermogensbelasting / Proposition de loi visant à instaurer une taxe sur le patrimoine (DOC 56 1298/001)
by: Dieter Vanbesien, Sarah Schlitz and seven other Ecolo-Groen members
summary: Introduces an annual tax on net wealth above EUR 2.5 million so that the financial burden of current social challenges is carried by the richest.
status: Pending (hangend) in the Chamber's Finance and Budget committee. It was taken into consideration on 22 January 2026; committee discussion started on 24 March 2026 and continued on 22 September and 6 October 2026. No vote is recorded (Chamber file read 12 November 2026).
overview:
The Ecolo-Groen bill creates an annual tax on net wealth above 2.5 million euro, the lowest threshold of the three Belgian bills. The first 2.5 million euro is taxed at 0%, then 0.4% on the slice from 2.5 to 5 million, 0.8% from 5 to 10 million and 1.2% above 10 million. It is written into the 1992 income-tax code as a new Title I/1 and covers real estate, financial instruments and business assets, after deducting the debts taken on to buy or keep them.

The valuation copies the tax on securities accounts. Real estate counts at its last sale value, indexed to the property price index. Financial instruments count at their average value on four reference dates (31 December, 31 March, 30 June and 30 September), and the taxpayer estimates assets that have no market price, with evidence. Business assets count at cost less the depreciation allowed for income tax. Belgian intermediaries send the taxpayer a yearly overview, and the securities-account tax paid is deducted from the new tax. Failing to file or pay is fined 10% to 200% of the tax.

The explanatory text says the wealthiest 1% own as much as the poorest 75%, that about 70% of wealth comes from inheritance, up from 45% in the 1970s, and that the top 1% by income pay lower average tax rates than any other group. It asks for the contribution to help finance lower taxes on labour. The bill gives no revenue estimate.

Dieter Vanbesien and Sarah Schlitz tabled it on 15 January 2026 with seven other Ecolo-Groen members: Staf Aerts, Meyrem Almaci, Rajae Maouane, Matti Vandemaele, Stefaan Van Hecke, Jeroen Van Lysebettens and Claire Hugon (listed as an author on the Chamber's file). Vanbesien is one of the committee's rapporteurs.

title: Studie over de belasting op grote vermogens (Study of the tax on large fortunes; DULBEA Policy Report 23.03)
by: Thérèse Bastin, Benoît Bayenet, Ilan Tojerow and Magali Verdonck (DULBEA, Université libre de Bruxelles), for the Federal Planning Bureau
summary: Defines the net wealth base, reviews how net wealth taxes work abroad and how wealth is taxed in Belgium, and assesses the behavioural effects and risks of a Belgian net wealth tax.

title: A one-off wealth tax for Belgium: Revenue potential, distributional impact, and environmental effects
by: Arthur Apostel and Daniel W. O'Neill
summary: Combines survey data with a Pareto model of the top tail to estimate the revenue, distributional and emissions effects of three one-off wealth tax designs for Belgium, finding the revenue larger than advocates estimated but inequality little changed.

title: 'Tax the rich'. Hoe denken Belgen over een vermogensbelasting?
by: Ellen Roelandts (KU Leuven), Samenleving & Politiek
summary: Uses the Belgian National Election Study 1999-2019 to show broad and stable public support for taxing large fortunes, including two in three for a tax on wealth above EUR 1 million in 2019.

title: PB 35 – Pajak Kekayaan: Menakar Potensi dan Peluang Implementasi di Indonesia (Policy Brief)
by: The PRAKARSA (Eka Afrina Djamhari, Irvan Tengku Harja, Rizky Deco Praha, Victoria Fanggidae, Herni Ramdlaningrum)
summary: Compares four wealth tax models and concludes that an annual progressive rate of 1% to 2% on high-net-worth individuals above IDR 144 billion is the most likely to be applied in Indonesia, with a one-off levy estimated at IDR 54 to 155.3 trillion.

title: PB 42 – Pajak Kekayaan untuk Mengatasi Distribusi Beban Pajak yang Asimetris (Policy Brief)
by: The PRAKARSA (Herni Ramdlaningrum, Eka Afrina Djamhari, Irvan Tengku Harja, Rizky Deco Praha, Victoria Fanggidae)
summary: Argues that Indonesia, the Philippines and Vietnam should adopt a wealth tax on high-net-worth individuals and estimates its potential revenue at US$8.18 billion in Indonesia, US$2.28 billion in the Philippines and US$3.09 billion in Vietnam.

title: Adjournment Motion: Taxation for a Dynamic and Fair 21st Century Economy
by: Jamus Lim (Workers' Party, Sengkang)
status: Adjournment motion debated at the sitting of 1 November 2021 (Question proposed); the Second Minister for Finance replied; the Official Report records no vote on the proposal. It is a debate on the motion for the House to adjourn, not a bill, and ended with the sitting.
summary: Proposes an annual tax of 0.5% on net wealth above S$10 million, 1% above S$50 million and 2% above S$1 billion, paid into a special-purpose foundation.

links.label: Reply by the Second Minister for Finance, Indranee Rajah (Ministry of Finance)

overview:
This is a debate, not a bill. On 1 November 2021 Jamus Lim, a Workers' Party member for Sengkang, used an adjournment motion at the end of the sitting to argue for a tax on wealth. His speech, "Taxation for a Dynamic and Fair 21st Century Economy", proposes a net wealth tax of 0.5% on wealth above S$10 million, 1% above S$50 million and 2% above S$1 billion.

Lim suggested the revenue could go to a special-purpose foundation required to spend its whole endowment over time on Government-approved uses that fit national priorities. He argued that returns on large fortunes typically exceed these rates, so the very rich should not expect their principal to fall. He answered the competitiveness worry by pointing to political stability in Hong Kong and to Switzerland, where the canton of Zürich applies wealth taxes starting at CHF 77,000 for singles, and said wealth taxes would diversify the Government's revenue and help manage the effects of rising inequality.

The Second Minister for Finance, Indranee Rajah, replied the same evening. She said Singapore already has one of the most progressive systems of taxes and transfers in the world, built on a competitive, fair and sustainable tax system. She gave taxes as about 13% of GDP, against an OECD average of 34%, and said the Government is continuously reviewing the tax system.

An adjournment motion ends the sitting without a vote, and the Official Report records none. No wealth tax followed. The Official Report of the sitting and the Minister's reply were read for this page.

title: ร่างพระราชบัญญัติภาษีความมั่งคั่ง พ.ศ. .... (Draft Wealth Tax Act)
by: Sirikanya Tansakun, Member of the House of Representatives, and colleagues
status: Prime Minister did not certify it (the Section 77 hearing page shows its status as not certified); a money bill proposed by members of the House, put to public hearing from 2 October to 3 November 2023. Without that certification the bill could not go on to the House; I found no later action.
summary: A new law introducing a wealth tax on Thai individuals with net wealth of at least 300 million baht, collected by the Revenue Department, with an asset and liability register, rates of up to 0.5% set by Royal Decree, assessment and penalties.

links.label: Draft Wealth Tax Act, as put to the Section 77 hearing (PDF, scanned)

overview:
The Draft Wealth Tax Act was proposed by Sirikanya Tansakun, a member of the House of Representatives, and colleagues. It is a money bill, and the House's hearing page lists its status as "Prime Minister did not certify", which stopped it from going on to the House.

The bill would set up a yearly tax on Thai individuals whose net wealth, assets less debts, was at least an amount fixed by Royal Decree and in no case below 300 million baht on 1 January. Rates are also fixed by Royal Decree, as a single rate or several rates by net wealth, and may not exceed 0.5%. The Revenue Department would collect it and the money would go to state revenue. Taxpayers would report their assets and debts to a register, valued under the Minister's rules or at market price where there are none. The bill also covers assessment, payment by instalments, a surcharge of 1% a month on late payment, fines, and prison of up to seven years and a fine of up to one million baht for evasion. A Royal Decree could suspend the tax for a single year.

The House ran a public hearing under Section 77 of the Constitution from 2 October to 3 November 2023. The hearing page shows 2,835 views and 28 participants, with 92.86% in favour. The hearing report counts 798 visitors and 32 people who commented. The bill's explanatory note says Thailand has a high concentration of wealth while tax is raised mainly on consumption and income, and that the state needs more revenue for economic and social programmes. Nothing further is recorded on the bill. The bill text is a scanned PDF and was read through OCR.

title: Wealth Tax Policy Note
by: Tayla Forward for Tax Justice Aotearoa
summary: A 32-page policy note for Tax Justice Aotearoa on the case for and design of a wealth tax in New Zealand, set against the Labour government's 2023 work on one.

title: Eine Vermögenssteuer als Antwort auf extreme Ungleichheit in Österreich
by: Ines Heck, Jakob Kapeller and Rafael Wildauer (A&W Blog, Arbeiterkammer Wien)
summary: Models an annual wealth tax with a 1-2-3-4 tariff (1% from EUR 1 million up to 4% from EUR 1 billion) that it puts at EUR 7.7 to 11.2 billion a year on estimated data and about 4% of households, and a steeper Piketty-style schedule.

title: Studie: Daň ze superbohatství
by: Miroslav Palanský, for the Strana zelených (Green Party)
summary: Models a Spanish-style tax on net wealth in Czechia with a 3.5% rate above CZK 111 million, which it estimates would hit about 4,200 people and raise roughly CZK 58 billion a year, plus progressive variants.

title: Wealth Tax as a Tool to Increase Tax Revenues in Polycrisis Times
by: Michal Radvan and Taisiia Chepys (Masaryk University), Studia Iuridica Lublinensia
summary: Tests whether a wealth tax could help Czech public finances in a polycrisis by comparing the wealth taxes of European countries and the Czech property taxes, and discusses how one would have to be designed (national, natural persons only, administrative costs).

title: Propunere legislativă pentru instituirea impozitului anual asupra averii (L361/2010)
by: Mugurel Surupăceanu (PSD)
summary: Legislative proposal to introduce an annual tax on wealth, tabled by a PSD deputy.
status: Rejected by the Senate on 11 October 2010 (13 for, 56 against, 20 abstentions) and finally by the Chamber of Deputies on 5 March 2013 (254 to reject, 28 against, 6 abstentions), as the Senate register shows
overview:
This legislative proposal, L361/2010 in the Senate (PLx 580/2010 in the Chamber of Deputies), was put forward by PSD deputy Mugurel Surupăceanu and presented to the Chamber's bureau on 16 March 2010. It would have created an annual wealth tax on individuals. Residents would owe it on assets held at home and abroad, and non-residents on assets in Romania, once their cumulative value passes EUR 500,000. The rate is 0.5% on the value above EUR 500,000, after deductions for debts on the assets and costs paid.

The bill counts only assets worth over EUR 1,000 each, exempts items such as financial investments, life insurance, copyright income, annuities, capitalised private pensions and agricultural machinery, and taxes married couples under community property together. People above the threshold would self-assess and file a declaration by 30 June of the following year, and failing to declare is treated as tax evasion. The explanatory memorandum argues for new revenue as the 2009 downturn pushed the budget deficit to 7.3% of GDP, and cites France and Norway as countries with wealth taxes.

The Legislative Council gave a favourable opinion, but the Government and the Senate's legal, human-rights and budget committees were negative. The Senate rejected it on 11 October 2010 (13 for, 56 against, 20 abstentions). The Chamber of Deputies, which had the final say, sent it back to committee several times in 2012 and rejected it on 5 March 2013 (254 to reject, 28 against, 6 abstentions), which ended the procedure.

title: Legea impozitării marilor afaceri și averi (L299/2025, PL-x 378/2025)
by: Liviu-Iulian Fodoca (senator, unaffiliated), Dumitrița Albu, Dumitru Coarnă, Andrei Csillag and Gheorghe-Petru Pîclișan (deputies, unaffiliated) and Călin-Florin Groza (deputy, PSD)
summary: Fiscal Code amendments whose explanatory memorandum introduces a Title on the tax on large fortunes: an annual 'solidarity tax' of 1%, 2% or 3% on the declared wealth of individuals above EUR 10 million, with higher rates at higher tiers, alongside rates on the income of very large taxpayers.
status: Rejected by the Senate, the first chamber notified, on 6 October 2025 (87 for rejection, 35 against, 2 abstentions) and sent on 13 October 2025 to the Chamber of Deputies, which is the deciding chamber. The Government's view was negative (30 October 2025), and on 10 March 2026 the Chamber's budget and industries committees filed reports of rejection. The Chamber page shows the stage as report filed, to go on the plenary agenda, and no Chamber vote (read 12 November 2026).

links.label: Chamber of Deputies, PL-x 378/2025 (decision stage, committee reports)

overview:
This is a private members' package by six Romanian parliamentarians, a "national solidarity law" that amends the Fiscal Code (Law 227/2015) and the offshore petroleum law (256/2018). Its wealth-tax part adds a new Title XI, "Tax on large fortunes". Individuals whose declared wealth at 31 December exceeds EUR 10 million pay 1% a year on all of it, 2% above EUR 100 million and 3% above EUR 1 billion. The rate applies to the whole declared wealth, and nobody under EUR 10 million pays. Those above the threshold file an annual wealth declaration by 25 March.

The same text taxes the turnover of large companies at 1% above EUR 10 million, 2% above EUR 100 million and 3% above EUR 1 billion, with 5% for companies extracting, refining or selling petroleum products, and taxes the part of pensions above 11 minimum gross wages at 90%. The memorandum says the aim is to raise revenue to pay for larger tax deductions for people with dependants, and to support births.

The initiators are Senator Liviu-Iulian Fodoca and Deputies Dumitrița Albu, Dumitru Coarnă, Andrei Csillag, Gheorghe-Petru Pîclișan and Călin-Florin Groza of the PSD. All six are in the register. The Senate registered the bill on 25 June 2025 and rejected it on 6 October 2025. The Chamber's page names the Chamber of Deputies as the deciding chamber, so the Senate's rejection does not end the bill, which stays pending there. Its committees recommended rejection on 10 March 2026 and no plenary vote has been held.

title: Servet Vergisi ve Temel Gelir Güvencesi Kanun Teklifi (2/2613)
by: Perihan Koca (DEM Parti, Mersin)
summary: Bill for an annual wealth tax on the real estate, luxury movables, bank deposits and other financial assets of individuals and companies worth TL 40 million or more (2% from TL 40 million, 3.5% from TL 100 million, 5% from TL 250 million, 7.5% from TL 500 million, 10% from TL 750 million), to fund a basic income guarantee for households below the hunger line.
status: Still in committee. The TBMM bill page gives the status 'KOMİSYONDA' (in committee); the bill went to the Plan and Budget Committee (lead) and the Health, Family, Labour and Social Affairs Committee on 17 October 2024. Perihan Koca, who dated it 15 October 2024 and filed it on 16 October 2024, is the only signer. No committee report or later action appears on the page (read on 12 November 2026).

links.label: Bill page with status, committees and signers (TBMM)
Bill text and general justification (TBMM, PDF)

overview:
Perihan Koca, a DEM Party member for Mersin, tabled this bill in the 28th term of the Grand National Assembly. She dated it 15 October 2024 and the Speaker's Office received it on 16 October 2024 as proposal 2/2613. She is the only signer. On 17 October 2024 it went to the Plan and Budget Committee as the lead committee and to the Health, Family, Labour and Social Affairs Committee. The assembly's bill page gives its status as "in committee", with no report or later step recorded.

The bill sets an annual wealth tax on natural and legal persons. The base is the combined value of their real estate, luxury movables, bank deposits and other financial assets. Article 1 sets five rates: 2% on holdings of TL 40 million to 99.99 million, 3.5% from TL 100 million, 5% from TL 250 million, 7.5% from TL 500 million and 10% from TL 750 million upward. The wording of the top step refers to deposits only; the other steps refer to all the assets above.

The revenue is ring-fenced. Article 2 makes the tax pay for basic income and creates a Basic Income Guarantee Fund when the law enters into force. Article 3 pays a monthly basic income to at least one member of each household with income below the hunger line that the statistics institute (TÜİK) calculates, women first, and never less than the monthly minimum wage. The central government finances the programme and runs it together with local authorities. The law takes effect on publication.

The general justification argues that about 70% of Turkey's tax revenue comes from indirect taxes and 30% from direct taxes, against direct taxes of about 65% in OECD countries. It cites Credit Suisse and UBS data that the richest 1% own 37% of the country's wealth, the highest share in Europe, and ranks Turkey second in Europe for the shares of the richest 5% and 10% and third on the Gini coefficient of wealth. It rests the case on article 73 of the Constitution, which requires equal tax from equal ability to pay and different tax from different ability, and calls taxing high wealth to give the poor extra income and jobs a first step.

title: Proposition de loi n° 246 visant à mettre en place une contribution exceptionnelle sur le patrimoine des contribuables les plus riches pour financer la transition écologique
by: Nicolas Sansu, André Chassaigne and the Gauche démocrate et républicaine group
status: Registered at the Assemblée nationale on 17 September 2024 and referred to the commission des finances. The Assemblée's text page and legislative dossier (read 12 November 2026) show only the filing and the referral: no committee examination, report or floor debate.
summary: A three-year exceptional levy on the net wealth of the richest taxpayers (2% from EUR 5 million, 6% from EUR 100 million, 10% above EUR 1 billion), to finance the ecological transition.

links.label: Text page, proposition de loi n° 246 (Assemblée nationale)

overview:
Proposition de loi n° 246 sets up a "contribution exceptionnelle sur les hauts patrimoines" to pay for the ecological transition. It is levied on the net wealth, on 1 January, of people tax-resident in France and of their minor children: all property, rights and securities, valued under the inheritance-tax rules. Business assets are included, because the levy is temporary; the only assets left out are those already covered by the real-estate wealth tax (IFI). The rates are 2% on the slice between 5 and 100 million euro, 6% between 100 million and 1 billion euro and 10% above 1 billion euro.

The explanatory memorandum says the levy would run for three years, and article 1 applies it until 31 December 2026. Its argument is that the transition needs public investment (55 to 85 billion euro a year according to I4CE, at least 66 billion euro according to the Pisani-Ferry and Mahfouz report), that at least half of it must come from public money, and that the cost must fall on the best off. It cites the Pisani-Ferry and Mahfouz estimate that a 5% levy over 30 years on the richest 10% of households would raise 150 billion euro. The text gives no revenue figure of its own.

Article 2 asks the government for a report within a year on a European version, since the authors say a levy of this kind should be set up at EU level to avoid tax competition. This follows the November 2023 information report on wealth taxation by the deputies Jean-Paul Mattei and Nicolas Sansu, which proposed exceptional, explicitly temporary European levies.

Nicolas Sansu, André Chassaigne and 15 other deputies of the Gauche démocrate et républicaine group tabled it on 17 September 2024. It differs from the "taxe Zucman" (n° 768), a permanent 2% floor on the richest households' wealth that the Assemblée passed in February 2025: this is a temporary levy with a top rate of 10% on billionaires.

title: Proposition de loi n° 359 instaurant un impôt de solidarité sur la fortune climatique
by: Eva Sas and the Écologiste group
status: Registered at the Assemblée nationale on 18 October 2022 and referred to the commission des finances; the text shows no later stage (16th legislature)
summary: Restores an annual solidarity wealth tax (ISF) from EUR 1.3 million of net assets with a climate bonus-malus that raises or lowers the bill by the carbon footprint of the holdings.

links.label: Text of proposition de loi no. 359 (PDF, Assemblée nationale)

overview:
Proposition de loi no. 359 brings back the annual wealth tax (ISF) as it stood on 31 December 2017, with changes, and adds a climate adjustment. The tax applies to households whose net assets exceed 1.3 million euro. The scale is 0 below 800,000 euro, 0.5% from 800,000 to 1.3 million euro, 1% from 1.3 to 8 million euro, 2% from 8 million to 1 billion euro and 3% above 1 billion euro. Professional assets are counted after an exemption of 2 million euro, works of art and intellectual-property rights are exempt only when worth under 250,000 euro, the principal home gets a flat abatement of 500,000 euro instead of 30%, private jets and large yachts are added to the base, and the cap that limits the tax to 75% of income is removed. Article 3 repeals the IFI.

The climate part adjusts the tax: homes in energy classes A and B by 0.5, classes C and D by 1, and classes E, F and G by 1.5. Until the end of 2023, financial holdings that meet one of six EU environmental objectives and do not fund nuclear or gas projects get a factor of 0.75, and all others 1.3. From 1 January 2024 the factor would follow a carbon score, which article 2 makes compulsory for portfolio managers from 2024.

The explanatory memorandum says the ISF raised 4.23 billion euro in 2017 and the IFI 1.67 billion euro in 2021, a gap of more than 2.6 billion euro a year, and that 77% of French people want the ISF back (Ifop). It also cites I4CE: 13 to 17 billion euro a year is missing to meet the national low-carbon strategy. The text gives no revenue figure of its own.

Eva Sas and members of the Écologiste group filed it on 18 October 2022. It was referred to the finance committee and the Assemblée's text shows no later stage in the 16th legislature.

title: Proposition de loi n° 648 visant à établir un impôt sur la très grande fortune
by: Marietta Karamanli, Boris Vallaud and the Socialistes et apparentés group
status: Registered at the Assemblée nationale on 15 December 2022 and referred to the commission des finances; the text shows no later stage (16th legislature)

links.label: Text of proposition de loi no. 648 (PDF, Assemblée nationale)

overview:
Proposition de loi no. 648 would turn the real-estate wealth tax (IFI) into an "impôt sur la très grande fortune" on all net wealth, at home and abroad, of people tax-resident in France. Assets are valued at market value and there are no exemptions, not even for the tool of work. The marginal rates are 1% from 20 to 50 million euro, 2% from 50 to 100 million, 3% from 100 to 250 million, 4% from 250 to 500 million, 5% from 500 million to 1 billion, 6% from 1 to 5 billion, 7% from 5 to 10 billion and 8% above 10 billion euro. Couples and cohabiting partners are taxed together, and the tax administration would send a pre-filled wealth return for the taxpayer to correct.

The explanatory memorandum says about 25,000 taxpayers, 0.05% of the population, would pay, and that the tax would raise about 25 billion euro a year, 1% of GDP, after allowing a 15% loss to avoidance. It says the 109 billionaires in the Challenges ranking own 792 billion euro, so the figure is cautious. It adds that the 370 largest French fortunes pay little income tax because they receive income through holding companies, and suggests that a person who leaves France with more than 20 million euro stay liable for a number of years. The loss of revenue would be offset by a tobacco levy (article 2).

Marietta Karamanli, Boris Vallaud and other deputies of the Socialistes et apparentés group filed it on 15 December 2022. It was referred to the finance committee and the Assemblée's text shows no later stage in the 16th legislature.

overview:
Early Day Motion 420 was tabled by Labour MP Richard Burgon on 10 September 2021 in the 2021-22 session. It calls on the Government to introduce a wealth tax as a progressive alternative to raising taxes on working people. It notes that almost a quarter of household wealth is held by the richest 1%, that UK billionaires' wealth rose by £106 billion since the start of the pandemic, and that the UK Wealth Commission's December 2020 report concluded a wealth tax would be preferable to raising income taxes. It also rejects the Chancellor's July 2020 remark that there would never be a time for a wealth tax.

It was signed by 43 Members, mostly Labour, plus Scottish National Party, Green, Liberal Democrat, SDLP, Alba and independent members, including John McDonnell, Jeremy Corbyn, Caroline Lucas and Diane Abbott. The first signatures came on the day it was tabled and the last on 28 February 2022. It has no amendments.

An early day motion is a non-binding statement: signing it is not a vote and it creates no tax. It lapsed with the session, but it is a dated record of cross-party support for a wealth tax in the Commons.

Early Day Motion 1909 was tabled on 15 September 2025 by Green Party MP Carla Denyer in the 2024-26 session. It says the UK should be alarmed by wealth inequality, with the top 1% owning as much household wealth as the bottom 50%, and that the tax system taxes income more than wealth.
