overview:
Stefania Prezioso Batou (Ensemble à Gauche) tabled motion 20.3335 on 6 May 2020. It instructs the Federal Council to submit a draft law for a time-limited federal solidarity tax on wealth from 2021, for three years, at 1% of wealth above 2 million francs, to help pay for the Covid-19 measures and the economic and social crisis.

The reasoning uses Federal Tax Administration figures for 2016: 128,010 taxpayers had net wealth over 2 million francs, together about 1,002 billion francs of it, so the 1% tax would raise about 10 billion francs a year. The author says the crisis hits the lowest-paid and front-line workers, mostly women, and should not be financed through earned income.

The Federal Council recommended rejection for the reasons it gave on the other Covid wealth-tax motions: a constitutional basis is missing, and a higher wealth tax would cut declared wealth through emigration and avoidance. It added that a tax starting in 2021 would have to be introduced retroactively, which would clash with legal certainty and the protection of legitimate expectations.

The National Council rejected the motion on 15 March 2022 by 127 votes to 66.

title: Initiative cantonale IN 185: Pour une contribution temporaire de solidarité sur les grandes fortunes
by: Initiative committee (Geneva)
status: Refused by the Grand Conseil on 26 January 2023 (57 no, 37 yes, 2 abstentions); the principle of a counter-proposal was refused 62 to 33. Rejected by Geneva voters on 18 June 2023: 47,369 yes, 58,170 no (55.1% no), on a turnout of 40.1% (110,872 voting cards from 276,401 eligible voters), per the Conseil d'État order of 21 June 2023.
summary: A ten-year solidarity contribution of 2.5 per mille on the part of net wealth above CHF 3 million, with higher social deductions.

links.label: Initiative text and explanatory memorandum, IN 185 (Grand Conseil)
Conseil d'État order with the result of the 18 June 2023 vote (Feuille d'avis officielle, 23 June 2023)

overview:
Geneva's initiative IN 185 would have added a ten-year "contribution de solidarité" to the cantonal wealth tax. The part of a taxpayer's wealth above 3 million francs would be charged 2.5 per mille, the same for married couples, which the initiators put at 4.5 to 5 per mille once the communal and cantonal additional centimes are added. The extra tax would end ten years after it takes effect. To shield smaller owners, the initiative also raised the social deductions to 250,000 francs for a single person, 500,000 for couples and 125,000 per dependent, raised the cap on the business-asset deduction to 1.5 million francs, and made the "tax shield" (the 60% ceiling on wealth and income taxes combined) count a net return on wealth of at least 2%.

The initiators say wealth above 3 million francs in Geneva tripled from 26 to 69 billion francs between 2011 and 2018 and now makes up 71% of declared wealth, a record in Switzerland. They expected about 350 million francs a year for the canton and 85 million for the communes, 35 million of it for the City of Geneva, to fund health, training, social policy and the ecological transition.

The initiative succeeded in March 2022 (the Conseil d'État noted this on 11 March 2022). The Grand Conseil refused it on 26 January 2023 and also refused to draw up a counter-proposal. On 18 June 2023 Geneva voters rejected it, 47,369 yes to 58,170 no.

title: Toward a Wealth Tax in Egypt
by: Nader Osama, Alternative Policy Solutions (American University in Cairo)
summary: Policy paper proposing a progressive comprehensive wealth tax from 1% on wealth over US$1 million to 5% over US$1 billion, estimated to raise about LE28 billion a year, with reform of the real estate tax and anti-evasion measures.

title: A Progressive Tax System to Fund a Fair Future: The Case for a Wealth Tax in Tanzania
by: Balozi Morwa Mollel, Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung Tanzania
summary: FES analysis of inequality and the taxation of the rich in Tanzania, concluding that the tax system is regressive and recommending wealth taxation as part of a more progressive system.

title: Оподаткування багатства в Україні: тест на солідарність (Wealth taxation in Ukraine: a test of solidarity)
by: Kostiantyn Shvabii, GROWFORD Institute
summary: Research piece arguing that introducing a wealth tax, as a temporary post-pandemic measure, is a test of solidarity for Ukraine's richest and of capacity for its political leaders.

title: European citizens' initiative: Taxing great wealth to finance the ecological and social transition
by: Citizens' initiative organisers (campaign site tax-the-rich.eu)
summary: Calls on the European Commission to establish a European tax on great wealth that would feed the Union's own resources and pay for the ecological and social transition and development cooperation.
status: Registered 11 July 2023; signature collection ran from 9 October 2023 to 9 October 2024 and is listed as unsuccessful on 29 October 2024, with 357,155 signatures reported by the organisers against the 1 million needed
overview:
This is a European citizens' initiative, a petition to the European Commission rather than a bill, titled "Taxing great wealth to finance the ecological and social transition". It asks the Commission to propose a European tax on great wealth. The tax would feed the Union's own resources and pay for the ecological and social transition and for development cooperation, cofunded by the Member States, to combat climate change and inequality. The organisers' campaign site is tax-the-rich.eu. The initiative page gives no rates or threshold.

The Commission registered it on 11 July 2023. Signature collection ran from 9 October 2023 to 9 October 2024. An initiative needs one million signatures from EU citizens, with minimum numbers in at least seven member states. The register lists it as an unsuccessful collection on 29 October 2024, with 357,155 signatures reported by the organisers and not verified by national authorities.

Three countries reached their national minimum: France with 111,106 signatures (199% of its minimum), Germany with 110,205 (163%) and Denmark with 10,473 (106%). Belgium reached 94%, Spain 71%, Slovakia 67% and Italy 63%. The organisers declared EUR 166,576 in support and funding, mostly from Oxfam organisations and the foundation FEPS, plus Europa-Nævnet.

The register's page for the initiative was read for this entry.

title: Tax the rich: from slogan to reality
by: Greens/EFA group in the European Parliament
summary: Study proposing a progressive wealth tax across the EU, modelled on a temporary Spanish measure, which it estimates would raise 213.3 billion euros a year, plus 59.5 billion from ending tax abuse through offshore wealth.

title: Resources for a Safe and Resilient Europe: The Case for Minimum Taxation of Ultra-High-Net-Worth Individuals in the EU
by: Quentin Parrinello, Giulia Varaschin and Gabriel Zucman (EU Tax Observatory)
summary: Policy note proposing a minimum tax of 2% or 3% on the wealth of people with more than 100 million or 1 billion euros; Oxfam's account of it gives 67 billion euros at 2% and 121 billion at 3% for 23 EU countries.

title: A European wealth tax for a fair and green recovery
by: Jakob Kapeller, Stuart Leitch and Rafael Wildauer (FEPS, Karl Renner Institut and AK Europa)
summary: Policy study arguing for an EU net wealth tax with exemption thresholds of 1 to 2 million euros, progressive rates and a broad base, taxing only the richest 1% to 3% of households, to help pay for the Covid-19 and climate response.

title: A Harmonized Net Wealth Tax in the European Union
by: Alexander Krenek and Margit Schratzenstaller (WIFO)
summary: Journal article (Jahrbücher für Nationalökonomie und Statistik) simulating an annual EU net wealth tax of 1% on net wealth from 1 to 5 million euros and 1.5% above, which it estimates would raise 165 to 177 billion euros after avoidance and evasion.

title: A progressive European wealth tax to fund the European COVID response
by: Camille Landais, Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman
summary: VoxEU column proposing a temporary, progressive, EU-wide tax on the net worth of the richest 1% that could repay about 10% of EU GDP in extra debt within ten years.

title: UN DESA Policy Brief No. 168: Net Wealth Taxes: How they can help fight inequality and fund sustainable development
by: Ilka Ritter, Laura Burt and Belisa Ferreira Liotti (UN DESA)
summary: Policy brief on the design of net wealth taxes: exemption thresholds, rates, avoidance through residency and undervaluation, and the value of international cooperation if the revenue is to fund sustainable development.

title: United Nations Handbook on Wealth and Solidarity Taxes
by: UN Committee of Experts on International Cooperation in Tax Matters
summary: Guidance approved by the UN Tax Committee in 2025 on taxing wealth; the Committee's Subcommittee on Wealth Taxation, set up in October 2025, builds on it, and the DESA brief on net wealth taxes cites it.

title: Bundesgesetz über die Harmonisierung der direkten Steuern der Kantone und Gemeinden (StHG), Art. 13 und 14: Vermögenssteuer
by: Bundesversammlung (SR 642.14)
summary: The federal framework for the cantonal wealth taxes: "Der Vermögenssteuer unterliegt das gesamte Reinvermögen" (Art. 13), valued at market value (Art. 14). The cantons set the tariffs, rates and allowances.
status: Consolidated text on Fedlex (Art. 13 and 14 as shown there); Switzerland has no federal wealth tax, the tax is levied by every canton

links.label: Wealth tax of natural persons, dossier of the Federal Tax Administration (ESTV), status 1 January 2026

overview:
Switzerland has no federal wealth tax. Every canton and its communes levy their own on individuals, and the Federal Act on the Harmonisation of Direct Taxes of the Cantons and Communes (StHG) sets the frame. Parliament passed it on 14 December 1990 to carry out a constitutional mandate of 1977 (today Art. 129 of the Federal Constitution). Art. 13 makes the whole net wealth of a person subject to the cantonal tax, and Art. 14 values assets at market value. The cantons keep the tariffs, rates and allowances, so Switzerland has 26 different wealth-tax regimes.

The Federal Tax Administration (ESTV) says no direct federal tax has been levied on individuals' wealth since 1959, because adding it to the cantonal and communal wealth taxes would have overburdened taxpayers. In 2024 the wealth tax raised 5,808 million francs for the cantons and 3,650 million for the communes, 9,458 million in total, which is 10.17% of all cantonal and communal tax revenue.

This is the law behind the Swiss debate: the Federal Council cites the existing cantonal wealth taxes when it rejects proposals for a federal one, and it said that motions 20.3174, 20.3203 and 20.3335 would first need an amendment to the Constitution.

title: Loi sur l'imposition des personnes physiques (LIPP, D 3 08), art. 46 ss: impôt sur la fortune (Geneva)
by: Grand Conseil de la République et canton de Genève
summary: The Geneva wealth tax: "L'impôt sur la fortune a pour objet l'ensemble de la fortune nette après déductions sociales" (art. 46). Art. 59 sets a progressive tariff in brackets, with a second, supplementary scale on top.
status: Consolidated text on the canton's legislation site: in force since 1 January 2010, text as amended to 1 January 2026
overview:
Geneva's Loi sur l'imposition des personnes physiques (LIPP, D 3 08) sets the canton's wealth tax in Articles 46 to 60. Article 46 taxes the whole net wealth after social deductions, and Article 47 lists what counts: property, shares and securities, cash and bank deposits, and similar assets.

From the net wealth the tax office deducts 82,200 francs for a single person, 164,400 for a couple and for single parents, and 41,100 for each dependent. It also deducts half of the assets invested in the taxpayer's own business, up to 500,000 francs (Art. 58). The tax is then worked out on a progressive scale (Art. 59): the base rate rises from 1.49 per mille on the first 111,059 francs to 3.83 per mille above 1,665,879 francs, and a second, supplementary scale is charged on top of it. A ceiling in Article 60 keeps the wealth and income taxes together, with communal and cantonal additional centimes, at no more than 60% of net taxable income, with the net return on wealth counted at no less than 1% of net wealth.

The law was passed on 27 September 2009 and has applied since 1 January 2010; the text on the canton's site is current to 1 January 2026. It is the law that Geneva's initiative IN 185 would have amended in 2023 with a ten-year solidarity contribution on wealth above 3 million francs, and Geneva voters rejected that on 18 June 2023.

title: Ley 19/1991, de 6 de junio, del Impuesto sobre el Patrimonio
by: Cortes Generales
summary: The Spanish net wealth tax: a direct, personal tax on the net wealth of individuals (art. 1), owed by residents on their worldwide net wealth and by non-residents on assets in Spain (art. 5).
status: Consolidated BOE text, last updated 28 December 2023 (the BOE page says it has no legal value); in force from 1 January 1992
overview:
Law 19/1991 of 6 June 1991 created Spain's net wealth tax (Impuesto sobre el Patrimonio), a direct personal tax on the net wealth of individuals. Spanish residents pay on their worldwide net wealth and non-residents only on assets in Spain. It was published in the BOE on 7 June 1991 and has applied from 1 January 1992.

The state default allows an exempt minimum of EUR 700,000 and taxes the rest on an eight-step scale from 0.2% up to 3.5% above EUR 10,695,996.06. A main home is exempt up to EUR 300,000, household goods are exempt, and so are business assets and qualifying family-company shareholdings. The combined bill with income tax cannot exceed 60% of the income-tax base, though this cannot cut the wealth tax by more than 80%. The regions can set their own exempt minimum, scale and deductions, and the tax can be ceded to them.

The 2022 Podemos bill in the register describes the tax's later history: a 2008 law (Law 4/2008) kept it on the books but gave a 100% rebate, and it was restored three years later. The same bill says the number of people declaring over EUR 1.5 million rose 36.4% between 2007 and 2019 while revenue fell 42.5%. Newer bills in the register build on this law. The BOE page is a consolidated text and the BOE says it has no legal value.

title: Ley 23.966, Título VI: Impuesto sobre los Bienes Personales (texto ordenado 1997)
by: Congreso de la Nación; texto ordenado by Decreto 281/1997
summary: The annual tax on personal assets held at 31 December, in the country and abroad: owed by residents on both and by people living abroad on assets in Argentina. Under Ley 27.743 the tax-free minimum is $100,000,000 (home $350,000,000) with rates from 0.50% to 1.25%, falling to a flat 0.25% in 2027.
status: AFIP's legal library lists the texto ordenado (Decreto 281/97) as in force; Ley 27.432 extended Título VI to 31 December 2022, and later laws (27.541, 27.667, 27.737, 27.743) changed the thresholds, rates and exemptions.

links.label: Texto ordenado of Ley 23.966 with amendments (AFIP legal library)

overview:
Argentina has taxed personal wealth for decades through Título VI of Ley 23.966, the Impuesto sobre los Bienes Personales. The consolidated text dates from 26 March 1997 (Decreto 281/97), and the tax falls on personal assets held on 31 December each year. It was first created for nine fiscal periods and has been extended since; Ley 27.432 pushed it to 31 December 2022, and AFIP's legal library lists it as in force.

Individuals who live in Argentina pay on assets at home and abroad, and non-residents pay only on assets in the country. Ley 27.541 replaced the old domicile test with a residence test from 2019. After the amendments of Ley 27.743 (2024), assets are taxed only above a minimum of $100,000,000, or $350,000,000 for a home, both adjusted each year by inflation. The tax on the excess follows a four-band scale of 0.50%, 0.75%, 1.00% and 1.25% for 2024. The same law lowers the rates each year and sets a single rate of 0.25% from fiscal period 2027. Exemptions cover, among others, diplomatic property, cooperative shares, rural land held by individuals and certain public securities and bank deposits.

It is consolidated law, not a recorded bill, so the register names no sponsors.

title: Skatteloven (lov 26. mars 1999 nr. 14), kapittel 4 Formue, § 4-1 Hovedregel om formue
by: Stortinget
summary: Defines taxable net wealth: the market value on 1 January of the assessment year of the taxpayer's assets with economic value, less the debts the taxpayer is liable for. The annual rates are set in the Storting's tax decision.
status: Consolidated text on Lovdata; chapter 4 Formue runs from § 4-1 to § 4-55
overview:
Chapter 4 of the Tax Act (skatteloven, law of 26 March 1999 no. 14) defines the base of Norway's wealth tax. It runs from section 4-1 to section 4-55 and covers the general rules, special valuation rules, tax-free wealth, the split of debt deductions, partnerships and other provisions.

Section 4-1 sets the main rule: taxable net wealth is the market value on 1 January of the assessment year of everything the taxpayer owns that has economic value, minus debts the taxpayer is liable for. Section 4-2 lists assets that are left out, such as certain insurance and pension rights. Section 4-3 lists debts that cannot be deducted. Section 4-1 was last amended by a law in force from 1 January 2024.

The Act does not set the rates. They are decided each year in the Storting's tax decision. For income year 2026 the state rate is 0.65% above NOK 1.9 million (0.75% above NOK 21.5 million), and the municipal rate is at most 0.35%.

title: Título 14: Impuesto al Patrimonio (IP), Texto Ordenado 2023, art. 4 Sujetos pasivos
by: Poder Ejecutivo (Decreto 101/024), consolidating the Título 14 of the Texto Ordenado 1996
summary: Creates "un impuesto anual que recaerá sobre el patrimonio" of the taxpayers listed in art. 4, for general revenue. Individuals, family units and undivided estates pay on net wealth above a tax-free minimum set each year, at rates running from 0.70% to 2.75% in the statutory scale, reduced annually; companies pay 1.5%.
status: Texto ordenado approved by Decreto 101/024 of 4 April 2024 (published 16 May 2024); the tax dates from the Título 14 of the 1996 text (Decreto 338/996)

links.label: Título 14, art. 4 and following (IMPO, Texto Ordenado 2023)

overview:
Uruguay has had an annual net wealth tax for decades. Título 14 of the Texto Ordenado 2023, approved by Decreto 101/024 of 4 April 2024 (published 16 May 2024), is the current consolidated text; the tax dates from the 1996 text, and the Tax Directorate keeps updating this one. Article 4 lists who pays: individuals, family units and undivided estates whose wealth exceeds a tax-free minimum, companies and similar entities, and foreign legal persons.

For individuals, family units and undivided estates the statutory scale starts at 0.70% on wealth up to the tax-free minimum and runs through 1.10%, 1.40%, 1.90%, 2.00% and 2.45% to 2.75% on the excess over fourteen times it. The same article then cuts those rates in steps from 2008, 2011 and 2016, down to a floor of 0.10%. The Executive fixes the minimum every year in line with the cost of living, and doubles it for a family unit. Other taxpayers, including companies, pay 1.5%, banks and financial companies 2.8%, bearer bonds 3.5% and entities in low-tax jurisdictions 3%. A surcharge of 0.70% to 1.50% applies to farm assets above 12 million indexed units. Public debt securities are not counted among the assets.

The text has been edited recently: Ley 20.446 of 16 December 2025 changed article 16 and article 23, and Ley 20.531 of 1 October 2026 adds a new article 70 bis to a different title. It is law in force, not a bill, so no sponsors are recorded.

title: Carpeta 804/2022: creación de una sobretasa de un 25% sobre el Impuesto al Patrimonio con destino al Fondo Nacional de Vivienda
by: Senators Oscar Andrade, Daniel Caggiani, Charles Carrera, Daniel Olesker, Uruguay Russi and Alejandro Sánchez
summary: Creates a permanent 25% surcharge on the Impuesto al Patrimonio, with all proceeds earmarked for the Fondo Nacional de Vivienda to finance social housing policies.
status: Introduced in the Senate on 17 October 2022 (Carpeta 804/2022, Distribuido 1227/2022) and sent to the Comisión de Vivienda y Ordenamiento Territorial, which discussed it on 1, 8 and 15 August, 14 November and 12 December 2023. Archived at the end of the 49th Legislature on 14 February 2025; the Senate plenary took it out of the archive on 11 March 2025 (Distribuido 79/2025). The committee heard the Facultad de Arquitectura, Diseño y Urbanismo on 9 September 2025, the latest entry on the Parliament's record (read 12 November 2026). No vote.
overview:
This bill, filed by six senators, creates a permanent surcharge of 25% on Uruguay's existing Impuesto al Patrimonio and sends all the proceeds to the Fondo Nacional de Vivienda. Its three articles are short. Article 1 creates the surcharge. Article 2 rewrites the Fund's resources in Ley 13.728 so that the surcharge's proceeds are one of them. Article 3 adds that when the Fund's annual resources from its payroll contribution and the surcharge fall below 2% of the public and private payroll, general revenue must make up the difference.

The explanatory statement starts from the right to housing in Article 45 of the Constitution. It says the Fund has lost resources since 1968: the 1% contribution of private-sector employers was dropped in 1992 and the 2007 tax reform did not make up for it. It cites the 2016 national Habitat III report, which counted 51,889 households in quantitative housing deficit and 169,573 in qualitative deficit in the 2011 census. The surcharge is meant to restore the Fund to the 2% of payroll that the 1968 law intended.

Because it is a surcharge on a tax that already exists, the bill sets no new threshold or base. What distinguishes it is that every peso goes to social housing. The bill lapsed with the legislature in February 2025, and the Senate revived it in March 2025. The committee's last recorded session on it was in September 2025. The text read here does not give a revenue estimate.

title: Ley 1357: Impuesto a las Grandes Fortunas (IGF)
by: Asamblea Legislativa Plurinacional
summary: Creates a national tax on the net fortune of individuals above Bs 30,000,000 at 31 December each year, at 1.4% up to Bs 40 million, 1.9% up to Bs 50 million and 2.4% above (arts. 5 and 9). Regulated by Decreto Supremo 4436 of 30 December 2020.
status: In force: the Chamber of Deputies' planning committee rejected the bill to repeal it on 10 February 2026 and the plenary approved only the repeal of the financial transactions tax; the tax authority extended the 2025 filing deadline on 24 March 2026. No later vote or repeal found; the government said it would insist (Oxígeno, 11 Feb 2026).

links.label: Ley 1357 (Lexivox transcription of the Gaceta Oficial)
RND 102600000009 extending the 2025 filing deadlines (Impuestos Nacionales, 24 March 2026)

overview:
Law 1357, the Impuesto a las Grandes Fortunas (IGF), was passed by Bolivia's Plurinational Legislative Assembly, sanctioned on 22 December 2020 and promulgated on 28 December 2020. It taxes the net fortune of individuals who hold more than Bs 30,000,000 on 31 December of each year. The tax applies from 2020 and the text sets no end date.

Residents, defined as people who stay more than 183 days in a 12-month period, pay on wealth in Bolivia and abroad. Non-residents pay on wealth located in Bolivia. Companies and other legal entities are outside the tax. The rates are 1.4% for a taxable base of Bs 30 to 40 million, 1.9% from Bs 40 to 50 million and 2.4% above Bs 50 million, with fixed deductions of Bs 150,000, 350,000 and 600,000 for the three bands. Loans from financial institutions regulated by ASFI can be deducted, household goods are excluded, and in a married couple each spouse's base includes half of the property acquired during the marriage. All the revenue goes to the national treasury. Decreto Supremo 4436 of 30 December 2020 regulates it.

The tax is still being collected. On 24 March 2026 the tax service issued a resolution extending the deadline to file and pay the IGF for 2025 to 30 April 2026 for residents and 29 May 2026 for non-residents. The register's status line records the 2026 move in the Chamber of Deputies to repeal the law and what became of it.

title: RND 102600000009: prórroga para el cumplimiento de obligaciones tributarias del Impuesto a las Grandes Fortunas (IGF), gestión 2025
by: Servicio de Impuestos Nacionales
summary: The tax authority extends the deadline to file and pay the IGF for 2025 to 30 April 2026 for residents and 29 May 2026 for non-residents.
status: Resolution of 24 March 2026, which shows the tax still being administered for the 2025 year
overview:
Resolución Normativa de Directorio 102600000009 is an administrative rule, not a bill. Bolivia's tax service (Servicio de Impuestos Nacionales) signed it on 24 March 2026 to extend the deadlines for the Impuesto a las Grandes Fortunas (IGF) for the 2025 tax year.

Under Decreto Supremo 4436, residents had to file and pay by the last business day of March and non-residents by the last business day of April. The resolution moves the deadline for residents, on Form 022, to 30 April 2026, and for non-residents, on Form 023, to 29 May 2026. The service gives the complexity of working out the tax base, and requests from taxpayers, as the reasons.

It matters because it shows the tax in active use more than five years after Law 1357 created it. The resolution recalls that the law taxes the fortune of individuals, that the taxable event arises on 31 December each year, and that Decreto Supremo 4436 of 30 December 2020 regulates it. It came into force on publication and changes nothing about who pays or how much.

title: Consideraciones sobre un gravamen al 1% más rico de la población uruguaya
by: Mauricio De Rosa and Joan Vilá (Instituto de Economía, Universidad de la República), letter to the PIT-CNT
summary: Two economists review the evidence on the wealth held by the richest 1%, estimate that a 1% tax on it could raise 0.75% to 1% of GDP (USD 600 to 800 million), and discuss evasion and a design built on the existing Impuesto al Patrimonio, concluding that the literature does not show such a proposal to be unviable.

title: Uruguay: Impuesto Mínimo Efectivo sobre la Riqueza
by: Vicente Silva (International Tax Observatory), with Friedrich Ebert Stiftung Uruguay
summary: Brief that simulates a minimum tax on the wealth of individuals with fortunes above USD 100 million (2% would raise about USD 260 million, 0.4% of GDP; 3% about USD 409 million) and notes the PIT-CNT's proposed surcharge on the Impuesto al Patrimonio.

title: Una señal regresiva y equivocada: eliminar el impuesto a las grandes fortunas profundiza la desigualdad en Bolivia
by: Oxfam en Bolivia
summary: Press release against the government's announced repeal of the Impuesto a las Grandes Fortunas, which it says reaches about 200 people and raises 240 million bolivianos a year.

title: Propuesta de creación de una sobretasa del Impuesto al Patrimonio de las Personas Físicas (IPPF) para financiar políticas para la reducción de la pobreza infantil y adolescente
by: Consultative commission of the PIT-CNT (Andrés Blanco, Juan Geymonat, Mauricio De Rosa, Gabriel Oyhantçabal, Andrea Vigorito, Joan Vilá, Alejandra Picco, Carlos Grau Pérez, Gustavo Viñales Guillama)
summary: Proposes an annual surcharge on the Impuesto al Patrimonio de las Personas Físicas for wealth above USD 1 million (about the richest 1%, some 25,000 people), with progressive rates and the proceeds going to a state fund against child poverty.

title: Expediente 22.113: Impuesto solidario a la riqueza, para reactivar el país ante la emergencia del COVID-19
by: Franggi Nicolás Solano (Partido Liberación Nacional)
summary: A one-off 1% tax on the capital declared to the tax administration by individuals holding more than US$2.5 million and by companies and trusts holding US$5 million or more, to fund the COVID-19 recovery.
status: Rechazado (Delfino.cr bill page, Comisión de Asuntos Hacendarios); date of the rejection not recorded

links.label: Press report on the bill (El Mundo CR, 29 July 2020)

overview:
Bill 22.113, the "Impuesto solidario a la riqueza", was presented in Costa Rica's Legislative Assembly on 29 July 2020 by Franggi Nicolás Solano of the Partido Liberación Nacional. It proposes a one-time tax of 1% on the capital value that taxpayers declared in their latest income-tax return.

According to the press report of its filing, the tax would hit individuals with assets above US$2.5 million and companies and trusts with assets of US$5 million or more, including business groups whose combined assets pass that mark. It covers movable and immovable property, intangible assets, financial assets and trusts. The revenue would go to paying public debt, reducing the state's debt to the social-security fund, housing, community and municipal development, the Bono Proteger programme, voluntary early retirement and mobility for public employees, public infrastructure, and rescue loans for small businesses. Social solidarity-economy organisations are exempt, and companies could get a lower rate if they invest in environmental or social projects.

The bill went to the Comisión de Asuntos Hacendarios. The Delfino.cr bill page lists it as rejected but does not give the date or the vote. The bill text itself could not be opened, so the figures above come from the press report of its filing.

title: Expediente 21.883: Ley de Contingencia Fiscal Progresiva y Solidaria ante la emergencia nacional del COVID-19
by: José María Villalta Flórez-Estrada (Frente Amplio)
summary: A package of 12-month surcharges on large companies, dividends, high self-employed incomes, salaries and pensions, plus (article 23) a one-off 0.1% tax on the net equity of commercial companies above CRC 95 million; only the equity levy is a tax on wealth.
status: Archivado (Delfino.cr bill page, Comisión de Asuntos Hacendarios); Servicios Técnicos opinion of 6 September 2021
overview:
Bill 21.883, the "Ley de Contingencia Fiscal Progresiva y Solidaria", was presented in Costa Rica's Legislative Assembly on 26 March 2020 by José María Villalta Flórez-Estrada of the Frente Amplio, in the first weeks of the COVID-19 emergency. It revives the logic of the 2002 Ley de Contingencia Fiscal (Ley 8343): temporary taxes on those with the most, to pay for the response.

Most of the package taxes income, not wealth. For 12 months, large taxpayers would pay 6 percentage points more tax on profits and large territorial companies 2 points more. Dividends from them would be taxed 5 and 3 points higher. Self-employed people earning more than CRC 36 million a year would pay 5% on the excess, and salaries and pensions above CRC 3 million a month would pay 5% on the excess.

The wealth part is article 23: a single tax of 0.1% on the net equity (assets minus liabilities) of registered commercial companies, on the part above CRC 95 million. Companies that made losses in 2020 are exempt, and the tax is not deductible from income tax.

The bill went to the Comisión de Asuntos Hacendarios and is marked archived on the Delfino.cr page, which lists the technical-services opinion of 6 September 2021 as its last text. The page does not give the archiving date.

overview:
After the earthquake of 16 April 2016 that devastated Manabí and part of Esmeraldas, Ecuador's President Rafael Correa sent the National Assembly a solidarity law, which it approved and which appeared in Registro Oficial Suplemento 759 on 20 May 2016. Article 4 is the wealth-tax part: a one-time "solidarity contribution" of 0.90% on the net wealth of individuals who held USD 1 million or more on 1 January 2016.

Residents pay on assets inside and outside Ecuador, non-residents on assets in Ecuador. Net wealth is assets minus liabilities, counting rights held through companies, nonprofits and trusts, and loans from related parties are not deductible unless shown to be genuine. People whose assets or business were directly hit by the earthquake and who live in Manabí, Muisne or other affected areas are exempt. The contribution was paid in three monthly instalments, with payment facilities of up to six months.

The same law also set other one-time contributions: one day of pay a month, for one to eight months, from employees earning USD 1,000 a month or more; 1.8% of the cadastral value of Ecuadorian property held by companies in tax havens; and 3% of company profits, based on 2015. As a one-off payment, there is nothing left to collect, which is why the register lists it as lapsed.

overview:
President Guillermo Lasso sent Ecuador's National Assembly the "Ley Orgánica para el Desarrollo Económico y Sostenibilidad Fiscal tras la Pandemia COVID-19" on 28 October 2021 as an urgent economic bill. Among its measures were two temporary contributions on net wealth, one for individuals and one for companies.

Individuals with net wealth of USD 1 million or more on 1 January 2021 pay, and the threshold is USD 2 million for the joint property of a couple. Up to USD 200,000 for a main home or unproductive farmland can be deducted. Vistazo reported that fewer than 6,000 people would pay. Companies with net wealth of USD 5 million or more at 31 December 2020 pay 0.8% of it; Vistazo counted 1,931 companies, a contribution lasting two years, and an expected yield of about USD 467 million.

The constitutional 30 days for an urgent economic bill passed without the Assembly approving any of the motions put to it, so on 29 November 2021 the president sent the law to the Registro Oficial, where it came into force in the Third Supplement of issue 587. overview:
The left party Radnička fronta (Workers' Front) submitted this proposal to the Croatian Parliament (Sabor) on 15 September 2023. It is a proposed parliamentary conclusion asking the Government to draft a Law on Net Wealth Tax. The draft law itself is not on the party's page; the page sets out the design.

The base is the market value of all assets in Croatia and abroad, minus tax-recognised debts, with foreign data coming from information exchange. Tax is due once a year above EUR 700,000, which the party sets at ten times the median household's assets. Rates rise from 1% (EUR 700,000 to 1.5 million), to 1.5% (to EUR 5 million), 2% (to EUR 20 million), 3% (to EUR 100 million) and 4% above EUR 100 million. A main home would count at 60% of its market price. Liability would follow citizenship rather than residence, as in the United States, and renouncing Croatian citizenship would trigger an exit tax of 40% of assets. The party estimates it would affect about 1% of households, roughly 12,000 to 15,000.

The initiative was left undebated when the 10th Sabor was dissolved in March 2024, as the register's status records from Nacional. The party's page does not describe any committee review or vote.

overview:
This bill, T/5575, would have set up a yearly "solidarity wealth tax" on the richest people living in Hungary. It taxes the net wealth of anyone who lives in Hungary and owns more than HUF 600 million after debts. Everything counts: property at home and abroad, valuables and art, securities, bank deposits, cash, and shares in Hungarian or foreign companies, with holdings in linked companies added together. The tax is progressive: 1.7% of the part between HUF 600 million and HUF 1.6 billion, 2.1% of the part between HUF 1.6 billion and HUF 2.9 billion, and 3.5% above that.

Six Párbeszéd (Dialogue) members of parliament submitted it on 11 October 2023: Bence Tordai, Sándor Berki, Tamás Mellár, András Jámbor, Rebeka Szabó and Tímea Szabó. The first payment would fall due in the year the law is promulgated, within 30 days of promulgation, and after that by 31 May each year. The Government would set the detailed rules by decree. The money would go to the cost-of-living crisis: pay rises for public-sector workers such as teachers, health and social-care staff, and support to offset inflation.

The bill's explanatory memorandum says the tax would reach only the richest half of one percent of the population. It rests on a Tax Justice Network study commissioned by the Greens group in the European Parliament, which the memorandum quotes as estimating about EUR 3,839 million, roughly HUF 1,500 billion, in revenue.

It never reached a debate. The Speaker sent it to the Economic Committee for a decision on whether to take it onto the agenda, and on 6 November 2023 the committee refused. The text above was read from archived copies of the three parliament.hu documents.

Net wealth is all assets after debts: property at home and abroad, valuables, securities, bank deposits, cash and company holdings, with linked companies added together. The rates rise in four bands as printed in the bill: 1% of the part above HUF 1 billion up to HUF 10 billion, 2% up to HUF 100 billion, 3% up to HUF 1,000 billion, and 98% of any wealth above HUF 1,000 billion.

Hvg, 6 October 2026: the consultation draft and how wealth is valued
Újpesti Hírmondó, 1 November 2026: the week's agenda and the revenue expected
Index, 28 October 2026: what changed between the draft and the bill

overview:
T/930, "A vagyonadóról" (On the wealth tax), is the Hungarian Government's bill for an annual tax on net wealth. Deputy Prime Minister Bálint Ruff filed it with the Speaker, Ágnes Forsthoffer, on 27 October 2026 at 21:27 "on behalf of the Government"; the Minister of Finance, András Kármán, is the presenter. The tax takes the part of a person's net wealth above HUF 1 billion. The rate is 1% on the part of the base up to HUF 100 billion and 1.5% on the part above it (§ 12). The law is to come into force on 15 December 2026 (§ 36).

The general justification states the aim: to bring "the economic capacity embodied in outstanding wealth" into sharing the public burden, on the principle that those with significant wealth can be asked for a larger contribution. The tax is charged once a year on the position on the last day of the year (§ 8). The base is the calculated value of all taxable assets less debts that are proven and backed by a law, a final ruling or a document of full evidential force (§ 9).

Who pays. Residents are taxed on all their assets at home and abroad; this includes Hungarian citizens with dual nationality who live abroad, unless they have lived abroad for at least ten years (§ 5). Non-residents are taxed only on Hungarian real estate and rights over it, and on stakes in Hungarian companies or in companies that hold Hungarian real estate (§ 7). Trusts, private foundations and similar structures are taxpayers in their own right. Linked structures set up by the same person or by relatives share a single HUF 1 billion threshold (§ 28).

What counts. Personal belongings and household fittings are left out, except art, collections and jewellery worth more than HUF 3 million each and vehicles worth more than HUF 10 million (§ 9). Co-owned assets count by share. Spouses' joint property follows their marriage contract or their joint election, and otherwise is split equally; a minor child's inherited and earned assets count with the parent who holds parental authority (§ 10). A holding in a pension insurance contract counts for the insured person at its surrender value (§ 25).

Valuation. Listed shares are valued at the closing price on the last trading day, or at the 180-day average if the close differs from it by more than 10% (§ 15). Unlisted company stakes follow the formula in Annex 1: V = (equity + 2 x earnings value) / 3 x ownership share. The earnings value is the average profit after tax of the last three years divided by a capitalisation rate of 15%. Equity is adjusted for hidden reserves above HUF 500 million; minority stakes get a 25% or 30% reduction; a company with equity up to HUF 100 million can use its equity share instead (§ 15(9)). Where the formula does not fit, an independent valuer that meets turnover conditions can be used (§ 15). Hungarian real estate is valued by a purchase price in the last twelve months, an indexed price from a purchase in the last ten years, or the tax authority's mass-valuation model, in that order of precedence (§§ 19-22). Foreign real estate starts from the purchase price and is raised each year by 3% or by the local property price index (§ 20).

Paying. Taxpayers assess, declare and pay themselves, through the tax authority's electronic platform, by 31 August of the following year; the first return and payment, for 2026, fall due by 31 August 2027 (§§ 29 and 38). A return is needed only when tax is due. The tax authority may defer payment for up to twelve months, or 24 in exceptional cases, if paying in one sum would be a disproportionate burden (§ 30). Fees paid for required valuations are credited at 50%, up to HUF 2 million, and local taxes and motor-vehicle tax paid on the taxed assets are deducted from the tax (§ 12).

Revenue. The tax goes to the central budget; a taxpayer may declare that 5% of the tax paid goes to the National Cooperation Fund (§ 35). The justification gives no revenue estimate.

Debate and vote. The bill text shows no committee or vote. Press reports put the general debate on the agenda of 3 November 2026; the parliament's own record of the debate, the committee report and the vote have not yet been read in this register.

overview:
The auðlegðarskattur ("wealth tax") was a temporary net wealth tax on individuals in Iceland. It was introduced in the government's revenue bill of the 2009–2010 session by finance minister Steingrímur J. Sigfússon and enacted at the end of 2009. It taxed net wealth, that is assets minus debts, regardless of income. The bill proposed it for three years at 1.25 per cent of net wealth above ISK 90 million for a single person and above ISK 120 million for a couple, saying the richest had enjoyed low taxation while ordinary people carried heavier burdens.

In its last form a single person paid nothing on the first ISK 75 million (couples ISK 100 million), 1.5 per cent on the band up to ISK 150 million (couples ISK 200 million) and 2 per cent above that. A supplementary wealth tax on the gap between the nominal and real value of shares applied for the 2013 and 2014 assessments. The tax was last assessed in 2014 on net wealth at the end of 2013.

The finance minister's written answer to Andrés Ingi Jónsson in the 154th session (2024) put the 2013 tax base at about ISK 4,060 billion and the tax at about ISK 9.6 billion in today's prices. It estimated that the same rules, with thresholds indexed to prices, would raise ISK 36.9 billion for 2023.

Both source pages (the 2009 bill and the 2024 answer) were read through web-archive copies, because althingi.is blocks scripted requests.

overview:
Bill 310 of 2020 in the Colombian Senate was filed on 27 May 2020 by 54 senators led by Luis Iván Marulanda and Roosvelt Rodríguez Rengifo. By its title it modifies Decreto Ley 518 of 2020, which created the Ingreso Solidario programme for households in poverty and vulnerability during the COVID-19 emergency, and turns it into an "emergency basic income". It was assigned to the Third Constitutional Commission of the Senate.

According to Semana, the bill proposed a transfer equal to one minimum wage for three months to about nine million households, paid for with a loan from the central bank and multilateral funds. The senators paired it with a call for a structural tax reform that includes a progressive wealth tax on individuals with net wealth from COP 2,000 million and higher rates on the richest companies. The bill is not itself a wealth-tax bill; the wealth tax is part of its stated financing and reform agenda.

The record lists rapporteurs for reports dated 12 and 16 June 2020. The register lists the bill as lapsed. The articles of the bill itself were not available in the sources read, so this page describes it from the Senate record and press coverage.

by: Ministry of Finance (Minister Germán Ávila Plazas), Petro government

The Cámara's tracking page (read 12 November 2026) shows it "en trámite en comisión"; the rapporteur for the first debate, Óscar Darío Pérez Pineda, was assigned on 1 October 2026 and his report recommends against the bill (Gaceta 1721/2026). overview:
Proyecto de Ley 004 de 2026 Cámara is the tax reform that the Petro government's Finance Minister, Germán Ávila Plazas, filed on 20 July 2026, with thirty representatives and nine senators as co-authors. Its explanatory statement aims to raise 21.9 trillion pesos (21.9 billones) in 2027, about 1.0% of GDP, through fewer tax exemptions, higher taxes on top incomes and wealth, and levies on environmental and health harms. One part is a wider wealth tax.

Colombia reintroduced a permanent wealth tax on individuals in 2022, and 32,397 people paid it in 2024. The bill lowers the entry threshold from 72,000 UVT to 40,000 UVT, which would bring in 105,332 taxpayers, 1.7% of income-tax filers. The marginal rates, on the wealth above each step, are 0.5% from 40,000 UVT, 1% from 70,000, 2% from 120,000, 3% from 240,000 and 5% above 2,000,000 UVT. The statement works out effective rates that reach 2.8% for the 2,956 taxpayers in the 3% step and 3.2% in the top step. It counts the wealth tax at 1,900 thousand million pesos of new revenue in 2027.

The bill went to the Comisión Tercera of the Cámara. Its assigned rapporteur recommends against it, and the Cámara's page shows no vote. The government that filed it left office in August 2026, and the new government is moving its own Rescate Económico bill. What distinguishes the Colombian bill from the others in the Americas is that it reshapes a wealth tax already in force, with five steps up to 5%, inside a larger reform.

title: Wet vermogensbelasting 2024 (36 173): progressive wealth tax
by: Luc Stultiens, Jimmy Dijk, Christine Teunissen and Laurens Dassen
summary: Private member's bill: €100,000 exempt per person, then 1% rising to 5% above €5 million; the initiators' estimate is about €5 billion a year.
status: Filed on 13 July 2022 by Nijboer, Alkaya, Van Raan and Gündoğan, with Maatoug co-defending from 25 August 2022. After they left the Kamer, Stultiens, Dijk and Teunissen took over the defence (21 May 2025) and Dassen joined (28 May 2025). links.label: Bill text and cover letter, 13 July 2022

Letter of 28 May 2025: Dassen joins the defence

overview:
The Wet vermogensbelasting 2024 would add a progressive tax on net wealth to Dutch law. It takes the assets of today's box 3 as its base (savings, investments, property other than the own home, cash and crypto), less debts, and taxes the wealth itself, not an assumed return on it. Each person has 100,000 euro exempt (200,000 for a couple). Above that the rate is 1% up to 500,000 euro, 2% to 1 million, 3% to 2 million, 4% to 5 million and 5% above 5 million. The own home and substantial-interest shares stay in boxes 1 and 2, and pensions fall outside. Only natural persons pay, including foreigners with Dutch assets such as a holiday home.

The initiators wrote it after the Hoge Raad's ruling of 24 December 2021, which held that box 3's flat deemed return had drifted too far from actual returns. They argue that the ruling could leave wealth untaxed, that Dutch capital is taxed lightly next to labour, and that wealth is far more unequally spread than income. They count about 9,300 taxpayers with more than 2.5 million euro. The tax was meant to start on 1 January 2024; the memorandum's estimate, from 2019 tax-return data, is about 4.4 billion euro in 2024 and about 5.2 billion euro a year in the long run.

Henk Nijboer (GroenLinks-PvdA), Mahir Alkaya (SP), Lammert van Raan (PvdD) and Nilüfer Gündoğan (independent) filed it on 13 July 2022; Senna Maatoug (GroenLinks-PvdA) joined the defence on 25 August 2022. All five have since left the Kamer. Luc Stultiens (GroenLinks-PvdA), Jimmy Dijk (SP) and Christine Teunissen (PvdD) took over on 21 May 2025, and Laurens Dassen (Volt) joined a week later.

Since the filing the bill has had no vote, and the Kamer's file shows no committee report or debate.

by: De Nationale Assemblée (promulgated G.B. 1960 no. 85, last amended S.B. 2004 no. 152)
summary: Suriname's core net wealth tax law, levying an annual direct tax of 0.8% (Sf. 8 per Sf. 1,000) on the net wealth of residents above a tax-free amount (Sf. 20,000 if single, Sf. 30,000 if married), and of non-residents on local assets.
status: In force (G.B. 1944 no. 185 as amended through S.B. 2004 no. 152)

links.label: Wet Vermogensbelasting 1944, consolidated text to S.B. 2004 no. 152 (De Nationale Assemblée, PDF)

overview:
Suriname's wealth tax law dates from 14 December 1944 (Gouvernementsblad 1944 no. 185) and has been amended several times, most recently in 2004 (S.B. 2004 no. 152). The version on the National Assembly's website is the consolidated text through that amendment. It imposes a direct tax, the Vermogensbelasting, on people who live in Suriname.

Residents pay on their net wealth, meaning everything with a money value minus debts, measured at the start of the tax year on 1 January. Gold and silverware, pearls and gems count only above a small limit; household goods, art, clothes, food, legal pensions and certain annuity and life-insurance policies are left out. Property is valued at sale value, shares at market value and farmland at its value as farmland. Non-residents are taxed only on Surinamese real estate, mortgage claims secured on it and the assets of a permanent business establishment. Business owners may value their business assets from their latest approved balance sheet.

The tax is Sf. 8 for every Sf. 1,000 of taxable wealth, that is 0.8%. Taxable wealth is net wealth minus Sf. 20,000 for a single person or Sf. 30,000 for a married one. The amounts are in the old Surinamese florin as written in the text; the consolidated text shows no indexation. The wife's assets are treated as her husband's unless the couple is separated or has separate property, a rule of the 1944 text. The register lists it as in force; no sponsors are recorded.

title: Lag (1997:323) om statlig förmögenhetsskatt

summary: Sweden's annual state tax on net wealth: 1.5% a year on the net wealth of a natural person above SEK 1.5 million (SEK 3 million for couples taxed jointly).

overview:
Law (1997:323) on state wealth tax was issued on 5 June 1997 and took effect on 1 July 1997, applying fully from the 1998 assessment. It was the basis of Sweden's national wealth tax until its repeal.

For a natural person, an estate or a family foundation the tax was 1.5% a year of net wealth above SEK 1.5 million; for couples and others taxed together the allowance was SEK 3 million. Other legal persons paid 1.5 per mille above SEK 25,000. Taxable wealth was all assets minus debts at the end of the year, including privately owned homes, listed and unlisted shares and other financial assets.

The law was repealed with effect from 1 January 2008 (by SFS 2007:1403), after it had been amended repeatedly, the last time by SFS 2007:545. Sweden has had no national wealth tax since.

by: Parliament of India

overview:
The Wealth-tax Act, 1957 gave India an annual tax on net wealth. It charged individuals, Hindu undivided families and companies. The Act's own text gives the later form: from the assessment year starting 1 April 1993, 1% of the amount by which net wealth exceeded ₹15 lakh, raised to ₹30 lakh from the assessment year starting 1 April 2010. Before 1993 the Act charged the graded rates set in its Schedule I.

It taxed only a listed set of assets. These were houses and farm houses near towns, motor cars, jewellery and bullion, yachts, boats and aircraft not used commercially, urban land, and cash above ₹50,000 for individuals and Hindu undivided families. Some houses were excluded, such as those let for at least 300 days a year, commercial property and houses used for the owner's business. Shares and bank deposits were not on the list.

The tax stopped in 2016. Act 20 of 2015, the Finance Act 2015, added the words "but before the 1st day of April, 2016" to the charging section, so the last assessment year was 2015-16 and nothing is charged after it. The text read for this page is the Act as modified on 12 November 2018, from the copy at thc.nic.in.

overview:
This was an amendment to the 2021 budget bill (A.C. 2790), not a bill of its own. It was signed first by Matteo Orfini of the Democratic Party (PD) and Nicola Fratoianni of Sinistra Italiana within Liberi e Uguali (LeU), and later by PD deputy Enza Bruno Bossio and Five Star Movement deputy Andrea Colletti. It would have abolished the IMU property tax and the stamp duty on bank accounts and securities and put a progressive annual tax on large fortunes in their place.

Il Fatto Quotidiano reports the rates as 0.2% on wealth from EUR 500,000, 0.5% from EUR 1 million, 1% from EUR 5 million, 2% from EUR 50 million, and 3% above EUR 1 billion from 2021, with fines of 3% to 15% of the amount for undeclared foreign assets. Fratoianni said the tax would use cadastral income, not market value, for property, so it would spare the middle class. The Chamber's page is the record of the budget bill itself and does not show the amendment's text, so the rates here come from the press.

The Budget Committee first ruled the amendment inadmissible, then readmitted it on 3 December 2020. The PD said it was an initiative of some deputies that did not commit the group, and the Five Star Movement and Italia Viva opposed it. On 16 December 2020 Luca Pastorino of LeU told the committee that it was withdrawn, along with a second LeU amendment by Federico Fornaro for a one-off 1% solidarity contribution on net wealth above EUR 1.5 million, excluding the main home. Open reports that both had received negative opinions from the rapporteurs and the government, and neither was voted.

title: Loi n. 2025-17 du 12 décembre 2025 portant loi de finances pour 2026, article 88 (impôt sur la fortune)
by: Presidency of the Republic (bill 2025/114); Minister of Finance Michket Salama Khaldi
status: Adopted 4 December 2025 (article 50 of the bill, 72 for, 14 against, 16 abstentions); published in the Official Gazette n. 148 of 12 December 2025 as article 88; returns due by 30 June each year
summary: Annual tax on the immovable and movable property of individuals: 0.5% on net wealth of 3 to 5 million dinars and 1% above, with the main residence, professional assets, cars up to 12 CV and deposits in banks and the post office exempt.
overview:
The 2026 finance bill (project 2025/114, tabled by the Presidency of the Republic) put an annual wealth tax in its article 50. It replaced the 2023 tax on real estate worth 3 million dinars or more with a tax on the immovable and movable property of individuals, including that of minor children in their care: 0.5% on property worth 3 to 5 million dinars and 1% above 5 million, charged on 1 January on the value after debts tied to the assets. The main residence and its furniture, professional property and goodwill in use, cars of up to 12 CV and money deposited in banks, financial institutions or the post office are exempt. Residents are taxed on property in Tunisia and abroad, non-residents on property in Tunisia.

The Finance Minister presented the article to the finance committee of the Assemblée des représentants du peuple on 11 November 2025. At the joint sitting of 21 November the committee of the Conseil national des régions et des districts accepted it with two amendments, while the ARP committee did not; the ARP committee dropped it with 10 votes against and 3 for. The plenary rejected it on 1 December (30 for, 14 abstentions, 69 against). The minister re-tabled a revised article under article 112 of the standing orders and the ARP adopted it on 4 December 2025 with 72 for, 14 against and 16 abstentions, before passing the whole law 89 to 23 with 12 abstentions.

The tax is article 88 of Law 2025-17 of 12 December 2025. The tax administration explained it in general note 13 of 2026, and the first returns were due by 30 June 2026.
